# 📍 Locality Research Guide: County Cork, Ireland — 1830s–1840s

**Jurisdiction:** Cork, Munster, Ireland | County type | Established 1606 | Province of Munster
**Target Period:** 1830–1849
**Source:** FamilySearch Wiki — [Ireland Genealogy Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)

---

## ⚠️ Critical Context: Record Destruction

Two catastrophes define pre-Famine Cork research:

1. **1922 Four Courts Fire** — Destroyed most pre-1901 census returns (including the 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 Irish censuses) and large numbers of wills, Church of Ireland registers, and government records held in Dublin. **There is no intact census for County Cork in the 1830s–1840s.** Land and church records are the mandatory substitutes.
2. **Great Famine (1845–1852)** — Dramatically disrupted recordkeeping and caused massive emigration from Cork ports; some record series thin out or have gaps in the late 1840s.

---

## 1. Civil Registration — ❌ NOT AVAILABLE for this period

| Record Type | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Births & deaths (civil) | From **1 January 1864** | No civil birth or death certificates exist for the 1830s–1840s |
| Roman Catholic marriages (civil) | From **1 January 1864** | Must use parish registers instead |
| Non-Catholic marriages (civil) | From **1845** | Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, and other Protestant marriages only |

**There are no civil vital records for this period.** Church registers are the only vital record source for the 1830s–1840s. *(Source: [Ireland Genealogy Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 2. Church Records — ✅ PRIMARY SOURCES

### Roman Catholic Parish Registers
The **core source** for the vast majority of County Cork families, who were Catholic.

- **What they contain:** Baptisms (including parents' names and sometimes mother's maiden name), marriages (including witnesses), rarely burials.
- **Coverage start:** Varies widely by parish. Many Cork parishes begin in the **1810s–1830s**; a few start earlier (1750s–1790s), and some begin only in the 1840s–1850s. Gap coverage is a real risk.
- **Language:** Latin (entries) with some Irish or English.
- **Access:**
  - **National Library of Ireland (NLI):** Free online digital images of Catholic registers to 1880 — [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie) — browse by parish. **Images only; not name-indexed on NLI — must be browsed parish by parish.**
  - **IrishGenealogy.ie** ([irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)): Provides a **name-searchable index** to the same Catholic registers, with links to images. Best starting point.
  - **FamilySearch:** Some Cork Catholic registers are digitized and partially indexed; check the FamilySearch Catalog under "Cork, Munster, Ireland — Church Records."
- **Key quirk:** You must know (or deduce) the civil parish or Catholic parish before searching — the NLI images are organized by diocese and parish, not by county or surname. Diocese of Cork and Ross, Diocese of Cloyne, and Diocese of Kerry all cover parts of County Cork.

### Church of Ireland (Anglican) Registers
- **What they contain:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — Church of Ireland community (Protestant minority).
- **Losses:** Many were held in the Four Courts and were destroyed in 1922. Surviving originals are at the **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)**, Dublin, or in local custody.
- **Access:** Check the **RCBL Parish Register Index** ([ireland.anglican.org](https://ireland.anglican.org)) to confirm whether a specific Cork parish register survived and where it is held. IrishGenealogy.ie also has some surviving Church of Ireland registers indexed online.

### Presbyterian and Other Nonconformist Registers
- Relevant if your ancestor was Presbyterian, Methodist, or Quaker (smaller communities in Cork).
- Presbyterian registers are held by the **Presbyterian Historical Society** (Belfast) or PRONI; Quaker records by the **Religious Society of Friends** in Dublin. Check survival for Cork specifically.

---

## 3. Census Substitutes — ✅ ESSENTIAL (No intact census survives)

### Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) — **Key source for the 1830s**
- **What they are:** Lists of occupiers of land liable to pay tithes to the Church of Ireland, compiled parish by parish.
- **Coverage:** Rural landholders; does **not** include landless laborers, cottiers without their own plot, or urban dwellers — a significant gap for poorer Cork families.
- **Access:**
  - **IrishGenealogy.ie** — free, searchable online.
  - **NAI (National Archives of Ireland):** Original volumes; microfilm on FamilySearch.
  - **FamilySearch:** Search "Ireland Tithe Applotment Books, 1823–1837."

### Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork c. 1851–1853) — **Key source for the 1840s**
- **What it is:** A comprehensive survey of every property occupied, listing householder, immediate lessor, land description, and valuation. Published slightly after the target period, but reflects occupancy in the early 1850s — useful for tracing families who survived the Famine.
- **Access:**
  - **AskAboutIreland.ie** ([askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie)) — free, searchable, with maps.
  - **Ancestry.com** — indexed and searchable.
  - **IrishGenealogy.ie** — also searchable.
- **Key quirk:** Griffith's reflects the post-Famine landscape; families who emigrated or died during 1845–1851 will not appear.

### 1841 & 1851 Census Fragments
- The 1841 and 1851 censuses were conducted but destroyed in 1922. A small number of **fragments and extracts** survive — mostly used to claim old-age pensions (the "Green Forms" at the NAI). Check the **NAI online catalog** for any Cork survivals.

---

## 4. Land, Estate & Property Records

### Registry of Deeds (from 1708)
- Records property transactions (leases, mortgages, conveyances). Primarily useful for **landowners and larger tenant farmers**, not for cottiers or laborers.
- **Access:** Physical at the Registry of Deeds in Dublin; **FamilySearch** has microfilm; some indexes are online at the NAI.

### Estate Papers / Landlord Records
- County Cork had many large estates (e.g., the Kingston, Bowen, Brodrick, and Longfield estates). Surviving estate papers (rent rolls, tenant lists, eviction records) can document families not in any other record.
- **Access:** Dispersed — check the **Cork City and County Archives (CCCA)**, NLI manuscripts, and the **NAI** catalog. The **National Register of Archives (Ireland)** lists known holdings.

### Poor Law Union Records (from 1838)
- The **Irish Poor Law Act of 1838** created a network of Poor Law Unions across Ireland, each with a Board of Guardians administering a workhouse. Cork had multiple unions (Cork, Bantry, Bandon, Clonakilty, Dunmanway, Fermoy, Kanturk, Kinsale, Macroom, Mallow, Middleton, Millstreet, Mitchelstown, Skull, Skibbereen).
- Records include **workhouse admission/discharge registers**, outdoor relief records, and rate books.
- **Key note:** These records become especially significant for the Famine years (1845–1852). Survival is uneven.
- **Access:** **Cork City and County Archives** holds many Board of Guardians records. Check the CCCA catalog online.

---

## 5. Emigration Records — ✅ ESPECIALLY RICH for this period

Cork (particularly **Cobh/Queenstown**) was one of Ireland's main emigration ports. Famine-era emigration (1846–1850) generated large passenger list series.

- **Departure records (Irish side):** Sparse before the Famine; some survive in newspaper notices and Lloyd's records.
- **Arrival records (destination side):**
  - **US ports:** Passenger manifests for ships arriving at New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Baltimore, New Orleans (on **Ancestry**, **FamilySearch**, **Fold3**). Pre-1820 lists are minimal; post-1820 lists grow significantly.
  - **Canadian ports (Quebec/Grosse Île):** Many Cork emigrants landed in Canada first. Records at **Library and Archives Canada** and some indexes at FamilySearch.
  - **Australian/New Zealand:** Assisted emigration schemes from Cork; records at state archives and the NAI.
- **FamilySearch Collections:** Search "Ireland Emigration and Immigration" and browse Cork-specific passenger lists.

---

## 6. Vital Notices in Newspapers

### Cork Examiner (founded 1841) / Cork Constitution
- Published birth, marriage, and death notices — primarily for middle-class and Protestant families, but not exclusively.
- **Access:**
  - **Irish Newspaper Archives** ([irishnewsarchive.com](https://irishnewsarchive.com)) — subscription, full-text searchable back to 1841.
  - **British Newspaper Archive** ([britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk](https://britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk)) — subscription.
  - Some issues are free on the **NLI's Newspapers** portal.

---

## 7. Wills & Probate

- **Pre-1858:** Probate was handled by Church of Ireland diocesan courts. The original wills were almost entirely destroyed in 1922. However:
  - **Will indexes** (testator name, year, diocese) survive and are searchable at the NAI and online via IrishGenealogy.ie.
  - **Will abstracts and copies** appear in collections such as the **Betham Abstracts** (at the NAI and Irish Genealogical Research Society) and the **O'Brien Abstracts**.
  - Wills required a minimum estate — not useful for very poor families.
- **Post-1858:** A new civil probate system began, with better survival rates, but that postdates the 1830s–1840s.

---

## 8. Military Records

- Many Cork men served in the **British Army** during this period.
- **UK National Archives (Kew):** Holds army service records, muster rolls, and pension records. Accessible at **Ancestry** and **Findmypast** (subscription) and some through **Fold3**.
- **Militia records:** Irish militia muster rolls, some at NAI.
- **FamilySearch:** Has some Irish military indexes.

---

## 9. National School Records (from 1831)

- Ireland's **National School system** was established in 1831. School registers often recorded the child's name, age, father's name, address, and religion.
- **Access:** **NAI** holds many surviving registers. The **Cork City and County Archives** may hold local school records. Coverage is incomplete.

---

## Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** | Catholic parish register images to 1880; newspapers; estate papers | [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie) — free |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Indexed Catholic & CoI registers; Tithe Books; civil reg (post-1864) | Free online |
| **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)** | Census fragments; wills; school registers; state records; estate papers | [nationalarchives.ie](https://www.nationalarchives.ie); catalog searchable online |
| **Cork City and County Archives (CCCA)** | Poor Law records; local government; deeds; estate papers | [corkarchives.ie](https://www.corkarchives.ie) — in-person and online catalog |
| **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)** | Surviving Church of Ireland registers | [ireland.anglican.org](https://ireland.anglican.org) — in-person; some digitized |
| **AskAboutIreland.ie** | Griffith's Valuation (free, with maps) | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Griffith's; passenger lists; some indexed Irish records | Subscription |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Catholic registers; Tithe Books; emigration records; various indexes | Free |
| **FindMyPast.com** | Irish records; British Army; newspapers | Subscription |
| **Irish Newspaper Archives** | Cork Examiner from 1841; other Irish papers | Subscription |

---

## Recommended Research Sequence for County Cork, 1830s–1840s

1. **Start with IrishGenealogy.ie** — search the indexed Catholic parish register database to locate the parish and find baptism/marriage entries.
2. **Identify the civil parish** — use the Civil Parish locator on [johngrenham.com](https://www.johngrenham.com) to map your townland to its civil and Catholic parish.
3. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books** — confirms land occupation in the 1820s–1830s and may give the townland.
4. **Search Griffith's Valuation** — anchors the family geographically just after the target period.
5. **Browse NLI parish register images** — for the specific parish once identified; many entries are not indexed.
6. **Search passenger records** — especially if emigration occurred around 1846–1855 (Famine period).
7. **Check Cork City and County Archives** — for Poor Law, estate papers, and local records not held in Dublin.

---

**Summary of Coverage:**
> For the 1830s–1840s in County Cork, **there are no civil vital records** and **no surviving census**. The three pillars of research are **(1) Catholic parish registers** (baptisms and marriages, many starting 1810s–1830s, freely indexed on IrishGenealogy.ie and imaged on the NLI), **(2) the Tithe Applotment Books** (1823–1837, land occupiers), and **(3) Griffith's Valuation** (c. 1851–1853, every householder). Emigration records from Cork/Queenstown are particularly strong for the Famine years. The 1922 Four Courts fire means many record classes that once existed — census returns, original wills, many Church of Ireland registers — are simply gone; surviving substitutes and estate papers are the workaround.

## Locality Research Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts — 1820–1850

### Jurisdictional Context

**Berkshire County** was established in **1761**, carved from Hampshire County. It is Massachusetts' westernmost county and shares long borders with:
- **New York** (west): **Rensselaer County, NY** (formed 1791) to the northwest and **Columbia County, NY** (formed 1786) to the southwest
- **Vermont** (northeast): **Bennington County, VT** (formed 1779)

This tri-state corner is critical for your research: families routinely crossed state lines for church membership, land purchases, and marriage. Records for the same household may sit in all three states simultaneously.

**Vital registration timeline — all levels:**
- **Town level (MA):** The Massachusetts General Court mandated town recording of births, marriages, and deaths in **1639**. Berkshire's towns were recording vital events continuously by the time of your 1820–1850 window. *(Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial))*
- **Statewide level (MA):** Massachusetts began centralized **statewide registration in 1841**, so for 1841–1850 a second, state-level copy exists in addition to the town record.
- **New York:** NY did not require statewide vital registration until 1880. A 1847 town-clerk law existed but was poorly enforced. For 1820–1850 NY events, church records and county records are the primary substitutes.
- **Vermont:** Statewide vital registration began in 1857. Town clerk records were required earlier but inconsistently kept; town copies are the primary source for 1820–1850.

---

### Births, Marriages, and Deaths — Priority Sources

#### 1. Massachusetts Town Clerk Vital Records ⭐ *Primary source*

**What:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by individual town clerks, mandated since 1639. Every Berkshire County town (Adams, Cheshire, Clarksburg, Dalton, Florida, Great Barrington, Hancock, Hinsdale, Lanesborough, Lee, Lenox, Monterey, Mount Washington, New Ashford, New Marlborough, North Adams/Williamstown, Otis, Peru, Pittsfield, Richmond, Sandisfield, Savoy, Sheffield, Stockbridge, Tyringham, Washington, West Stockbridge, Windsor, etc.) kept its own register.

**Published compilations:** The NEHGS / Topsfield Historical Society **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series covers over 200 Massachusetts towns, including Berkshire County towns. These were printed and indexed volumes; many are digitized.

**On FamilySearch:**
- **Collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (Collection ID [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)) — reported ~3.4 million records spanning 1620–1890.
- **Volume IGN 004500891:** Town Clerk Vital and Town Records for Berkshire County, covering **1761–1850**, 512 images. ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.

**Where held physically:** Original town clerk volumes remain with each town clerk's office or have been transferred to the **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** or the **Berkshire Registry of Deeds / Probate Court (Pittsfield)**.

**NEHGS:** The [New England Historic Genealogical Society](https://www.americanancestors.org) (Boston) holds the largest regional genealogical library and has microfilm and digital copies of many town vital records. *(Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military))*

---

#### 2. Massachusetts Statewide Registration (1841–1850)

**What:** From 1841, town clerks forwarded annual reports to the Secretary of State. This creates a **second copy** for events 1841–1850 — invaluable when a town volume is damaged or missing.

**Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston). Also partially available through the town vital records collections on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

#### 3. Church Records ⭐ *Essential substitute and supplement, especially 1820–1840*

Before 1841, and wherever a family was unchurched or a town clerk was lax, baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded by congregations are often the only evidence of a vital event.

**On FamilySearch:**
- **Collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (Collection ID [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)) — ~987,000 records.
- **Volume IGN 004500892:** Congregational Church Records for **Pittsfield, Berkshire County, 1791–1850**, 274 images. ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.

**Denominations active in Berkshire County 1820–1850:** Congregational (dominant), Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, and Quaker (smaller presence in the southern towns). Each kept its own register; not all are yet digitized. Check:

- Local church archives
- NEHGS microfilm holdings

#### 4. Federal Census Records

The **1820, 1830, 1840**, and **1850** federal censuses all enumerate Berkshire County households. Note:
- 1820–1840 censuses name only the head of household; other members are counted by age and sex brackets only.
- **1850 is the breakthrough census** — the first to list every person by name, age, sex, birthplace, and occupation. It is the most powerful indirect birth-date and birthplace source for your period's survivors.

FamilySearch and Ancestry both have fully indexed, imaged 1820–1850 censuses for Berkshire County. Search at [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Cross-Border Research — New York and Vermont

Because the user's family lived **close to both the NY and Vermont lines**, do not limit searching to Massachusetts alone.

**New York side (Rensselaer and Columbia Counties):**
- NY statewide vital registration did not begin until 1880. For 1820–1850, rely on **church records** (Reformed Dutch, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist), **county court records**, and the 1820–1850 **federal censuses** for NY counties.
- Rensselaer County records (formed 1791): County clerk in Troy, NY.
- Columbia County records (formed 1786): County clerk in Hudson, NY.
- FamilySearch has NY church records and some county-level collections. Ancestry.com has strong NY indexes for this period.

**Vermont side (Bennington County):**
- Vermont town clerk vital records predate statewide registration (which began in 1857), but coverage is uneven. **Town copies are the primary source** for 1820–1850.
- Bennington County records (formed 1779): Vermont State Archives and town clerks.
- FamilySearch and Ancestry have Vermont vital records indexes.

### Searcher's Quirks and Gotchas

1. **Browse-only volumes on FamilySearch:** Both digitized Berkshire volumes found (IGN 004500891 and IGN 004500892) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — you must browse them image by image. The indexed FamilySearch collections (Town Vital Records 2061550, Church Records 1921657) are the faster starting point.

2. **Two-tier vital records before 1841:** For events 1820–1840, search the town clerk's register directly — there is no state-level copy for those years. For 1841–1850, a state-level copy exists alongside the town record.

3. **"Vital Records to 1850" printed series:** These NEHGS-published books are often the fastest path to pre-1850 births, marriages, and deaths and are available at major genealogical libraries and through NEHGS digital holdings.

4. **Berkshire County has three deed districts:** Deeds are split among Northern (Adams), Middle (Pittsfield), and Southern (Great Barrington) registries. Know which district your town falls in before searching land records.

5. **Cross-border NY church records:** Families near the NY line often belonged to congregations across the border in Rensselaer or Columbia County. NY did not require civil vital registration until 1880 — church registers are the primary source for NY-side events in this period.

6. **Vermont cross-border events:** Families near the VT line may have events recorded in Bennington County town clerk records. Vermont statewide registration began 1857; for 1820–1850 events in VT, go directly to individual town clerk records or the Vermont State Archives.

7. **Pittsfield Sun newspaper:** Published continuously from 1800, the *Pittsfield Sun* carried birth, marriage, and death notices that often predate or supplement official records. Search it on [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/).

8. **1850 census is the watershed:** If the family was present in Berkshire County in 1850, the Seventh Census names every person — treat it as a mandatory first search because it gives birthplaces and ages that anchor all earlier record searching.

## Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — 1840s–1860s

### Jurisdictional Context

**Schuylkill County** was created in 1811 from parts of Berks and Northampton Counties, so by the 1840s it was a mature jurisdiction with over three decades of its own records. The county seat is **Pottsville**. During the target period the county was the epicenter of Pennsylvania's anthracite coal industry, drawing large immigrant waves — Welsh, Irish, German, and others — which makes church records, naturalization filings, and immigration sources especially important alongside standard civil records.

No boundary changes affecting Schuylkill County occurred during 1840–1870; records from those decades belong unambiguously to this county. Pre-1811 events for the same territory would be found in Berks or Northampton County records.

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

#### 1. 🟢 Federal Census — **Indexed + Images (96%)**

| Source | Details |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch volume IGN 007621224 | 412 images · Schuylkill County · 1850–1860 · **96% name-indexed** · full-text searchable |
| Ancestry | [1850 United States Federal Census – Schuylkill County](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) |

The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are well-covered and name-indexed, making them the natural starting point for any Schuylkill County research. The 1850 census was the first to list all household members by name. The **1850 Mortality Schedule** (recording deaths in the year preceding the enumeration) exists as a separate schedule and is worth consulting for death dates and causes in the early 1850s.

**The 1860 census is not confirmed as a separate volume** in the tool results — only the 1850–1860 range appears in a single volume, so both years may be consolidated there.

---

#### 2. 🟡 Probate Records — **Full-text searchable; minimally name-indexed (4%)**

| Source | Details |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch volume IGN 004812990 | 286 images · Schuylkill County · **1845–1880** · 4% name-indexed · **full-text searchable** |
| FamilySearch collection 1999196 | *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* · 2,304,118 records and images |

Only 4% of the Schuylkill County probate volume is name-indexed, so it will **not** surface reliably in a standard record search. However, it **is** full-text searchable — use FamilySearch's full-text search tool rather than the indexed record search. Probate files from this era typically include wills, inventories of personal property, letters of administration, and guardian appointments, all of which can reveal family relationships, neighbors, and economic standing.

---

#### 3. 🔴 Church Records (Lutheran) — **Browse-only; bilingual English/German**

| Source | Details |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch volume IGN 004288771 | 198 images · Schuylkill County · **1840–1875** · **0% name-indexed** · NOT full-text searchable · English and German |

This is the only digitized church-record volume returned for Schuylkill County in this period, and it is **browse-only** — there is no name search and no full-text search. A researcher must open the volume and page through image by image.

⚠️ **Language warning:** The volume is recorded in both English and German. Records for German immigrant families will likely be in German, requiring a researcher able to read 19th-century German script (often *Kurrent* or *Kurrent*-influenced handwriting).

Given Schuylkill County's large German immigrant population and the absence of Pennsylvania statewide civil vital registration before the 20th century (see Vital Records section below), this Lutheran register is likely to be a **critical substitute source** for births, marriages, and deaths in German-heritage families. Other denominations — Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Irish Catholic, Welsh Calvinist Methodist — also had active congregations but **no digitized volumes** appeared in the tool results for those faiths. Their records may exist as undigitized microfilm or physical registers.

---

#### 4. ⚫ Vital Records (Civil) — **Gap: No indexed civil records for this period**

Pennsylvania did not have **statewide civil vital registration** during the 1840s–1860s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania all returned only generic content and did not confirm Pennsylvania-specific registration dates, so this guide cannot cite a specific FamilySearch source for that date. No indexed Pennsylvania vital-records collection for Schuylkill County in this window appeared in either the collections search or volume search.

**Substitutes for vital events:**
- Church records (Lutheran volume above; other denominations in physical repositories)
- Probate records (often name spouse, children, heirs)
- Federal census (age data allows approximate birth year calculation)
- Newspaper obituaries and announcements (Pottsville papers; check the Schuylkill County Historical Society)
- Cemetery records (not confirmed as a digitized online collection in tool results)

---

#### 5. 🔴 Tax Records — **Predates target period / physical**

| Source | Details |
|---|---|
| Ancestry | [Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) |

This Ancestry collection covers **1768–1801** — well before the 1840s target window — but can be useful for establishing a family's pre-migration Pennsylvania presence or for families who were in the county before Schuylkill was carved out in 1811. County tax assessment records **for 1840–1860 are not confirmed as digitized** in the tool results; they may exist as physical records at the Schuylkill County Courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives.

#### 6. ⚫ Land and Deed Records — **Not confirmed as digitized**

No digitized land or deed volumes for Schuylkill County appeared in the tool results. Deed books are typically held at the **Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds** (Pottsville) and may be partially indexed by the county or available on microfilm. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds some colonial-era land records, but Schuylkill County land records from the 1840s–1860s are not confirmed as online.

#### 7. ⚫ Court Records & Naturalizations — **Not confirmed as digitized**

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or federal courts — so Schuylkill County naturalization records for immigrant miners and their families from this period may be scattered across multiple court dockets. No digitized court or naturalization collection for Schuylkill County appeared in the tool results. The **Schuylkill County Courthouse** and the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (which holds federal court records) are the primary repositories.

For the 1840s–1860s, relevant military record classes include:
- **Mexican War (1846–1848):** Service records and pension files at NARA
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Service records, pension files, and the 1862–1863 draft registrations at NARA; Pennsylvania's Civil War records are also at the Pennsylvania State Archives

No digitized Pennsylvania or Schuylkill County military collections for this period appeared in the tool results.

---

#### 9. ⚫ Immigration Records — **Not confirmed as digitized locally**

Schuylkill County's coal economy drew massive immigration in this era, with Philadelphia and New York as primary ports of entry. Philadelphia passenger arrival records and New York lists are held at NARA and are widely indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch — search those indexes by name rather than by Schuylkill County. No county-level immigration collection appeared in the tool results.

### Researcher Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No statewide civil vital registration in this period.** Church registers are the primary substitute — and the only digitized church volume on FamilySearch is Lutheran, browse-only, and partially in German.
2. **Lutheran church records require German-reading ability.** The IGN 004288771 volume is bilingual; German script entries will not be decipherable without reading knowledge of 19th-century German.
3. **Probate records are not name-indexed — use full-text search.** A standard FamilySearch record search at 4% indexing will miss most entries; full-text search on IGN 004812990 is the right approach.
4. **Pre-1811 events belong to Berks or Northampton County.** For families present in the area before Schuylkill County's formation, look in those predecessor counties' records.
5. **Naturalization records are dispersed across multiple courts.** Search Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal court records separately — no single index exists.
6. **Welsh, Irish, and German denominational records are likely in physical repositories.** Welsh Congregational, Catholic, and Methodist records for the coal-region congregations were not confirmed as digitized online.
7. **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content** in this survey — confirm Pennsylvania-specific registration dates and repository holdings directly at [FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy) before planning searches.
8. **Check adjoining counties.** Berks County (southeast) and Northumberland County (northwest) border Schuylkill County; families straddling those lines may have records in both jurisdictions.

| Tax Records | 1768–1801 only | 🔴 Predates target window | Ancestry |
| Military Records | 1846–1865 | ⚫ NARA / state archives | Physical / NARA request |
| Naturalizations / Court | — | ⚫ Not confirmed digitized | County courthouse / NARA |
| Immigration | — | ⚫ County-level not found | NARA / Ancestry by name |

---

**Bottom line for 1840s–1860s Schuylkill County research:** Start with the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses (well indexed), then use FamilySearch's full-text search on the probate volume, then browse the Lutheran church records image by image for vital events in German immigrant families. For Welsh, Irish, and Catholic families, plan a physical visit or correspondence with the Schuylkill County Historical Society and relevant denominational archives, as those records are not confirmed as online.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (circa 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Around 1800 there was no single jurisdiction called "Alabama." The territory now comprising the state was divided between overlapping administrations:

- **Mississippi Territory (1798–1817):** Most of present-day northern and central Alabama fell under this U.S. territory, established by Congress in 1798. Washington County (1800) was the first county organized in the portion that is now Alabama.
- **Spanish Mobile District (1780–1813):** The southwestern corner — the Mobile Bay area — remained under Spanish colonial rule until U.S. forces seized Fort Charlotte in April 1813. An ancestor near the coast around 1800 was in a *different sovereign jurisdiction* than one in the interior.
- **Alabama Territory (1817–1819):** When Mississippi achieved statehood in 1817, the eastern portion was reorganized as the separate Alabama Territory. Alabama was admitted to the Union on **December 14, 1819**.

Per the FamilySearch Wiki: Alabama "was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then became the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819. Territorial records include land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records." ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))

**Economy:** Overwhelmingly agricultural — cotton was beginning its dominance in the south, subsistence farming and cattle ranging in the interior, active maritime trade in the Mobile area.

**Religious denominations:** Catholic tradition in the Mobile area (French/Spanish colonial origin); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders were the primary denominations among American settlers in the interior.

---

## Boundary Changes

This period involves a **geographic split** within what we now call Alabama, not merely a temporal succession. The two halves generated records in entirely different archives:

- **Mobile area (southwestern Alabama):** Under Spanish jurisdiction until 1813. Records from circa 1800 were created under Spanish authority and are held in European archives and their copies — not in Alabama courthouses.
- **Interior and northern Alabama:** Mississippi Territory from 1798. County organization was sparse; Washington County was established in 1800 as the first.
- **After 1817:** Alabama Territory records diverge from Mississippi Territory records held in what is now the state of Mississippi.

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** Before routing any search, determine whether your ancestor lived near the Mobile coast (→ Spanish colonial records track) or in the interior (→ Mississippi Territory records track). The two paths lead to entirely different repositories on different continents.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in the territorial period. Alabama did not require **statewide** civil registration of births and deaths until **1908**. Marriages were recorded at the county level beginning when each county was organized — the earliest Alabama counties formed in 1809 (Madison, Baldwin).
- **What exists for 1800–1819:** County marriage records begin in 1809. FamilySearch holds **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** ([collection 1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)) — 612,345 records, 306,172 images. **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only source for births, baptisms, and burials in this period.

### Church Records
- **Denominations and holdings:**
  - *Catholic (Mobile area):* Spanish colonial sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are part of the Mobile District records held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress** and microfilm at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
  - *Protestant (interior):* FamilySearch holds **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** ([collection 1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)) — 156,789 records, 78,394 images. **Digitization level: Indexed + images (partial).** Early Baptist and Methodist records may also survive only at local churches or in denominational archives.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the Spanish period are in Spanish and/or Latin. Researchers unfamiliar with these languages should seek published transcriptions or engage a specialist.

### Census Records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Spanish colonial census:** Mobile District census returns under Spanish administration are held in the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville), with copies at the Library of Congress. ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Federal census:** The first federal enumeration to include present-day Alabama is **1810** (filed as Mississippi Territory). The 1820 census is the first taken after statehood.
- **FamilySearch index:** **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** ([collection 2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)) — 287,634 records; **0 images — index only, no image verification possible online.** Includes territorial census substitutes (tax lists, etc.) alongside federal enumerations.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Date range:** Begin with county formation. Washington County formed 1800; most other Alabama counties formed 1809 and after.
- **FamilySearch:** **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** ([collection 1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)) — 438,210 records, 219,105 images. **Digitization level: Indexed + images (partial).** The 1809 start reflects the earliest-formed county courts.
- **Territorial court records:** Pre-county territorial court records are held at **ADAH** and in NARA's Territorial Papers series.
- **Value in this period:** With no civil vital registration, probate files are often the richest source of family relationship data — wills name children and grandchildren; estate inventories and guardianship files reveal family structure.

### Land Records
- **System:** Alabama is a **federal-land (public domain) state.** Land was distributed through U.S. federal land offices, not a state land office.
  - First federal land office in present-day Alabama: **St. Stephens Land Office**, opened 1803.
  - Second: **Huntsville Land Office**, opened 1811.
  - Federal land patents are searchable free at **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Colonial land grants:** Spanish and British grants in the Mobile area are documented in the **Archivo General de Indias** and at the **Library of Congress**; local land claims filed after U.S. takeover were adjudicated in federal courts.
- **Territorial records:** Land grants and entries from the Mississippi Territory period are held at **ADAH**. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **County deeds:** Metes-and-bounds deed books from county formation forward are at county courthouses; some are microfilmed at ADAH.

### Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; many settlers were Revolutionary War veterans who received bounty land grants in the frontier territories.
- **Territorial militia rolls:** Noted as part of the territorial records at ADAH. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Federal records:** Service records and pension files at **NARA** (Washington, D.C.); many are digitized on **Fold3** (subscription — listed in the external links for Alabama in this period). Pension files routinely include birthplace, age, physical description, and family member names, making them the best pre-Alabama biographical source for veterans.
- **Bounty land warrants:** Veterans of the Revolution and later conflicts could claim federal land in the Mississippi/Alabama territory; these application files at NARA are a prime source.

### Cemetery Records
- **Coverage:** Most burials in this period were in family plots or churchyards, with no formal sexton records. Organized cemeteries with maintained registers are largely a post-statehood development.
- **Online:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com — listed in the curated external links for Alabama) has volunteer-submitted headstone transcriptions, but pre-1820 burial coverage is sparse.
- **Physical records:** The DAR and Alabama county historical societies have transcribed some early cemeteries; check ADAH's holdings and the published *Alabama Cemetery Survey*.

### Newspaper Records
- **Earliest Alabama papers:** The *Mobile Centinel* (1811) was among the first in the territory. No newspapers existed in the interior before approximately 1810.
- **Where held:** Early Alabama newspaper runs on microfilm at ADAH and major research libraries. Newspapers.com (listed in the external links for Alabama) has digitized some early runs.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale announcements, and estate administrator notices are the primary genealogical content in this era; formal obituaries were uncommon before the 1820s.

### Immigration / Emigration Records
- **Context:** Virtually all settlers arriving in present-day Alabama around 1800 came **overland** from Georgia, the Carolinas, Tennessee, and Virginia — not by sea. Ship passenger lists do not apply to this migration. Your next step is to trace the family back to their state of origin, where earlier records will be found.
- **Mobile port:** The Spanish colonial Mobile District records include some arrivals by sea; these are in the **Archivo General de Indias** records. ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalization records could be filed in any court of record. Territorial court records at ADAH and NARA may contain petitions for foreign-born settlers.

### Tax Records
- **Types:** Property and poll tax lists from county and territorial administration.
- **Date range:** Begin with county formation (Washington County, 1800).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the **single most useful census substitute** for this period — they name heads of household annually, effectively filling every year between sparse territorial enumerations. This is especially critical given the 1790–1810 gap for this territory.
- **Where held:** ADAH; partially included in the **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** ([collection 2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)).

### Other Record Types
- **Territorial Papers of the United States:** NARA holds the original Mississippi Territory administrative records; published in print by the U.S. Government Printing Office. These document governance, land petitions, and individual claims.
- **Indian land cession records:** Around 1800 the interior was still largely Creek and Cherokee territory. Land cession treaties (1805, 1814, 1816 onward) generated federal records. If an ancestor was Native American or intermarried, Cherokee and Creek tribal records are a parallel source.
- **Town and county histories:** Many 19th- and early 20th-century local Alabama histories reprint early tax lists, pension abstracts, and biographical sketches — sometimes the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevant holdings for Alabama pre-1819 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | County Marriages 1809–1950; Probate Records 1809–1985; Census Substitutes Index 1810–1890; Church Records 1803–1950 | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1810 Mississippi Territory; 1820 Alabama) | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military pension files; War of 1812; Creek War service records | Subscription |
| **BLM–GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from St. Stephens (1803+) and Huntsville (1811+) offices | Free |
| **Library of Congress** (loc.gov) | Copies of Spanish Mobile District records (census, land grants, church registers) | Free (finding aids; some digitized) |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL | Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, court records; early county records | In-person; mail requests; catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| **NARA – Southeast Region**, Atlanta, GA | Federal records for Alabama territory; pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person; online request |
| **NARA – Washington, D.C.** | Territorial Papers (Mississippi Territory); military pensions and service records | In-person; Fold3 online |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records: Mobile District census, church registers, land grants (1780–1813) | In-person; finding aids + some digitized material via the Pares portal (pares.mcu.es) |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records, Mobile area (1702–1763) | In-person; microfilm copies at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives**, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records; local church and government records | In-person |
| **County probate courts** | Original deed books, probate files, marriage registers from county formation | In-person / mail |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following records are known to exist for this period but are **not** available in major online databases:

- **Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808)** — ADAH only; not on FamilySearch or Ancestry
- **Spanish Mobile District records** (census, sacramental registers, land grants, 1780–1813) — originals in Seville; Library of Congress copies not fully digitized online
- **French colonial records** (Mobile area, 1702–1763) — originals in France; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives only
- **Early territorial court minute books** (Washington County and the handful of pre-1819 counties) — at ADAH or original county courthouses
- **Militia and muster rolls** from the territorial period — largely at ADAH; some survive only in published transcriptions

---

## Known Record Losses

- **Sparse pre-county record creation:** Before Washington County was organized in 1800, essentially no civil records exist for the interior of present-day Alabama — the land was minimally administered. The absence of records is structural, not a destruction event.
- **Uneven early county survival:** Individual early county courthouses should be contacted to confirm what survives from their founding decade. No single catastrophic courthouse loss has been documented in the tool results for this period, but piecemeal attrition is likely.
- **Split custody of territorial records:** Records from the Mississippi Territory period are split between ADAH, NARA, the state of Mississippi's archives (for the western portion of the territory), and published transcriptions. Some records may be unlocatable or missing.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Pin down location first.** Whether your ancestor was near Mobile (→ Spanish colonial track) or in the interior (→ Mississippi Territory track) determines the entire repository strategy. ([Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); [Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))

2. **Start with the census substitute index.** The **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** on FamilySearch ([collection 2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)) includes tax lists and territorial enumerations — often the earliest documentary trace of a family in the territory. Be aware it has no images; treat hits as pointers to ADAH originals.

3. **Follow the ancestor backward to their origin state.** Most settlers around 1800 came from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, or Tennessee. Records for birth, early marriage, and family relationships will almost certainly be in those states, not in Alabama.

4. **Mine pension and bounty land files aggressively.** Many early Alabama settlers were Revolutionary War or War of 1812 veterans. Their pension application files at NARA (on Fold3) routinely contain the richest pre-Alabama biographical data available — birthplace, age, family members' names, affidavits from neighbors.

5. **Work tax lists as a year-by-year census.** With territorial censuses only in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810, annual tax lists at ADAH effectively substitute for the missing census years.

6. **For the Mobile area: plan for multilingual research.** Spanish colonial records are in Spanish; the earlier French records are in French and Latin. Seek the published transcriptions and translations produced by the Historic Mobile Preservation Society and the Alabama Historical Quarterly before committing to original archival research in Europe.

7. **Check the BLM-GLO for land patents.** The St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices issued the first federal patents in Alabama territory. A land patent entry at glorecords.blm.gov places an ancestor in the territory at a datable moment and names the exact parcel — useful for narrowing county of residence before counties multiplied.

8. **County formation dates control everything.** No county courthouse records predate the county's formation. For 1800–1819, only a handful of counties existed: research the precise formation date of the county you're targeting and search the parent county (or territorial administration) for events before that date.

## 📍 Locality Research Guide
### Arkansas Region — Pre-1800 (French & Spanish Colonial Era, ~1686–1800)

---

### Jurisdictional History

The territory that became the U.S. state of Arkansas (admitted 1836) passed through three colonial regimes before American rule:

| Period | Sovereign | Administrative Jurisdiction |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | France | La Louisiane (French Louisiana) |
| 1763–1800 | Spain | Louisiana (Luisiana) — Upper Louisiana district, administered from New Orleans |
| 1800–1803 | France (briefly) | Louisiana (ceded back by Treaty of San Ildefonso) |
| 1803–1819 | United States | District / Territory of Orleans, then Missouri Territory |
| 1819–1836 | United States | Arkansas Territory |

**The single most important settlement for genealogical research is Arkansas Post** (*Poste de Arkansas* / *Poste aux Arkansas*), established 1686 in present-day Arkansas County — the only substantial European community in the region during the colonial era. Records were generated at the post level and routed administratively through New Orleans. **There was no Arkansas-level jurisdiction before 1819** — all pre-1800 records belong to Louisiana/Spanish Louisiana record series, not an "Arkansas" series.

---

### ⚠️ Critical Research Quirk — Two Overlapping Record Series

The Arkansas Post colonial records form **one continuous research trail across two administrations**, but the records are held in different places and languages:

- **French period (pre-1763):** Catholic sacramental registers in French/Latin, held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and the **Arkansas History Commission**; transcriptions available at the Commission.
- **Spanish period (1763–1800):** Sacramental registers and civil records in Spanish, held at the **Arkansas History Commission**, **Library of Congress** (microfilm), and the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville). FamilySearch has digitized one browse-only volume (see below).

Do not treat these as separate record sets — search both together as a single lineage of post records, working backward from Spanish into French administration.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. 🏛️ Sacramental Registers — Arkansas Post (Spanish Colonial, 1763–1800)
- **FamilySearch volume:** Image Group **008814402** — 64 images
  - Coverage: *Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, United States*, 1763–1800
  - Record type: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) — baptisms, marriages, burials
  - **Access level: Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be reviewed image by image.
  - **Language: Spanish** — researcher must read Spanish or use a translator; no English index exists on FamilySearch.
  - 🔗 Browse at: `https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=008814402`

#### 2. ⛪ French-Period Catholic Sacramental Registers (Pre-1763)
- French Catholic missionaries maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s, covering both European settlers and Native Americans.
- **Access level: Physical/microfilm only** — not on FamilySearch in digitized form.
- **Held by:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock; transcriptions at the Arkansas History Commission.
- **Language: French and Latin.**
- Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Arkansas Genealogy*, "Church Records" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))

#### 3. 📜 Spanish Colonial Civil Records — Padrones, Land Concessions, Military
- Under Spanish administration, the commandant at Arkansas Post generated:
  - **Padrones** (household censuses) — name, age, household members, sometimes occupation and origin
  - **Land concessions** (grants and surveys)
  - **Military post records** — muster rolls, correspondence
- **Access level: Physical/microfilm — not on FamilySearch.** Surviving records are held at:
  - **Arkansas History Commission**, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR 72201 — [https://www.arkansas.gov/ahc](https://www.arkansas.gov/ahc)
  - **Library of Congress**, Manuscript Division (microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Louisiana records)
  - **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain — the primary Spanish imperial archive; holds original Louisiana colonial administrative correspondence, military records, land files. Partially digitized via the PARES portal ([http://pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es)).
- Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Arkansas Genealogy*, "Colonial Records" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

#### 4. 📋 Louisiana Church Records, 1718–1925
- **FamilySearch Collection 1612905** — *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925*
  - 987,654 records; 493,827 images
  - Date range overlaps the target period beginning 1718
  - Covers Louisiana-administered parishes; may capture persons who also transacted business at Arkansas Post or relocated between the Arkansas district and lower Louisiana
  - **Access level: Indexed + images**
  - 🔗 [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)

#### 5. ⚖️ Louisiana Probate Records, 1756–1984
- **FamilySearch Collection 2078341** — *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984*
  - 456,789 records; 228,394 images
  - Begins 1756 — spans the Spanish colonial period
  - Relevant for settlers who may have had legal or estate connections routed through New Orleans courts
  - **Access level: Indexed + images**
  - 🔗 [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)

#### 6. 🗺️ No Pre-1800 Indexed Arkansas Collections on FamilySearch
- FamilySearch's three Arkansas-scoped indexed collections begin no earlier than 1819 (the earliest, *Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870*, collection 2085124). **No name-indexed FamilySearch collection exists specifically for pre-1800 Arkansas.** This is an honest digitization gap, not an absence of records — the records exist, they are just in physical repositories or in the single browse-only volume noted above.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) | Spanish padrones, land concessions, sacramental register transcriptions, microfilm of colonial records | In-person / written inquiry; some digitized finding aids online |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original French-period sacramental registers (pre-1763) | Contact diocesan archives |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, D.C.) | Microfilm of Spanish colonial Louisiana records, including Arkansas Post | On-site and some via interlibrary loan |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish imperial records — Louisiana / Upper Louisiana series | PARES online portal (partially digitized); in-person for full access |
| **FamilySearch** | 1 browse-only image volume (008814402), Arkansas Post 1763–1800; Louisiana church and probate collections from 1718/1756 | Free online |
| **NARA** (National Archives) | Post-1803 territorial records; some earlier Spanish land claim adjudication files | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |

---

### Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Records are filed under Louisiana, not Arkansas.** Before 1819, no "Arkansas" jurisdiction existed. Search Louisiana-scoped series and route your research through New Orleans administrative records.
2. **Arkansas Post is the research hub.** Nearly all pre-1800 European-descent and mixed-ancestry families in the region appear in Arkansas Post records — not scattered county courthouses (counties did not exist yet).
3. **Spanish records are in Spanish; French records in French/Latin.** The FamilySearch browse-only sacramental register volume (008814402) has no English index. You must read the original images, or commission a translation.
4. **The browse-only FamilySearch volume (008814402) must be browsed image by image** — 64 images, no name search possible. Plan time to page through it systematically.
5. **The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds irreplaceable originals.** For land grants, military appointments, and gubernatorial correspondence, PARES ([http://pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es)) is the starting point; the *Papeles de Cuba* and *Audiencia de Santo Domingo* sections are the most relevant series for Louisiana/Arkansas colonial records.
6. **No pre-1800 population or census data is available on FamilySearch** for Arkansas — the padrones (Spanish censuses) must be sought at the Arkansas History Commission and Library of Congress microfilm.
7. **After 1800, the research trail continues in Missouri Territory records** before Arkansas Territory was split off in 1819. A family present at Arkansas Post in 1800 would next appear in Missouri Territory records (1804–1819), then Arkansas Territory (1819–1836).

---

### Topical Breadth — Additional Leads

- **Native American connections:** Arkansas Post records document interactions with the Quapaw, Osage, and other nations. The Quapaw tribe maintained a presence throughout the colonial era; their members appear in some sacramental registers.
- **Enslaved persons:** Spanish colonial census padrones and inventories sometimes name enslaved individuals. Check the Arkansas History Commission holdings and the *Papeles de Cuba* series at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Military service:** Spanish garrison records for Arkansas Post survive among the *Papeles de Cuba* (AGI Seville). Fold3 ([https://www.fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) and NARA hold some compiled service file materials for the post-1803 period.
- **Land claims:** After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners adjudicated pre-existing French and Spanish land grants. These proceedings generated English-language summaries of the original grants and are held at NARA and partially digitized at the BLM General Land Office ([https://glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)).

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Period | FamilySearch Access | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers | 1763–1800 | ⚠️ Browse-only (vol. 008814402) | Spanish |
| French-period Sacramental Registers | ~1700–1763 | ❌ Not digitized | French/Latin |
| Spanish Padrones & Land Records | 1763–1800 | ❌ Not on FamilySearch | Spanish |
| Louisiana Church Records | 1718–1925 | ✅ Indexed + images (col. 1612905) | French/Spanish/English |
| Louisiana Probate Records | 1756–1984 | ✅ Indexed + images (col. 2078341) | French/Spanish/English |
| AGI (Papeles de Cuba, etc.) | 1763–1800 | ⚠️ Partial via PARES portal | Spanish |

---

**Bottom line:** For pre-1800 Arkansas, your primary research axis runs through **Arkansas Post → New Orleans → Seville**. The FamilySearch browse-only volume (008814402) and the two Louisiana-scoped indexed collections (1612905, 2078341) are your digital starting points. For padrones, land concessions, and military records, you will need to work with the **Arkansas History Commission** and the **Archivo General de Indias** — either in person, via microfilm at the Library of Congress, or through the PARES online portal.

---

# 📍 Locality Guide: Ohio (Pre-Statehood) — c. 1790

---

## 1. Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

**Ohio did not exist as a political unit in 1790.** The land was part of the **Northwest Territory**, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 7 July 1787. This ordinance established the framework for organizing the territory north of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi, which eventually became Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota.

### County Formation — the critical boundary problem

Records for any event in this territory are filed under the **county that held jurisdiction at the moment of the event**, not under today's county. The county map changed dramatically and rapidly:

| County | Established | Approximate area covered in 1790 |
|---|---|---|
| **Washington County** | 1788 | Entire eastern and northern region; seat at Marietta (Ohio Company settlement) |
| **Hamilton County** | 1790 | Southwestern region; seat at Cincinnati (Fort Washington area) |

> ⚠️ **Geographic split — search both.** In 1790 the entire territory of present-day Ohio was divided between Washington County (east/north) and Hamilton County (southwest). Which county holds a given record depends entirely on *where within the territory* the event occurred. Do not assume a single county — determine the settlement location first, then match it to the county boundary of 1790. All subsequent Ohio counties were carved from these two originals, so records for any event before the carved county existed will be in the parent county (Washington or Hamilton).

Ohio statehood was formally granted **1 March 1803** — after that date, county-level Ohio records replace territorial records.

### Land Districts — a second jurisdictional layer
Ohio's territory was further divided into distinct **land survey systems**, each generating its own record series at different repositories:

| District | Location | Survey system | Primary record repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ohio Company Purchase** | Around Marietta (Washington Co.) | Rectangular/PLSS | Ohio History Connection; NARA |
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds | Virginia State Library; NARA |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Township grid | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **U.S. Military District** | Central Ohio | Rectangular | NARA; Bureau of Land Management GLO |
| **Symmes Purchase** | Between the two Miami rivers | Rectangular | Hamilton County records; NARA |
| **Congress Lands** | Remainder | PLSS rectangular | Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (online: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) |

> ⚠️ **Quirk — Virginia Military District warrants predate Ohio statehood.** Virginia Military District bounty land warrants were issued from Virginia, not the Northwest Territory. These records are at the **Virginia State Library**, *not* Ohio repositories, and use a metes-and-bounds system incompatible with the rectangular PLSS surveys covering the rest of Ohio. [FamilySearch Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)

> ⚠️ **Quirk — Connecticut Western Reserve.** Northeastern Ohio was claimed by Connecticut under its colonial charter. Records are at the **Western Reserve Historical Society** in Cleveland, separate from the Ohio History Connection. [FamilySearch Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)

---

## 2. Population Context

No indexed FamilySearch population data was returned for Ohio in the 1780–1803 window — a coverage gap in the tool's fixture. Historically, settlement in 1790 was very sparse and concentrated at two nodes: **Marietta** (established 1788 by the Ohio Company, in Washington County) and **Cincinnati / Fort Washington** (established 1788–1789, in Hamilton County). The 1790 federal population was perhaps a few thousand non-indigenous residents scattered across an enormous, largely uncharted territory.

---

## 3. Records Available

### A. Vital Records — **Major gap; no civil registration**

There was **no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths** in the Northwest Territory in 1790 — or in Ohio until:
- **Marriages:** County-level registration began after statehood (1803); the earliest FamilySearch collection begins **1789** (see below), reflecting early county court marriage bonds and registers.
- **Deaths:** No statewide civil death registration until **1867** at the state level.
- **Births:** No statewide civil birth registration until **1908** at the state level.

For 1790, **church records and marriage bonds are the only vital-event substitutes.**

**FamilySearch collection:**
- 📋 [Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) — 1,523,678 indexed records; 761,839 images. The 1789 start date reflects early Washington County marriage bonds. **Indexed + images** — searchable by name.

### B. Church Records — **Prime source for 1790 vital events**

Early Ohio settlements had active Protestant congregations almost from founding. Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker congregations were established in the 1788–1800 period. Baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the primary evidence of birth, marriage, and death for this era.

**FamilySearch collection:**
- 📋 [Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) — 678,234 indexed records; 339,117 images. Starts 1787. **Indexed + images.** Note: pre-1800 coverage within this collection is likely sparse — treat a negative result as a gap to note, not a conclusion of non-existence.

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Church records are often indexed only at the county level on FamilySearch — search Washington County or Hamilton County rather than a specific township.

### C. Land Records — **The most important record class for 1790**

In a frontier territory with no civil vital registration, **land records are the single most productive record class.** They name heads of household, establish presence in a location, and often record witnesses and neighbors (the FAN cluster).

**FamilySearch collections:**
- 📋 [Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) — 234,567 indexed records; 117,283 images. Starts 1787. **Indexed + images.**

**Digitized browse-only volumes (volume_search results):**
- 🗂️ **ImageGroup 005112233** — *Northwest Territory, United States — Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799* — 51 images. **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable. Browse-only image-by-image.** This is a critical pre-statehood volume; there is no shortcut — every image must be examined manually.

**Additional repositories (not on FamilySearch):**
- **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO)** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — Original land entry patents for Congress Lands and U.S. Military District, fully searchable online.
- **NARA (National Archives)** — Original land entry case files [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) — paper files with affidavits, witnesses, and survey plats.
- **Virginia State Library** — Virginia Military District warrants and surveys.
- **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland** — Connecticut Western Reserve land records.
- **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** — Early territorial and county land records, court records.

### D. Tax Records

Tax lists name heads of household and are invaluable substitutes for census records, especially for the 1788–1790 gap before any census enumeration in this territory.

**FamilySearch collections:**
- 📋 [Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) — 345,890 indexed records; 172,945 images. Starts **1800** — does not reach back to 1790, but covers the last years of the territorial period.

**Digitized browse-only volumes:**
- 🗂️ **ImageGroup 005112240** — *Washington County, Ohio — County Tax Records, 1799–1803* — 73 images. **12% name-indexed; not full-text searchable. Mostly browse-only.** Only about 9 images are name-searchable; the rest must be browsed image-by-image.

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Tax records for 1790 specifically may exist only in physical form at the **Ohio History Connection** or **Washington County Courthouse** — a zero result in FamilySearch does not mean they don't survive. Contact the Ohio History Connection directly.

### E. Census Records

- **1790 Federal Census:** The Northwest Territory settlements *were* enumerated in the 1790 U.S. Federal Census, but coverage was extremely incomplete for this frontier region. Washington County (Marietta area) has the best survival. Hamilton County coverage is sparse. Available via [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- **No territorial census** is known for Ohio between federal censuses.
- The **1800 Federal Census** is the first reasonably complete enumeration of the Ohio territory and is the practical starting point for name-by-name coverage.

### F. Military Records — **High value for pre-statehood settlers**

Most adult male settlers in Ohio's earliest communities were **Revolutionary War veterans**. Military pension files at NARA are exceptionally rich — they include depositions naming family members, places of residence, and migration paths. These often substitute for missing vital records.

- **NARA Revolutionary War pension files** — [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) (subscription) or NARA directly [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)
- **Bounty land warrant files** — especially relevant for Virginia Military District settlers; warrants issued by Virginia pre-statehood.

### G. Probate & Court Records

The Northwest Territory had a functioning court system from 1788. Territorial court records, where they survive, are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus. These include wills, estate inventories, guardianship records, and civil cases — all name-rich sources.

- ⚠️ **Coverage gap:** FamilySearch's [Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1417891) starts in **1840** and does not cover 1790. Do not rely on it for the pre-statehood period.
- For 1790 probate, contact the **Ohio History Connection** directly or check county courthouse microfilm for Washington and Hamilton Counties.

### H. Newspapers

Historical newspapers from the Marietta and Cincinnati areas exist from the early 1790s:
- *Centinel of the Northwestern Territory* (Cincinnati, est. 1793) — the first newspaper in the Northwest Territory; [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) may have partial holdings.

### I. Cemetery Records

- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many early Ohio pioneer cemeteries, though pre-1800 inscriptions are often weathered or absent.

---

## 4. Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What they hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** | Territorial & early county court, land, probate records | In-person + some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **Bureau of Land Management GLO** | Federal land patents (Congress Lands, U.S. Military District) | Free online: glorecords.blm.gov |
| **NARA (National Archives)** | Land entry case files, military pension files, 1790 census | In-person + Ancestry/Fold3 |
| **Virginia State Library, Richmond** | Virginia Military District warrants & surveys | In-person + some microfilm |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland** | Connecticut Western Reserve land & early records | In-person |
| **Washington County Courthouse, Marietta** | County-level records from 1788 | In-person |
| **Hamilton County Courthouse, Cincinnati** | County-level records from 1790 | In-person |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections + browse-only volumes listed above | Free online |

---

## 5. Key Quirks & Research Warnings

1. **Ohio did not exist in 1790** — all records were created under the **Northwest Territory**, then filed under **Washington County** or **Hamilton County** depending on the settlement's location. Determine location first, then identify the correct county.
2. **There is no statewide vital registration for 1790** — church records and marriage bonds are the only substitutes for birth, marriage, and death evidence.
3. **County boundaries changed constantly, 1788–1820** — always identify which county held jurisdiction *at the event date*, not today's county. Every subsequent Ohio county was carved from Washington or Hamilton.
4. **The Virginia Military District uses metes-and-bounds, not the PLSS rectangular system** — its land records are at the Virginia State Library, not at Ohio repositories. Settlers with Virginia land grants in this district generate a separate Virginia records trail.
5. **Connecticut Western Reserve records are in Cleveland**, not Columbus — northeastern Ohio settlers need the Western Reserve Historical Society, not just the Ohio History Connection.
6. **ImageGroup 005112233 (Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799) is 0% indexed** — must be browsed image by image; no name search is possible.
7. **The 1790 Federal Census covered Northwest Territory settlements incompletely** — a missing ancestor is not proof of non-residence; they may simply not have been enumerated. Cross-check tax lists and land records.
8. **Revolutionary War pension files at NARA are often the richest single source** for 1790 Ohio settlers — they routinely name spouses, children, and migration history. Search them even if military service itself is not the research goal.

---

| Record Type | Date Range (for 1790) | Digitization Level | FamilySearch Link |

| Church Records | 1787–1803 | ✅ Indexed + images | [2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) |
| Land Records | 1787–1803 | ✅ Indexed + images | [1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) |
| Territorial Land Records (vol.) | 1788–1799 | ⛔ Browse-only (0% indexed) | ImageGroup 005112233 |
| Washington Co. Tax Records (vol.) | 1799–1803 | 🔶 Mostly browse-only (12% indexed) | ImageGroup 005112240 |
| Tax Records (collection) | 1800–1850 | ✅ Indexed + images | [1987542](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) |
| County Death Records | 1840+ only | ❌ Does not cover 1790 | [1417891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1417891) |
| BLM GLO Patents | 1787+ | ✅ Free searchable online | glorecords.blm.gov |
| Military Pensions | 1775–1800s | ✅ Searchable (Ancestry/Fold3/NARA) | fold3.com / archives.gov |
| 1790 Federal Census | 1790 | ✅ Indexed (incomplete coverage) | Ancestry / FamilySearch |

---

## 7. Research Strategy for 1790 Ohio

Given the documentation gaps, a recommended sequence:

1. **Pin the settlement location** (which of the two 1790 counties — Washington or Hamilton?) using the land district map.
2. **Search BLM GLO and Ohio Land Records** — land is the primary evidence of presence.
3. **Check the Territorial Land Records browse-only volume** (ImageGroup 005112233) for any record of the specific family.
