# 📜 California Gold Rush Era — Locality Research Guide
**Place:** California, United States
**Period:** 1848–1865 (Gold Rush onset through early statehood)
**Prepared:** 2026-08-25

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, on January 24, 1848 — still under Mexican jurisdiction, just nine days before the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred California to the United States. California was admitted as the 31st state on **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely. That unusual path has direct consequences for records:

- **No U.S. territorial records exist for California.** Unlike Arizona or New Mexico, there was no territorial legislature, territorial court series, or territorial census. Everything jumps from Mexican-era records to state-level records in 1850.
- **County formation was explosive.** The legislature created 27 counties in 1850; many more were carved out through the 1850s and 1860s. A mining camp that was in one county in 1851 might be in a different county by 1856. Always verify county boundaries for the specific year using a historical map source (e.g., the David Rumsey Map Collection or the Historical County Boundary Database).
- **Civil vital registration did not exist statewide in the 1850s.** County-level recording of births and marriages began in 1850, but compliance was very uneven. Death registration was especially poor. Statewide registration came much later. A missing vital record does not mean the event didn't happen.

---

## Record Classes

### ⭐ 1. California State Census, 1852 — *Most Important Gold Rush-Era Source*

The **only state census California ever conducted**, taken at the peak of the Rush.

| | |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch volume | imageGroupNumber 006601001 |
| Images | 522 |
| Name-indexed | **88%** |
| Full-text searchable | **Yes** |
| Coverage | California statewide, 1850–1852 |

This is the single most valuable record for locating miners and settlers who had moved on or died before the 1860 federal census. Source: FamilySearch volume_search.

---

### 2. Federal Census — 1850 and 1860

⚠️ **Critical caveat on 1850:** The 1850 federal census — the *first* taken for California — was partially destroyed. Some county returns are missing entirely. Per the FamilySearch Wiki California Genealogy article, the 1852 state census was taken partly as a response to this problem. Check which counties' 1850 returns survive before assuming an ancestor is absent.

- The **1860 census** is complete and fully indexed.
- **Mortality schedules** accompanied both censuses (1850 and 1860), recording deaths in the prior year — an important source for miners who died during the Rush itself.
- Available indexed and free at FamilySearch; also on Ancestry.com.

---

### 3. Mining Claim Registers — 🔍 Browse-Only

| | |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch volume | imageGroupNumber 006601002 |
| Images | 340 |
| Name-indexed | **0%** |
| Full-text searchable | **No** |
| Coverage | San Francisco area, 1849–1855 |

**Must be browsed image by image — no search capability.** The FamilySearch Wiki California Genealogy article notes that mining claim records are held at **county recorders' offices** in the Mother Lode counties (El Dorado, Placer, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, etc.). Physical research at those county offices is required for the bulk of this record class.

---

### 4. Port Arrival Registers — 🔍 Browse-Only

| | |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch volume | imageGroupNumber 006601003 |
| Images | 298 |
| Name-indexed | **0%** |
| Full-text searchable | **No** |
| Coverage | Sacramento / San Francisco area, 1849–1858 |

**Must be browsed image by image.** For sea arrivals, a better entry point is Ancestry.com's indexed U.S. passenger lists. The **National Archives Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA)** holds the primary series of San Francisco passenger manifests for the Gold Rush period, documenting the "Forty-Niners" who arrived by ship. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, these are a key Gold Rush source. Source: wiki_search result, FamilySearch Wiki California Genealogy article, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California\_Genealogy#Gold\_Rush\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).

---

### 5. Vital Records — County Level (Indexed on FamilySearch)

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| California, County Births, 1850–1919 | [2017276](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) | 789,456 indexed + images | Full target period |
| California, County Marriages, 1850–1952 | [1452832](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) | 567,890 indexed + images | Full target period |

⚠️ No equivalent county-level **death** collection appears in FamilySearch's California holdings for this period. Death registration was sparse in the 1850s — substitute sources include mortality census schedules, cemetery records, and probate files.

---

### 6. Great Registers (Voter Registration), 1866–1910

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records |
|---|---|---|
| California, Great Registers, 1866–1910 | [1923340](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340) | 1,345,678 indexed + images |

⚠️ **Starts in 1866 — after the Gold Rush era.** Cannot document a miner's presence *during* the Rush, but invaluable for men who stayed. Each entry typically includes name, birthplace, occupation, physical description, age, and county of residence — a rich biographical snapshot for connecting a Gold Rush arrival to his later settled life in California.

---

### 7. Mission Records, 1769–1850 — Pre-Gold Rush Background

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records |
|---|---|---|
| California, Mission Records, 1769–1850 | [1804372](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) | 98,765 indexed + images |

Franciscan friar records of baptisms, marriages, and burials for Native Californian and settler (Californio) populations. Relevant only as **background context** for families with California roots before the Gold Rush — not a prime source for 1850s miners and migrants.

---

### 8. Land Records

- **Federal land patents** for California are free and searchable at the **BLM General Land Office** website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — relevant for settlers who filed homestead or pre-emption claims.
- **Rancho grants** from the Spanish/Mexican era were adjudicated by the U.S. Land Commission after 1851; case files are at the National Archives.
- **County deed books** documenting subsequent land transfers are held at county recorders' offices — mostly physical, not widely digitized for the 1850s.

---

### 9. Probate Records

- Held at county Superior Courts (or predecessor courts).
- Relevant for miners who died with property — estate files can name heirs, state birthplace and prior residence, and list personal property (including mining equipment).
- **Not systematically digitized for the 1850s.** Requires physical research at county courthouses or the California State Archives.

---

### 10. Military Records

- **Mexican-American War (1846–1848):** Veterans who remained in California can be traced through NARA pension and service records (Fold3, Ancestry).
- **Civil War:** California furnished Union volunteers (1st–8th California Infantry, California Cavalry). Service records at NARA; indexed on Fold3.
- **State adjutant general records** at the California State Archives.

---

### 11. Newspapers

Active Gold Rush-era newspapers included the *Alta California* (San Francisco) and the *Sacramento Union*. These are searchable via:
- **Newspapers.com** — subscription
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection (CDNC)** at [cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu) — free, searchable full text
Obituaries, ship arrival notices, mining company news, and legal notices frequently name individuals.

---

### 12. Church Records

Predominantly Catholic in the pre-Gold Rush population; Protestant denominations proliferated rapidly after 1848. Catholic registers are held at the **Archdiocese of San Francisco** and **Diocese of Sacramento**. Most denominational records are **not digitized** — contact individual parishes or denominational archives directly.

---

### 13. Naturalization Records

Pre-1906 naturalizations could occur in *any* court of record — federal district court, state court, or county court. For California in the 1850s, look at county court files. FamilySearch has some naturalization volumes; physical records at county courthouses and NARA San Bruno.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | 1852 state census, county births/marriages, Great Registers, Mission records, browse-only mining/arrival volumes | Free online |
| **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** | SF ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalizations, land commission files | Physical; some via Ancestry/Fold3 |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State agency records, adjutant general, legislative files | Physical; some digitized |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, newspapers, photographs | Physical + online catalog |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Extensive Gold Rush manuscript collections, diaries, company records | Physical; finding aids at [oac.cdlib.org](https://oac.cdlib.org) |
| **County Recorders / Superior Courts** | Mining claim records, deeds, probate, naturalization | Mostly physical |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses, indexed passenger lists, military | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free online |
| **Newspapers.com / CDNC** | Historical California newspapers | Subscription / Free |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Access Level | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| California State Census, 1852 | ✅ **Indexed + images (88%)** | Also full-text searchable |
| County Births, 1850–1919 | ✅ **Indexed + images** | 789K records |
| County Marriages, 1850–1952 | ✅ **Indexed + images** | 568K records |
| Great Registers, 1866–1910 | ✅ **Indexed + images** | Begins *after* Gold Rush |
| Mission Records, 1769–1850 | ✅ **Indexed + images** | Pre-Gold Rush background |
| Mining Claim Registers | 🔍 **Browse-only** | 0% indexed, no full-text |
| Port Arrival Registers | 🔍 **Browse-only** | 0% indexed, no full-text |
| Federal land patents | ✅ **Online (BLM GLO)** | Free |
| Probate records | 📦 **Physical/microfilm only** | County courthouses |
| Church records | 📦 **Physical/microfilm only** | Contact parish/diocese |
| Naturalization (pre-1906) | 📦 **Mostly physical** | NARA San Bruno + county courts |
| Military (Civil War) | ✅ **Online (NARA/Fold3)** | Subscription for Fold3 |
| Newspapers | ✅ **Online (CDNC free; Newspapers.com paid)** | CDNC is free and searchable |

---

## Research Quirks

1. **The 1850 federal census has gaps** — some California county returns were lost. The 1852 state census (88% indexed) is the essential substitute.
2. **No statewide vital registration in the 1850s.** County recording was inconsistent, and death registration was especially poor. Use mortality schedules, church registers, cemetery records, and probate files as substitutes.
3. **Mining claim records are browse-only** on FamilySearch. The bulk of this record class sits undigitized at county recorders' offices in the Mother Lode counties.
4. **County boundaries shifted rapidly.** Determine the correct county for a given mining camp at a given date before searching deed, probate, or court records.
5. **Great Registers don't start until 1866.** They are invaluable for men who *stayed* in California but cannot document the Rush itself.
6. **Many miners were transient.** An ancestor may appear in California records only briefly. Always search the *origin* state's records — a miner from Ohio who returned home after the Rush will appear in Ohio records, not California's.
7. **Bancroft Library and California State Library hold unique unpublished material.** Diaries, letters, mining company rosters, and overland trail journals are not in standard genealogical databases. Search their online finding aids (Online Archive of California, [oac.cdlib.org](https://oac.cdlib.org)) for manuscript collections.
8. **FamilySearch volume_search returned 14 total volumes for California 1848–1865 but only 3 on the first page.** Additional digitized volumes — possibly covering tax, court, or naturalization records — may exist. Run a targeted `volume_search` for specific record-type groups to surface them.

---

This guide covers the major record classes confirmed by FamilySearch's collections and volume data, the FamilySearch Wiki California Genealogy article ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California\_Genealogy#Gold\_Rush\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)), and Wikipedia's California Gold Rush article. The most productive starting sequence for most researchers is: **(1)** 1852 state census → **(2)** 1860 federal census → **(3)** county births/marriages → **(4)** Great Registers (for post-Rush location) → **(5)** ship passenger lists at Ancestry/NARA → **(6)** Bancroft/State Library manuscript finding aids.

# Locality Guide: New York City (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Jurisdiction:** New York City (standardPlace: *New York, New York, United States*), in its 1700s form essentially coterminous with **New York County (Manhattan)**. Established 1624 as Dutch New Amsterdam; taken by the English in 1664 and renamed New York.
- **Administrative status:** Provincial capital of New York Province (royal colony) under British rule for the entire 1700s.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic commercial port, trade, crafts, and merchant activity.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, Jewish, and a significant enslaved African population — multiple languages and record streams run in parallel.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous registers), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran (Dutch and German), French Huguenot, Quaker, and Jewish congregations.
- **Key events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763) generated militia records; American Revolution / British occupation of NYC (1776–1783) disrupted civil life and some record-keeping; Gradual Emancipation Act of 1799 at period's end.
- **Population:** No FamilySearch population data returned for this fixture — colonial-era provincial censuses/musters survive for some years (see Census section).

---

## Boundary changes

| Date | Change | Research implication |
|------|--------|----------------------|
| 1664 | English seize Dutch New Netherland; city becomes New York | Dutch Reformed registers continue in Dutch language |
| 1683 | Province divided into counties; NYC ≈ New York County (Manhattan) | Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, and Richmond (Staten Island) become separate counties with their own courts and records |
| 1776–1783 | British military occupation | Civil record-keeping disrupted; Loyalist and military records now relevant |
| 1788 | Province becomes State | Prerogative Court (provincial probate) replaced by county Surrogate's Courts |

> **Quirk:** The "five boroughs" of modern New York City did not exist in the 1700s. Brooklyn, Staten Island, and Queens were entirely separate jurisdictions. A family near the colonial city's edge may have generated records in Kings, Queens, or Richmond Counties — search those separately.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration during the 1700s. New York State did not require statewide vital registration until 1880.
- **What exists for this period:** None — church registers are the only organized vital record source.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials), newspaper notices, and court records are the substitutes.

---

### Church records ⭐ *Most important source class for this period*
No civil registration means church registers are your primary evidence for births, marriages, and deaths throughout the 1700s.

**Denominations confirmed by tool results** ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)):

| Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|
| Dutch Reformed | Continuous registers from 1639; records in **Dutch** through much of the 18th century |
| Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church) | Founded 1697; baptisms, marriages, burials |
| Presbyterian | Individual congregational records |
| Lutheran (Dutch & German) | Denominational archives |
| French Huguenot | Huguenot Society of America holds records |
| Quaker | Meeting records |

**FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Church Records, 1640–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) (collection 1469062) — approximately 2.3 million records and 1.17 million images. **Indexed + images** (verify indexing by sub-collection).

**Specific digitized volume from `volume_search`:**
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, 1700–1776** (image group 007733180) — 211 images
  - **⚠ Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
  - **⚠ Language: Dutch** — reading Dutch is required; no translated index exists on FamilySearch

**Physical repositories:** New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS); New-York Historical Society; Trinity Church Archives (contact for Anglican registers from 1697); individual parish archives.

---

### Census records
- **Federal census:** First enumeration is 1790 — after this period. Not applicable for most of the 1700s.
- **Colonial enumerations:** New York Province conducted periodic population musters/censuses (not household-level enumerations). These survive for some years and are held at the New York State Archives.
- **Enslaved population:** Enslaved people appear in some colonial enumerations and ward-level tax lists.
- **Access:** Colonial musters are largely microfilm or physical at the NY State Archives; some transcribed in published genealogical works. The first fully usable federal census for NYC is 1790.

---

### Probate and court records
**⚠ Critical quirk:** During the colonial period, probate was NOT handled at the county level. It was handled by the **Prerogative Court of New York** — a province-wide court. After the Revolution (1788+), county Surrogate's Courts took over.

- **Prerogative Court wills (colonial-era):** Indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)). Start here for any pre-1788 decedent.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) (collection 1542780) — approximately 987,000 records and 493,000 images. **Indexed + images.**
- **Mayor's Court:** NYC's colonial civil and criminal court. Records held at the NYC Municipal Archives ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)). **Physical only** — not digitized online.

---

### Land records
- **System:** Metes and bounds. Colonial land grants issued by the provincial governor; conveyances recorded at the county level.
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Land grants, patents, and provincial land documents held at the New York State Archives ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).
- **FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Land Records, 1630–1975](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) (collection 2078654) — approximately 1.57 million records and 783,000 images. **Indexed + images** (verify sub-collection coverage for the 1700s).

---

### Military records

| Conflict | Record types | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Queen Anne's War (1702–1713) | Provincial militia musters | NY State Archives |
| French & Indian War (1754–1763) | Militia rolls listing men of military age | NY State Archives; NARA |
| American Revolution (1775–1783) | Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants | NARA; Fold3.com |
| British occupation (1776–1783) | Loyalist muster rolls; Loyalist claims | British National Archives (Kew, UK) |

Provincial militia rolls are confirmed as a source for identifying male residents ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)).

**Access:** [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) for Revolutionary records; [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) (free in person, some digitized).

---

### Cemetery records
- **Trinity Churchyard** (Manhattan, from 1697): One of the oldest surviving colonial burial grounds in the city.
- **Dutch Reformed burial grounds:** Associated with church registers.
- **African Burial Ground** (lower Manhattan, active pre-1700s through ~1794): Significant for African American lineages; re-discovered 1991.
- **Online coverage:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial colonial NYC entries. Physical sexton records vary by churchyard.

---

### Newspaper records
- **New York Gazette** (founded 1725): First newspaper in New York City; confirmed as a colonial-era source by Wikipedia tool result.
- **Later papers:** New York Mercury (1752+), New-York Journal (1766+), New York Packet.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, runaway slave advertisements, ship arrivals, marriage and death announcements.
- **Access:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) has some historical NYC papers; the New York State Library and New-York Historical Society hold microfilm of colonial-era papers.

---

### Immigration records
- **Port of New York:** Primary Atlantic port of entry. Colonial passenger arrivals are recorded in the New York Colonial Manuscripts and published transcriptions.
- **Naturalization (pre-1906):** Could be filed in any court of record — Mayor's Court, colonial supreme court, county courts. Records are scattered.
- **Huguenot arrivals:** The Huguenot Society of America holds relevant passenger and church records.
- **Access:** [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) — some colonial passenger lists; in-person or partial digitization.

---

### Tax records
- **Type:** Ward-level tax assessment lists survive for some years ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)).
- **Substitute value:** In the absence of any census before 1790, ward tax lists are among the best year-by-year locators for NYC residents during the 1700s.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) (collection 1678432) — catches only the very tail of the period. Earlier lists are physical at the NYC Municipal Archives and NY State Archives.

---

### Enslaved persons records
- New York had a substantial enslaved population throughout the 1700s. Gradual emancipation began with the 1799 Act.
- **Key sources:** Enslavers' wills and estate inventories (naming individuals), runaway advertisements in newspapers, church baptism records, manumission records (post-1780s), colonial census enumerations.
- **Repositories:** NYGBS; New-York Historical Society; NYC Municipal Archives.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640–1940 (coll. 1469062); Land Records 1630–1975 (coll. 2078654); Probate Records 1629–1971 (coll. 1542780); Tax Rolls 1799–1804 (coll. 1678432) | Free |
| [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) | Federal census from 1790; additional NY colonial transcriptions | Subscription |
| [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) | Revolutionary War service, pension, and Loyalist records | Subscription |
| [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com) | Colonial-era churchyard burials (partial coverage) | Free |
| [NARA online](https://www.archives.gov) | Some colonial passenger lists; Revolutionary War records | Free / Fold3 subscription |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NYC Municipal Archives | Mayor's Court records; ward tax lists; colonial city records | In-person; some digitized |
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial court records; militia rolls | In-person; some digitized |
| New-York Historical Society | *Abstracts of Wills*; church record transcriptions; colonial newspapers | In-person; membership |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Compiled colonial records; Dutch Reformed transcriptions; *NY Genealogical and Biographical Record* | In-person + online subscription |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican baptism, marriage, burial registers from 1697 | Contact archives |
| British National Archives (Kew, UK) | Loyalist claims and muster rolls (1776–1783) | In-person; partial online via Fold3 |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Most colonial-era ward tax lists (pre-1799):** Physical at NYC Municipal Archives and NY State Archives
- **Mayor's Court records (colonial civil/criminal cases):** NYC Municipal Archives — physical
- **Non-Reformed church registers** (Anglican, Lutheran, Huguenot, Quaker): Held by individual congregations, NYGBS, or denominational archives — mostly microfilm or physical
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** (provincial government records): NY State Archives — partial digitization only
- **Manumission and enslaved persons records:** Scattered across municipal, court, and church archives

---

## Known record losses and gaps

- **British occupation gap (1776–1783):** Military occupation caused disruptions in civil record-keeping; some records were lost or left uncreated during this period.
- **Dutch Reformed registers: browse-only and in Dutch.** The only FamilySearch-digitized volume covering NYC for the 1700s (image group 007733180, 1700–1776) is 0% name-indexed and in Dutch — a significant practical barrier for researchers without Dutch-language ability.
- **FamilySearch `volume_search` returned only one volume** specifically covering NYC in this period. Coverage of colonial NYC on FamilySearch is sparse compared to later periods; the bulk of colonial records remain on microfilm or in physical repositories.
- **No population data** was returned by FamilySearch for this period — colonial-era population counts are found in published provincial muster records rather than the standard place-population tool.

---

## Research tips

1. **Church records first, always.** There is no civil registration for the 1700s. Dutch Reformed, Trinity (Anglican), and Presbyterian registers are your primary vital record substitutes. Start with [FamilySearch Church Records 1640–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062).

2. **Colonial probate goes to the Prerogative Court, not the county surrogate.** Before 1788, wills were proved at the provincial level. Use the New-York Historical Society's *Abstracts of Wills* series as your first index for colonial decedents. The FamilySearch [Probate Records collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) (1629–1971) spans the period.

3. **The Dutch Reformed registers (1700–1776) are browse-only and in Dutch.** Image group 007733180 (211 images) on FamilySearch cannot be name-searched. You must scroll image by image and read Dutch script. Consider engaging a Dutch-language genealogist or using NYGBS transcriptions.

4. **Use ward tax lists as a census substitute.** There is no household-level federal census before 1790. Colonial ward tax lists are the best annual locator for NYC residents — held at the NYC Municipal Archives and NY State Archives ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)).

5. **The NYGBS is indispensable.** The *New York Genealogical and Biographical Record* (published from 1870) and NYGBS compiled abstracts cover thousands of colonial families — often more thoroughly than any online database.

6. **Check adjacent colonial county records.** Brooklyn (Kings County), Staten Island (Richmond County), and Queens County had separate courts, churches, and record-keepers. A family near the city's edge will require searching all applicable county records.

7. **Loyalist records for the occupation years (1776–1783).** Families who remained in British-held NYC appear in Loyalist muster rolls, provision lists, and claims at the British National Archives (Kew). These are a frequently overlooked source for American colonial research and are partially accessible via Fold3.

8. **African Burial Ground and manumission records for African American lineages.** Church baptism registers, estate inventories, newspaper advertisements, and post-1780s manumission records are the primary sources. NYGBS and the New-York Historical Society hold the most comprehensive collections.

9. **Search the New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the NY State Archives for land grants, patents, and provincial administrative records touching your family ([New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).

---

## 📜 Virginia, 1775–1783 — Revolutionary War Genealogy Research Guide

**Place:** Virginia, United States
**Period:** 1775–1783 (American Revolutionary War)
**Focus:** Military service, wartime activities, and connected family records

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies and maintained **county-level record-keeping from the 1630s**, making it among the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in America. During the Revolution, it contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony, and major actions — including the decisive siege at Yorktown (1781) — were fought on Virginia soil. All civil records during this period were created and held **at the county level**; there was no statewide vital registration. Researchers must identify the specific county of residence to target the right record sets.

> ⚠️ **Critical gap:** Virginia's **1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The **1782–1785 personal property tax lists** are the standard substitute and are essential for locating families immediately after the war.

> ⚠️ **West Virginia boundary note:** Counties in what is today **West Virginia** were Virginia counties until 1863. If your ancestor lived in western Virginia, their pre-1863 records are filed under Virginia county names — search accordingly.

---

### 1. 🎖️ Military Service Records

These are the primary sources for establishing a soldier's service.

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Continental Army service records & muster rolls** | NARA, Record Group 93 | Physical + digitized on Fold3 |
| **Virginia militia records** | Library of Virginia, Richmond | Physical; partial microfilm at FamilySearch |
| **Pension & bounty-land warrant applications** | NARA, Record Group 15 | Digitized on Fold3; indexed on Ancestry |
| **Virginia State Navy records** | Published volumes | Print; copies at LVA and major libraries |
| **Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783** | FamilySearch ([collection 1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)) | Online — verify searchability per volume |

**Key facts (from [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)):**
- Continental Line service records and muster rolls are at **NARA RG 93**
- Virginia militia records are held at the **Library of Virginia in Richmond**
- Pension and bounty-land warrant files are at **NARA RG 15** — these files often contain extensive family data (widow's pension applications in particular name children, marriage dates, and neighbors who gave depositions)
- Published **Virginia State Navy records** cover naval service

---

### 2. 🏡 Bounty Land Records (Post-War)

After the Revolution, Virginia awarded bounty-land grants to its veterans in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** (a tract set aside in present-day Ohio). These records bridge military service and post-war settlement.

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Bounty-land warrants & survey records** | Library of Virginia / Virginia State Library | Physical; some digitized |
| **Ohio entry & survey records** | Ohio History Connection; BLM GLO website | Partially online |

**Key tip (from [FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)):** Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their land claims. If your ancestor disappeared from Virginia after the war, check Ohio for migration tied to bounty-land grants.

---

### 3. 📋 Tax Lists (Critical Substitute for the Missing 1790 Census)

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Personal property tax lists, 1782–1850** | FamilySearch ([collection 1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723)) | Online — indexed |
| **Land tax lists, 1782–1850** | Library of Virginia; FamilySearch | Online — browse/indexed |

The **1782–1785 personal property tax lists** are the single most important substitute for the missing 1790 census. They list heads of household by county, enumerate taxable property (slaves, horses, carriages), and can reveal family structure and relative wealth. They also appear immediately after wartime — making them useful for confirming that a veteran returned home.

---

### 4. ⛪ Church Records (Vital Events)

Virginia had no civil vital registration during this period. **Anglican/Episcopal parish registers** are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials.

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Church Records, 1680–1929** | FamilySearch ([collection 1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)) | Online — indexed |
| **Vestry books & tithe lists** | Library of Virginia; local Episcopal archives | Physical; some microfilm |

Nonconformist congregations (Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist — all grew rapidly during the Revolution) kept separate registers. Check denominational archives and local church histories if your ancestor was not Anglican.

---

### 5. 📜 Land, Marriage & Will Records

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Land, Marriage & Will Records, 1600–1900** | FamilySearch ([collection 1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)) | Online — indexed |
| **County deed books** | County courthouses; Library of Virginia | Physical; some digitized |

Land records are especially valuable for wartime Virginia. Bounty-land grants, debt sales, and estate administrations tied to soldiers killed in action all appear in deed and will books. Marriage bonds (rather than certificates) are the standard marriage record form in Virginia for this period.

---

### 6. 🏛️ County Court Records

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Virginia County Court Records, 1650–1920** | FamilySearch ([collection 2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)) | Online — indexed |
| **County order & minute books** | Library of Virginia; county courthouses | Physical; partial microfilm |

County court order books recorded a wide range of wartime activities: appointments of overseers of the poor for soldiers' families, apprenticeships of orphans, estate administrations for men killed in service, and loyalty-related proceedings. These are underused sources for wartime family research.

---

### 7. 🗞️ Newspapers & Published Sources

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical newspapers (Virginia Gazette, etc.)** | Newspapers.com; Library of Virginia; Chronicling America (LOC) | Online — searchable |
| **Published muster rolls & rosters** | Print; HathiTrust; Internet Archive | Online |

The *Virginia Gazette* (published in Williamsburg) carried enlistment notices, casualty reports, and estate notices throughout the war.

---

### 8. 🪦 Cemetery Records

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Cemetery transcriptions** | FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) | Online — searchable |
| **DAR grave registration files** | DAR Library, Washington DC | Physical; partial online |

The Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) conducted extensive grave-registration surveys for Revolutionary War veterans — their files can confirm service and identify burial location.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia (LVA), Richmond** | Virginia militia records, tax lists, county court records, land grants | [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov/) |
| **NARA, Washington DC** | Continental service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized collections 1598230, 1734285, 1945678, 1456723, 2134567 | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/) |
| **Fold3** | Digitized NARA pension files, service records | [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Various Virginia collections, indexed pension abstracts | [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/) |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records, DAR grave registrations | [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| **Newspapers.com** | Virginia Gazette and other colonial/state newspapers | [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) |

---

### ⚠️ Researcher's Checklist of Quirks

1. **No 1790 census for Virginia** — use the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723) as the direct substitute.
2. **No statewide vital registration** in this period — church records (collection 1598230) are the only systematic source for births, marriages, and deaths.
3. **County is required** — all records are organized at the county level; identify the county before searching.
4. **Pension widow's files** are often richer than the soldier's own file — widows had to prove marriage and often submitted family Bibles, neighbor depositions, and correspondence.
5. **Bounty land may mean Ohio migration** — if a veteran disappears from Virginia after 1783, check the Virginia Military District of Ohio records and Ohio county records.
6. **West Virginia split (1863)** — ancestors in western Virginia counties have records filed under their original Virginia county names before 1863.
7. **Loyalist families** left few military records but appear in county court forfeiture proceedings and escheat records — check the Library of Virginia's colonial papers for these.

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. Start with **NARA RG 15 pension files** on Fold3 — they are the richest single source and often contain family narratives.
2. Check **FamilySearch collection 1945678** (Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783) for service documentation.
3. Pull the **1782–1785 tax lists** (collection 1456723) to place the family in a specific county.
4. Search **county court order books** (collection 2134567) for wartime estate and guardianship actions.
5. Consult **church records** (collection 1598230) for baptisms and marriages that anchor family relationships.
6. Check the **Library of Virginia** directly for militia records not yet digitized.
7. Search **Fold3 and Ancestry** for digitized NARA service records and pension abstracts.

---

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (c. 1800–1840)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Founded / Standard Place:** New Orleans, Orleans, Louisiana, United States — founded by the French in 1718
- **Governing jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish (coterminous with the city of New Orleans; Louisiana uses parishes, not counties)
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans itself
- **Legal tradition:** Civil law under the Napoleonic Code — **not** English common law. This is the single most important structural fact for researchers: probate is called "successions," guardianship is "tutorships," competency proceedings are "interdictions," and the central legal instrument is the notarial act rather than the recorded deed
- **Sovereignty timeline during the target period:**
  - French colony → Spanish control (1763) → briefly returned to France (~1800) → **Louisiana Purchase, 1803** (becomes U.S. Territory of Orleans) → **Louisiana statehood, 1812**
  - These sovereignty transitions directly govern which record systems were in use and which archives hold the records
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this fixture. Consult published census schedules and local histories for population figures
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic and Gulf port; trade, shipping, sugar and cotton agriculture, enslaved labor
- **Ethnic/linguistic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, Anglo-American settlers (post-1803), enslaved Africans and African Creoles, free people of color (*gens de couleur libres*), German and Irish immigrants arriving through the port
- **Language of records:** French and Spanish predominate for pre-1803 and early post-1803 records; English increasingly appears after statehood (1812). The one FamilySearch volume of surviving notarial acts (1803–1820) is catalogued as bilingual French/English
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was dominant and officially established under French and Spanish rule. St. Louis Cathedral on Jackson Square was (and remains) the central parish church, with sacramental registers dating to 1731

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Pre-1803:** New Orleans was not U.S. territory. No U.S. federal records were created; Spanish colonial administration (the Cabildo) and the Catholic Church maintained the primary records
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — city absorbed into the U.S. as part of the Territory of Orleans
- **1812:** Louisiana admitted as a state; Orleans Parish formally established under the state constitution. Before this date, records may be styled under "Territory of Orleans" rather than "State of Louisiana"
- **Practical split for researchers:** Records created before 1803 run under French or Spanish colonial provenance; records from 1803–1812 under U.S. territorial provenance; records from 1812 onward under state of Louisiana provenance. All three streams must be searched — they do not overlap cleanly

---

## Known Record Losses — Disasters, Fires, and Floods

This is the foundational challenge of New Orleans research and must be understood before any search strategy is designed.

### The Great Fires (1788 and 1794)

According to the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)) and Wikipedia ([New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans); [Orleans Parish, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orleans_Parish,_Louisiana)):

- **Good Friday Fire, 1788:** Destroyed most of the French Quarter and a significant portion of the city's colonial-era built environment and records
- **Barracks Street Fire, 1794:** A second catastrophic fire, further destroying what the 1788 fire had not

These fires occurred **before** the primary 1800–1840 window but are directly relevant because they destroyed the records that would have documented the parents and grandparents of people alive in the early 1800s. A researcher tracing an 1810 New Orleans family backward will quickly hit a fire-caused wall.

### Ongoing Threats: Yellow Fever, Hurricanes, and Floods

Wikipedia notes that "repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings." New Orleans' below-sea-level topography and tropical climate made surviving physical records chronically vulnerable to moisture, mold, and periodic flooding throughout the nineteenth century.

---

## What Survived — and Where to Find It

### ✅ St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers (SURVIVED)

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)):

- Baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded at St. Louis Cathedral **from 1731**, though with gaps caused by the fires
- These registers are the **primary substitute for civil vital registration** during the entire early 1800s period, since no statewide civil registration system existed in Louisiana during this window
- Records are in **French and Spanish** for the colonial and early territorial era; partially in English after 1812
- **Partial access via FamilySearch:** The collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) contains 987,654 records with images — **indexed + images**, covering the target period
- **Physical originals and full register runs:** Held by the **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives**, New Orleans, Louisiana. Contact the archives for volumes not yet digitized

> **Substitute strategy:** When fire damage creates a gap in sacramental registers, check whether a **duplicate register** was maintained (the Catholic Church often required duplicate copies kept at the diocese level) and look for **notarial acts** that reference baptisms or marriages.

---

### ✅ New Orleans Notarial Archives (SURVIVED — mostly)

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)):

- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts dating to 1734
- Notarial acts in Louisiana's civil law system are not equivalent to deeds; they are the instrument for virtually all legal transactions: sales, purchases, mortgages, leases, contracts, manumissions (freedom papers for enslaved people), marriage contracts, successions, tutorships, and more
- Think of the notarial archives as the combined deed office, probate court, and contract registry for early New Orleans

**FamilySearch digitization (partial):**
- Volume_search returned **1 volume**: imageGroupNumber 004990115 — *Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)*, Orleans, Louisiana, **1803–1820**, 167 images
  - **Access level: Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed page by page
  - Language: French and English
- This one volume represents only a microfilm sample; the full archive (30M+ pages) is physically held at:

> **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
> 1340 Poydras St., Suite 500, New Orleans, LA 70112
> [www.notarialarchives.org](http://www.notarialarchives.org)
> Holdings include acts from 1734 onward; the archive has an internal index system for the early period

---

### ✅ Cabildo Records (SURVIVED)

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)):

- The Cabildo was the Spanish colonial governing body; its records survived and document the pre-1803 administrative period
- Held by the **Louisiana State Museum** (the Cabildo building on Jackson Square, New Orleans) and the **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge
- Relevant to researchers tracing families in the 1790s–1803 window just before U.S. acquisition

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Civil registration in the early 1800s:** Louisiana did **not** have a functioning statewide civil vital registration system during most of the 1800–1840 window. The FamilySearch "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection [1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892)) begins in 1819 but is an index only — **no images**, 2,345,678 indexed entries. What exactly the 1819 index derives from (local registers, church records, etc.) is not specified in the tool result
- **Pre-registration substitute:** Use St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (see above) as the primary vital record substitute for the entire target period
- **Parish Marriages collection:** FamilySearch "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection [1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)) — starts 1837, so it covers only the tail end of the 1800–1840 window; **indexed + images**, 567,890 records. Useful for marriages from 1837 onward

---

### Church Records

- **Primary denomination:** Roman Catholic — St. Louis Cathedral is the central repository for sacramental registers
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — **indexed + images**, ~987,654 records and ~493,827 images. Covers the full target window
- **Language:** French and Spanish dominate pre-1812; English increases afterward
- **Access to originals:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives for volumes not yet on FamilySearch

---

### Census Records

- **1800 federal census:** New Orleans was not U.S. territory — **no U.S. census applies**
- **1810 federal census onward:** New Orleans was included beginning with the 1810 enumeration (first U.S. census after statehood of the Territory of Orleans). The collections_search did not return any census collection for Louisiana in the 1800–1840 window — this is a coverage gap on FamilySearch. The Ancestry external link returned by the tool ([U.S. Federal Census Collection — Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) is the primary online access point for federal census schedules
- **Territorial and local enumerations:** The Louisiana State Archives holds territorial-era records; check their catalog for any pre-statehood enumeration that may have been conducted under the Territory of Orleans

---

### Probate and Succession Records

- In Louisiana's civil law system, probate is termed "**successions**"; guardianship is "**tutorships**"; competency proceedings are "**interdictions**" — per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — **indexed + images**, ~456,789 records and ~228,394 images. Covers the full 1800–1840 window
- **Physical holdings:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Orleans Parish Civil District Court records

---

### Notarial Records (Louisiana-specific — central legal record type)

- See the full discussion under "What Survived" above
- **FamilySearch:** 1 browse-only volume of surviving microfilm, 1803–1820, 167 images (imageGroup 004990115) — must be browsed image by image, bilingual French/English, **not name-indexed**
- **Physical access:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30M+ pages, internal finding aids)
- Notarial acts serve functions handled in other states by deed books, probate files, and contract courts — this is the record type to prioritize when vital records and census are absent

---

### Land Records

- Louisiana is a **civil law state**; land transfers are documented through **notarial acts** rather than deed books in the common-law sense. There is no distinct "deed book" series separate from the notarial archives
- **Federal land patents** (after the U.S. acquired Louisiana): Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — applicable for federal public-domain land grants in Louisiana after 1803
- **Cabildo records** document Spanish-era land grants and concessions (pre-1803)

---

### Military Records

- **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (January 1815):** A major event affecting New Orleans directly. Service records and pension files at NARA; also accessible via **Fold3** ([www.fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)), which appeared as a curated external link for this place
- **NARA (National Archives):** holds federal military service records and pension files — [www.archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov), also returned as a curated external link

---

### Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave** ([www.findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) returned as a curated external link for this place — search for New Orleans cemeteries including St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789, the oldest surviving cemetery in New Orleans) and St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), both of which contain interments from the early 1800s
- **Physical sexton records:** Orleans Parish holds some burial registers; check the Archdiocese of New Orleans for church burial records tied to sacramental registers

---

### Newspaper Records

- **Newspapers.com** ([www.newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) returned as a curated external link for this place
- New Orleans had active French- and English-language newspapers in the early 1800s (*Le Moniteur de la Louisiane*, *Louisiana Gazette*, and others); obituaries, legal notices, and manumission announcements are valuable substitutes for missing vital and court records

---

### Immigration / Port Records

- New Orleans was one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States during the early 1800s
- **Passenger lists:** Held at NARA ([www.archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)); also accessible via Ancestry's U.S. Federal Census and related collections
- **Note:** Examine full manifests for all household members, not just the head of family — infants and children traveling with parents are listed

---

### Enslaved Persons Records

Per the wiki_search result ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)):

- Manumission documents (freedom papers) were recorded as **notarial acts** — making the New Orleans Notarial Archives a critical repository for African American family history in this period
- The FamilySearch volume_search tool includes an "Enslavement" record type group; the one returned volume (notarial acts, 1803–1820) covers this type within its pages
- Records of the enslaved also appear in succession/probate inventories (estates listed enslaved people by first name, age, and sometimes origin) within the FamilySearch "Louisiana, Probate Records" collection

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for New Orleans / Orleans Parish | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 ([1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 ([2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 ([1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892)) — index only; Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 ([1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)); 1 browse-only notarial acts volume (1803–1820) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. Federal Census (1810–1840 for New Orleans); passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records and pension files; War of 1812 records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Louisiana newspapers | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records including St. Louis Cemeteries No. 1 and No. 2 | Free |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Passenger lists; military records; federal land patents | Free / varies |
| **BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)** | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (1340 Poydras St., Suite 500, New Orleans) | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734; the primary legal record series for early New Orleans | In-person; internal finding aids; [notarialarchives.org](http://www.notarialarchives.org) |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Full runs of St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; other parish registers | In-person / by correspondence |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records; successions; civil district court; Cabildo-era documents | In-person / some online finding aids |
| **Louisiana State Museum — The Cabildo** (Jackson Square, New Orleans) | Spanish colonial Cabildo records; pre-1803 governance records | In-person / research inquiries |
| **NARA — Southeast Regional** (Atlanta, GA) | Federal records for Louisiana: census, land, court, military | In-person / online requests via archives.gov |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following record types are confirmed to exist (from tool results) but are **not fully available** in any online database:

- **Notarial acts beyond the 1803–1820 microfilm sample** — the New Orleans Notarial Archives' 30M+ pages are overwhelmingly physical-access only; only 167 images appear on FamilySearch
- **Full runs of St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — partially on FamilySearch (collection 1612905) but complete originals require contact with the Archdiocese of New Orleans
- **Cabildo records** — held by the Louisiana State Museum and Louisiana State Archives; not found in the FamilySearch volume search
- **Territorial (pre-1812) court and administrative records** — the Louisiana State Archives holds these; limited online presence
- **Spanish colonial land concessions** — part of the Cabildo records

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with notarial acts, not deeds.** Louisiana's civil law system means the New Orleans Notarial Archives ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)) is the single most important repository for the early 1800s — it holds legal transactions of every kind, including manumissions, marriage contracts, and property transfers that would appear in completely different record series in common-law states.

2. **The 1788 and 1794 fires affect research backward in time, not forward.** For the 1800–1840 window itself, the fires are background context; the main issue for researchers is that the fires erased records needed to trace the *parents* of people alive in the 1800s. Post-1794 records in the Cathedral and notarial archives are largely intact. ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

3. **Read records in French and Spanish.** Pre-1812 records and many early post-statehood records are in French or Spanish. Engage a translator or use Latin/French genealogical glossaries before assuming a document says what it appears to say in English. The one FamilySearch notarial volume (1803–1820) is explicitly catalogued as bilingual.

4. **Know the civil law vocabulary.** Searching for "probate" in Louisiana databases may miss results filed as "successions"; "guardianship" may be filed as "tutorship." Use Louisiana-specific terminology when searching the FamilySearch Probate Records collection ([2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) and the Louisiana State Archives catalog. ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))

5. **Search succession records for family relationships.** Because civil vital registration was absent for most of this period, Louisiana succession records (probate inventories and family meetings) are one of the richest sources for identifying parents, siblings, and children — they name heirs and often describe family relationships explicitly.

6. **No 1800 census applies to New Orleans.** New Orleans was French/Spanish territory at the time of the 1800 U.S. federal census. The earliest U.S. federal census to include New Orleans is 1810. For the 1800–1810 gap, rely on notarial acts, sacramental registers, and any territorial enumerations held at the Louisiana State Archives.

7. **Check newspapers for legal notices and manumissions.** New Orleans newspapers in the early 1800s published legal notices (estate sales, court proceedings, debt announcements) and manumission notices that document people who appear in no other surviving record series. Use Newspapers.com ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)).

8. **For enslaved and free-colored ancestors, prioritize notarial acts and succession inventories.** Manumission documents were notarial acts; free people of color (*gens de couleur libres*) also appear as parties to notarial contracts. Succession inventories listed enslaved people by name, age, and sometimes origin — searchable within FamilySearch's Probate Records collection ([2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)).

9. **The FamilySearch notarial volume is browse-only.** The single volume returned by the volume search (imageGroup 004990115, 1803–1820, 167 images) has **0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image in French and English. For any systematic search of notarial acts, plan a visit or correspondence with the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.

10. **Cross the Mississippi: check adjoining parishes.** Families in early New Orleans frequently owned property, worshipped, or were buried across the river in Jefferson Parish or St. Bernard Parish. Records for those parishes are separate and held at their respective parish courthouses and church archives.

---

Here is your locality research guide for tracing immigrants who entered through the Port of Boston in the 1840s.

---

# Locality Research Guide: Port of Boston — Immigrant Arrivals, 1840s
**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period:** 1840s (with supporting records extending to 1850s for post-arrival tracing)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Boston is situated in **Suffolk County, Massachusetts** (standardPlace: *Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States*). Massachusetts entered the Union in 1788; Suffolk County has existed continuously since colonial times. During the 1840s, Boston was one of the five major US ports of entry and received some of the largest immigration waves of the 19th century — most prominently Irish Famine refugees (ca. 1845–1852), as well as arrivals from Germany, England, Canada, and elsewhere.

A critical quirk for vital records: Massachusetts town clerks were ordered by the General Court to record births, marriages, and deaths as early as **1639** (town level), while **statewide** registration began in **1841**. Both levels of records were being created simultaneously during the 1840s; do not assume that the statewide series superseded the town series. Cross-check both.

---

## 1. 🚢 Passenger Lists (Port of Boston)
**Access level: Indexed collection + 1 digitized volume (full-text searchable, near-zero name indexing)**

This is the first record to consult for any immigrant arriving through Boston.

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891*** (Collection ID 1784312)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312
  Searchable by name. Covers the Port of Boston for the full 1840s decade.

- **FamilySearch digitized volume** — Image Group Number **003345210** (389 images)
  Coverage: *Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850*
  ⚠️ **Only 3% name-indexed** — standard name search will miss most arrivals in this volume. However, it **is full-text searchable** via FamilySearch's fulltext search tool — use that rather than the standard record search.

- **Originals:** National Archives **Record Group 36** — Customs Passenger Lists. The physical originals are held at the **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA** (in-person access required for originals).

- **Also available on:** Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com — subscription required)

**What 1840s lists contain:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only. Unlike later Ellis Island–era manifests (post-1895), these lists do *not* name a specific home village, list relatives, or identify a person to contact. The arrival record alone will rarely pinpoint an immigrant's exact origin — pair it with Irish civil registration (begins 1864) or church records held in Ireland.

*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)*

---

## 2. 📜 Naturalization Records
**Access level: Indexed collection**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906*** (Collection ID 1459213)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213

⚠️ **Critical quirk — pre-1906 naturalization in ANY court:** Before the Naturalization Act of 1906 centralized the process, an immigrant could naturalize in *any court of record* — federal, state, or local. In Boston this means records may be found in the **US District Court**, the **Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas**, the **Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court**, or Boston municipal and police courts. Search all of these, not just federal court holdings.

**What naturalization records provide:** The **Declaration of Intent** ("first papers") often includes port and date of arrival, country of origin, and sometimes a hometown. This makes it an invaluable bridge back to the passenger list and to records in the country of origin. The full Petition for Naturalization followed, usually several years later.

---

## 3. 🏛️ Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
**Access level: Indexed collection**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890*** (Collection ID 2061550)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550

Since statewide registration launched in 1841, both town- and state-level records exist for the 1840s. Early years of statewide registration were often incomplete, so the town series can be more reliable for events in the first few years after 1841. Search both.

---

## 4. ⛪ Church Records
**Access level: Indexed collection + physical parish archives**

Catholic parish registers are **essential** for tracing Irish and other Catholic immigrants of the 1840s. They document baptisms, marriages, and burials — often before civil vital registration was reliable, and with more biographical detail than civil records.

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920*** (Collection ID 1921657)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657

- **Key Boston parishes for Irish immigrants:**
  - Cathedral of the Holy Cross (downtown Boston)
  - St. Patrick's Church
  - Original registers are held at the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — contact them directly for pre-digital records

*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)*

---

## 5. 📊 Federal Census Records
**Access level: Indexed; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry**

| Year | What it records | Value for immigrant research |
|---|---|---|
| **1840** | Head of household + age/sex tallies only | Confirms household presence in Boston; does not name all members |
| **1850** | **Names all individuals**, ages, occupations, and birthplaces | The pivotal record — immigrant household members will show a foreign birthplace; anchor your research here |

The 1850 census is especially powerful: it is the first to list every person by name and birthplace, giving you a snapshot of an immigrant family roughly 0–5 years after Famine-era arrivals.

---

## 6. ⚖️ Probate Records
**Access level: Indexed collection**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991*** (Collection ID 1678901)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901

Suffolk County Probate Court records are included. Even immigrant families without significant estates may have probate files — these can name heirs, relationships, and places of origin.

---

## 7. 🎖️ Military Records
**Access level: Physical at NARA; partial online via Fold3**

The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and state militia records are the relevant military sources for the 1840s. Some newly arrived immigrants enlisted. Service records and pension files are at **NARA (Washington, D.C.)** and are partially accessible via:
- Fold3: https://www.fold3.com/

---

## 8. 📰 Newspapers
**Access level: Partial digitization**

Boston newspapers of the 1840s frequently published **passenger arrival notices** — ships and their passengers were often listed. Obituaries and naturalization notices also appeared. Key titles include the *Boston Daily Advertiser*.

- Newspapers.com: https://www.newspapers.com/

---

## 9. ⚰️ Cemetery Records
**Access level: Partial online; physical at individual cemeteries**

Catholic cemeteries served Irish immigrant communities. Find A Grave indexes many Boston-area cemeteries:
- https://www.findagrave.com/

For Irish Catholic immigrants, also check Catholic cemeteries such as **Holy Cross Cemetery** (Malden, MA, est. 1859) and earlier Catholic burial grounds in the city.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Passenger lists (RG 36), federal court naturalizations | In-person; selected holdings on FamilySearch/Ancestry |
| **FamilySearch** | Passenger lists, naturalization, vital, church, probate | Free — familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists, census, vital records | Subscription |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** | State vital records, state court records | In-person; some online |
| **City of Boston Archives** | Municipal records (almshouse, city directories, etc.) | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers | Contact required |
| **NARA (Washington, D.C.)** | Military service/pension records | In-person or via Fold3 |

---

## Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **The 1840s passenger list volume (IGN 003345210) is only 3% name-indexed.** Use FamilySearch's **fulltext search** on this volume — standard name searches will miss nearly every arrival.
2. **Pre-1906 naturalization could be filed in any court.** Search Suffolk County courts, city municipal courts, and federal courts — don't limit yourself to NARA federal court holdings.
3. **Statewide vital registration (1841) was new and initially underreported.** Town-level records may be more complete for early 1840s events; check both series.
4. **1840s passenger lists give country (not village) of origin.** The arrival record alone won't identify an immigrant's townland. Pair it with naturalization declarations of intent, church records, and Irish civil/church records.
5. **The 1850 census is your most powerful post-arrival anchor.** It's the first federal census to name everyone and record birthplaces — use it to locate immigrant families before working backward.
6. **Irish Famine arrivals (ca. 1845–1852) dominate Boston's 1840s immigration.** The **Boston Pilot Missing Persons database** (1831–1921) is a well-known Irish-specific finding aid; check the Boston Pilot and NARA for access details if tracing Irish ancestors specifically.

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Access Level | Primary Online Access |
|---|---|---|
| Passenger lists, Port of Boston (1820–1891) | Indexed collection | FS col. 1784312; Ancestry.com |
| Passenger list volume 1840–1850 (IGN 003345210) | Fulltext searchable only (3% name-indexed) | FamilySearch fulltext search |
| Naturalization records (1790–1906) | Indexed collection | FS col. 1459213 |
| Town vital records (1620–1890) | Indexed collection | FS col. 2061550 |
| Church records (1630–1920) | Indexed collection | FS col. 1921657 |
| Probate records (1635–1991) | Indexed collection | FS col. 1678901 |
| Federal census (1840, 1850) | Indexed | FamilySearch; Ancestry.com |
| Military records | Physical + partial online | NARA; Fold3 |
| Newspapers | Partial digitization | Newspapers.com |
| Cemetery records | Partial | Find A Grave |

---

**Recommended first search sequence** for a newly located Boston immigrant arrival:
1. **Passenger list** (FS col. 1784312 + fulltext search on IGN 003345210) → confirms arrival and gives country of origin
2. **1850 census** → locates full household, ages, and all birthplaces
3. **Naturalization declaration of intent** (FS col. 1459213, also check county courts) → may give specific arrival details and hometown
4. **Church records** (FS col. 1921657 + Archdiocese archives) → baptisms, marriages, burials with additional family detail
5. **Vital records** (FS col. 2061550) → births, marriages, deaths after settlement in Boston
