---

## Locality Research Guide
### Native American Families in Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) · c. 1830–1900

---

### Jurisdictional Context

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma did not exist as a U.S. state — **it was Indian Territory**, a federally designated region created under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until **1907**. This has profound implications for genealogical research:

- Standard county-level civil registration (birth, marriage, death) did **not** apply in Indian Territory. Vital events were recorded — if at all — by tribal governments, federal agents, or missionaries.
- Records were created by four distinct authorities: **the federal government** (Bureau of Indian Affairs / Indian agents), **tribal governments**, **Christian missionaries**, and occasionally **the U.S. military**.
- The **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were the dominant groups relocated to Indian Territory and produced the richest genealogical record sets. Tribes west of that zone (Osage, Comanche, Kiowa, Cheyenne, Arapaho, etc.) were not removed under the same act and have sparser mid-1800s documentation.

> **Critical quirk:** Because Oklahoma was Indian Territory before 1907, searching "Oklahoma" county records for the mid-1800s will yield nothing for tribal families. All research in this period routes through federal (BIA/NARA), tribal, and missionary record sets — not county courthouses.

---

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls 🟢 Indexed + Images

The single most important record class. FamilySearch holds the collection **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (collection [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)) — 567,890 records with images — covering both the in-period rolls and the later Dawes enumeration. Key rolls within this window:

| Roll | Date | Tribe | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Old Settler Cherokee Roll** | 1851 | Cherokee | Covers Cherokees already in Indian Territory before the main removal |
| **Drennen Roll** | 1852 | Cherokee | Covers the Eastern Cherokee who arrived via Trail of Tears |
| **Annuity Rolls** | Various, 1830s–1880s | All Five Tribes | Payment rolls listing heads of household by name; BIA-created |
| **Dawes Rolls** | 1898–1914 | All Five Tribes | The most widely used enrollment; documents blood quantum, family groupings, and "Old Settler" vs. "Eastern" status — essential even for mid-1800s research because it captures family structure across generations |

> **Quirk:** The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) postdate the mid-1800s, but they are the essential starting point for any Five Civilized Tribes family because they explicitly note earlier tribal status (e.g., "Old Settler," "Delaware Cherokee") and connect living individuals to their mid-1800s ancestors. Always start with the Dawes Rolls and work backward. The FamilySearch Wiki discusses these at [Oklahoma Native American Records — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).

Volume search also returned a digitized series: **image group 002298871** — "Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870" — 940 images, **99% name-indexed and full-text searchable**. Reachable via `record_search` and `fulltext_search` on FamilySearch.

---

### 2. Land Records 🟢 Indexed + Images

**"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (collection [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. This collection covers land grants and allotment records within the territory. Land allotments accelerated after the **Dawes Act of 1887**, which subdivided tribal lands and required each enrolled member to receive an individual allotment — creating voluminous records naming family members and heirs. The General Land Office records (Bureau of Land Management, [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) also hold federal land patents for Indian Territory. NARA's Southwest Region in Fort Worth holds the original allotment jackets.

---

### 3. Mission and Church Records 🟢 Indexed + Images

**"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)) — 123,456 records, 61,728 images. Christian missionaries established churches and schools among the relocated tribes beginning in the 1820s. The wiki confirms that **Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian** missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)). These are often the only record of births and deaths in the mid-1800s period. Records are predominantly in English.

---

### 4. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records ⚠️ Primarily Physical / Microfilm

The BIA maintained extensive records at each agency: **annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records, ration rolls, and census counts**. These are among the richest mid-1800s sources for tribal families — annuity rolls in particular list heads of household by name and are effectively annual censuses for the period.

**Where held:** The bulk of Indian Territory BIA records are at **NARA's Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas** (the confirmed location per the FamilySearch Wiki). Some series have been microfilmed and are available on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) and [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

> **Quirk:** BIA records survive unevenly by agency and tribe. Cherokee records are the most complete; Seminole records are sparsest. Agency record availability should be verified at NARA Fort Worth before assuming a series exists for your tribe and decade.

---

### 5. Treaty Records ⚠️ Physical at NARA / Some Digitized

The federal government negotiated dozens of treaties with the Five Civilized Tribes and with Plains tribes in the mid-1800s. Treaty documents sometimes include signatories' names and are at **NARA in Washington, D.C.** (Record Group 75, Bureau of Indian Affairs). Some are transcribed at the [Oklahoma Historical Society](https://www.okhistory.org) and [Tribal websites](https://www.cherokee.org). Treaties set the legal framework for annuity payments, land boundaries, and enrollment — so understanding which treaties apply to your ancestral tribe directly determines which BIA record series to search.

---

### 6. Federal Census Records 🟡 Partially Indexed

Standard U.S. federal censuses (1860, 1870, 1880) enumerated **some** Indian Territory residents, particularly non-Indian settlers in border zones. Tribal members living within organized tribal nations were often recorded separately in tribal censuses rather than the federal enumeration. The **1880 Special Indian Census** and related schedules are the most useful for identifying family units in this period. These are within the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" collection on FamilySearch ([collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)).

---

### 7. Military Records ⚠️ Physical at NARA / Some on Fold3

Native American men served in the Union and Confederate armies during the Civil War (1861–1865) — the Five Tribes were split between both sides. Service records and pension files are at **NARA** and indexed on **[Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)**. Indian scouts who served with the U.S. Army also generated pension records. Fold3 is identified by FamilySearch as a curated external resource for this jurisdiction.

---

### 8. Newspapers and Published Sources ⚠️ Specialized

The **Cherokee Phoenix** (1828–1834) and its successor **Cherokee Advocate** were tribal newspapers that published obituaries, land notices, and community news. Some issues are digitized. **[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)** is a curated external resource for Oklahoma, though coverage before 1890 is sparse. The **Oklahoma Historical Society** (OHS) holds significant manuscript and newspaper holdings relevant to Indian Territory.

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)) | Tribal rolls (1851–1959), land records (1834–1907), mission records (1820–1965) — indexed | Free online |
| **NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth TX** | BIA agency records, allotment jackets, Dawes enrollment originals | In-person or copy request |
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** | Treaty records (RG 75), military service & pension files | In-person or FOIA/copy request |
| **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) | Military records, some BIA records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com)) | Dawes Rolls, federal census records | Subscription |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** ([okhistory.org](https://www.okhistory.org)) | Manuscripts, newspapers, Indian Territory records | Free online portal + in-person |
| **Tribal Archives** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole nations) | Tribal-held enrollment records, council minutes, citizenship records | Varies by tribe — contact directly |

---

### Suggested Research Sequence for Mid-1800s Tribal Families

1. **Start with the Dawes Rolls** (1898–1914) — FamilySearch [collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432). Even though they postdate the mid-1800s, they are the essential anchor: they establish tribal affiliation, blood quantum, and family groupings that point directly to earlier rolls.
2. **Work back to the 1851–1852 rolls** (Old Settler Cherokee / Drennen) and any annuity rolls for the relevant tribe within the same collection.
3. **Search the Tribal Enrollment Cards volume** (image group 002298871, 1840–1870) — 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable on FamilySearch.
4. **Search mission/church records** — FamilySearch [collection 1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) — for baptisms, marriages, and burials not captured by tribal rolls.
5. **Search land records** — FamilySearch [collection 1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) — for allotment and treaty land grant evidence placing the family geographically.
6. **Contact NARA Fort Worth** for BIA agency records not yet digitized — annuity rolls and correspondence can name individuals the digitized collections miss.
7. **Contact the relevant tribal nation's citizenship/enrollment office** — several tribes hold their own historical records and can confirm or extend enrollment lineage.

---

### Coverage Gaps to Note

- The **FamilySearch Wiki does not yet have Oklahoma-specific place pages** for the four standard research sections (home, getting-started, online records, research tips) — all returned generic content. The Oklahoma-specific resource is the article at [Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records).
- BIA agency records for many tribes are **not digitized** and require direct NARA access.
- **Freedmen** — people of African descent enslaved by tribal members and their descendants — also appear on tribal rolls (the "Freedmen Rolls" within the Dawes series). If your research involves this community, search the Freedmen Rolls explicitly alongside the main enrollment rolls.
- Records for **non-Five-Tribes nations** (Osage, Comanche, Kiowa, Cheyenne, Arapaho, etc.) are substantially sparser for the mid-1800s. These groups' agency records at NARA are the primary source; digitization coverage is limited.

## Pennsylvania Quaker Research Guide — Late 1700s (c. 1750–1800)

**Jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States | **Period:** c. 1750–1800
**Focus:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) / meeting records

---

### Why Quaker Records Are Your Primary Source

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration of births or deaths until 1906**, and no mandatory county-level vital registration in this period either. For the late 1700s, **Quaker monthly meeting registers are the functional equivalent of civil vital records** — often the only systematic documentation of births, marriages, and deaths for member families. This makes them essential, not supplementary.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))*

---

### 1. 🏆 Quaker Meeting Records — Core Source

**What they contain:**
Monthly meetings kept meticulous records across several record types, each genealogically rich:

| Record Type | What It Documents |
|---|---|
| **Birth registers** | Name, date, parents — often more complete than any civil record |
| **Marriage certificates** | Date, meeting, names of **both families** — signed by **every witness present** (often 50–100 names) |
| **Death registers** | Name, date, sometimes age and parentage |
| **Certificates of Removal** | Issued when a family moved between meetings — names the origin meeting, destination meeting, and family members. Tracks migration. |
| **Disownment proceedings** | Records members expelled for marrying outside the meeting, joining the military, or other violations — names the individual and the offense |
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Business proceedings; name members involved in disputes, applications, committee appointments |

**The meeting hierarchy matters for research:**
- **Monthly Meeting** → the record-keeping unit; where to start
- **Quarterly Meeting** → groups of monthly meetings (oversight)
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** → top of the Pennsylvania/Delaware/New Jersey structure

**Core Quaker counties (late 1700s):**
- **Philadelphia** — the center; Philadelphia Monthly Meeting and its branches
- **Chester County** — exceptionally dense Quaker settlement from the 1680s
- **Bucks County** — northeast of Philadelphia; strong Quaker communities
- **Delaware County** — carved from Chester County in **1789**; records before that date are in **Chester County** meeting/civil records
- **Lancaster County** — further inland; smaller but active Quaker presence

---

### 2. Where the Records Are Held

#### 🏛 Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA
The **largest collection of American Quaker records** in existence. Holds originals and microfilm of monthly meeting registers, minutes, removal certificates, and disciplinary records for Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and beyond.
- Website: [swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)
- Many records available by appointment; some microfilm copies at FamilySearch

#### 🏛 Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College, Haverford, PA
Second major repository for Pennsylvania Quaker manuscript records and printed works.
- Website: [haverford.edu/quaker-special-collections](https://www.haverford.edu/quaker-special-collections)

#### 🖥 FamilySearch (Online)
FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers. The confirmed digitized volume for this period is:

| Volume | Coverage | Images | Indexed? | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes** (IGN 001188322) | Philadelphia, PA — 1750–1800 | 145 | ❌ 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable | **Browse-only** — image by image |

This volume must be browsed page by page — there is no name search. Additional monthly meeting registers are held on FamilySearch microfilm (some not yet digitized); check the FamilySearch catalog by county and meeting name.

#### 🏛 Published Abstracts — Hinshaw's Encyclopedia
**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes** — abstracts (not full transcriptions) of meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states. An excellent name-indexed entry point to identify which meeting holds a record before going to the original. Available at major genealogical libraries, the Allen County Public Library, and online through some library databases.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Church Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))*

---

### 3. ⚠️ Critical Research Quirks

**a) The Quaker calendar — a dating trap**
Quakers refused to use pagan month and day names. Their records use **numbered months and days**. The critical complication: before **September 1752** (when Britain and its colonies adopted the Gregorian calendar), the Quaker year began in **March**. So:

- Before Sept. 1752: "1st Month" = **March**, "2nd Month" = April … "12th Month" = February
- After Sept. 1752: "1st Month" = **January**, "2nd Month" = February, etc.

A record dated "12th mo. 1749" means **February 1750** in the modern calendar. Always convert before recording dates.

**b) Removal certificates are migration trackers**
When a Quaker family moved — even to the next county — their monthly meeting issued a certificate of removal to the receiving meeting. These certificates travel with the family in the *destination* meeting's records, not the origin meeting's. To follow a family westward (e.g., Chester County → Lancaster County), search the *receiving* meeting's incoming removal file, not just the origin.

**c) Disownments often document non-conforming events**
A member who married a non-Quaker in a civil ceremony, or who served in the Revolutionary War militia, was often disowned. Disownment minutes name the individual, the offense, and sometimes family connections — a useful negative record that still places the person in the community.

**d) Delaware County records before 1789 are in Chester County**
Delaware County was formed from Chester County in 1789. Any civil or meeting record for what is now Delaware County before that date will be found under Chester County jurisdiction.

**e) Marriage records in Quaker records are uniquely rich**
Quaker marriages were not performed by clergy — they were witnessed by the entire meeting. Marriage certificates carry **all attending witnesses' signatures**, sometimes 50–100 names. This is frequently the most complete cluster of family names you will find for an 18th-century Pennsylvania Quaker family.

---

### 4. Supporting Records (Non-Quaker)

Since no civil vital registration existed, these fill gaps:

#### County Marriage Records (Marriage Licenses & Bonds)
- Kept at the **county courthouse** (now often at the county Historical Society or State Archives) from the colonial period
- FamilySearch collections covering this period:
  - **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** — [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) — 312,045 records; some images
  - **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** — [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) — 198,765 records; name-indexed; no images
- ⚠️ Note: Quakers who married within the meeting usually did NOT obtain a county marriage license — the meeting record was their documentation. County marriage records are most useful for Quakers who married outside the meeting (and were often disowned for it).

#### Probate Records
- Held at the **county Register of Wills** from the colonial period onward
- FamilySearch: **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** — [Collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records; images available
- Wills frequently name multiple generations and relationships; estate inventories document household goods

#### Land Records
- **Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg):** Warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's original grants (1681 onward)
- County deed books at the **county courthouse / Recorder of Deeds**
- Source: [Pennsylvania Land Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)

#### Tax Records (Pre-1790 Census Substitute)
- Pennsylvania tax assessment lists survive from the **1690s** in some counties
- The **1693 Chester County tax list** is one of the earliest surviving colonial tax records
- These are the primary population substitute before the first federal census
- Held at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch

#### 1790 Federal Census
- The **first federal census (1790)** covers the end of your research window
- Lists heads of household with household structure (free white males/females by age bracket, enslaved persons)
- Available on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and at NARA

#### Revolutionary War Military Records
- Many Quakers were **pacifists and refused service** — but some did serve, and many paid substitution fines or were fined/disowned for refusal
- Service records and pension files at **NARA** (Fold3 for digitized access)
- Pension files (post-war) are especially rich: applicants narrated their service and family history
- Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level militia muster rolls

#### Newspapers
- *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, 1728–1815) published birth, marriage, and death notices — useful for prominent Quaker families. Available on Newspapers.com and via Readex (Early American Newspapers).

---

### 5. Research Strategy — Recommended Order

1. **Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia** — identify which monthly meeting(s) your family belonged to (volumes are indexed by surname)
2. **Go to the meeting register** — search birth, marriage, death, and removal records at Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or on FamilySearch microfilm
3. **Browse the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes** (FamilySearch IGN 001188322, 145 images, browse-only) for committee or disciplinary references to your family
4. **Follow removal certificates** — trace each move by searching the *destination* meeting's incoming removal file
5. **Cross-check county marriage records** — especially if a family member married outside the meeting
6. **Search probate and land records** — for property relationships and inter-generational transfers
7. **Use tax lists** for pre-1790 household placement by county
8. **Check the 1790 census** as a baseline for late-period family structure

---

### 6. Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Original meeting registers, minutes, removals | In person / by appointment; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| Quaker & Special Collections, Haverford College | PA Quaker manuscripts | In person / by appointment |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, tax lists, some county records | In person; some online via PHMC |
| County Register of Wills / Courthouse | Probate, deeds, marriage licenses | In person; FamilySearch microfilm |
| FamilySearch (online) | Microfilmed meeting registers, probate, civil marriages | Free online; browse-only for most pre-1800 volumes |
| NARA / Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Online (Fold3, subscription) |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 census, compiled marriages, some PA church records | Subscription |

---

**Bottom line:** For Pennsylvania Quakers in the late 1700s, the monthly meeting register is your civil registration system — it did not exist at the state level until 1906. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore is your primary archive; Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* is your name index into it. The calendar quirk (numbered months, pre-1752 year start in March) is the single most common dating error researchers make — convert every date before recording it.

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: Pittsburgh & Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Era (c. 1870–1910)

**Place:** Pittsburgh (county seat), Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, United States
**FamilySearch Standard Place:** `Pittsburgh, Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States`
**Target Period:** c. 1870–1910 (peak steel industry immigration and expansion)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Allegheny County was formed in **1788** from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh became the county seat and grew into the center of American steel production in the Gilded Age under Carnegie, Jones & Laughlin, and other firms. The massive labor demand drew waves of immigrants — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian — most concentrated in Pittsburgh proper and nearby mill towns along the Monongahela, Allegheny, and Ohio river valleys.

**Critical registration boundary:**
- Allegheny County recorded **births and deaths from 1870** — earlier than Pennsylvania's statewide vital registration mandate of **1906**.
- **Marriage licenses** are available from **1885** at the Allegheny County Courthouse.
- Pre-1906 state-level vital registrations are largely absent outside county records.

---

## 1. 🏭 Industrial & Occupational Records *(the key focus)*

This is where Pittsburgh diverges from a standard county survey. Sources confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)):

| Source | What It Contains | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Hire dates, department, pay, sometimes birthplace and nationality | **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) & **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** archives | Physical; fragmentary — many did not survive |
| **Union membership lists** | Member name, local number, sometimes dues records and nationality | Various union archives; some at Heinz History Center | Physical |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Employee counts, nationalities, conditions by mill; may name supervisors | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Physical |
| **City directories (Pittsburgh, 1813–)** | Name, occupation, employer, home address, annual snapshots | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (complete run); also on Ancestry.com and Internet Archive | Digitized (some indexed) |

⚠️ **Gap warning:** Corporate employment records are highly fragmentary. Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and Westinghouse records survive unevenly. Do not assume a specific mill's records exist — contact the Heinz History Center or Rivers of Steel directly to confirm before planning a research trip.

---

## 2. 📊 Census Records

The federal census is the backbone of any Pittsburgh industrial-worker search. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Census section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)):

| Census Year | Key Fields | FamilySearch Availability |
|---|---|---|
| **1870** | Name, age, birthplace, occupation, real/personal estate value | Indexed + images (free) |
| **1880** | Name, age, birthplace, **parents' birthplaces**, occupation, relationship to head | Indexed + images (free) |
| **1900** | Name, age, birthplace, parents' birthplaces, **immigration year**, **years in US**, occupation | Indexed + images (free) |
| **1910** | Name, age, birthplace, parents' birthplaces, immigration year, occupation, **employer/self/wage** | Indexed + images (free) |

The **1890 federal census was largely destroyed** by fire — a major gap for this exact boom decade. Pennsylvania did not conduct a substitute state census.

**Mortality schedules (1870, 1880)** record deaths in the year preceding each census, including cause of death — useful for confirming industrial accident deaths.

---

## 3. 📜 Vital Records

Pennsylvania **did not require statewide** birth and death registration until 1906. Allegheny County began its own recording in **1870**. Marriage licenses are available at the **county courthouse from 1885**.

**FamilySearch collections confirmed (from `collections_search`):**

| Collection | Date Range | Records | FamilySearch Link |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | [Collection 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) |
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | [Collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) |

⚠️ Death certificates begin **1906** — for deaths before that year, look to county-level records, church burial registers, and cemetery records. County birth and death records from 1870–1905 are held at the **Allegheny County Health Department** and the **Pennsylvania State Archives**.

---

## 4. ⛪ Church Records *(critical for immigrant families)*

For steel-industry immigrant families, church records are often the **best or only** source for births, marriages, and deaths before civil registration. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Vital and Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)):

- **Catholic parishes** served specific ethnic communities and kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the **1840s onward**
- Key ethnic communities and their parishes: **Slovak** (e.g., St. Elizabeth of Hungary), **Polish** (e.g., St. Stanislaus Kostka), **Croatian**, **Italian**, **Irish** (e.g., St. Patrick's)
- Originals are held at the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** — contact them directly for access
- Protestant denominations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran for German families) kept similar registers — held at denominational archives or deposited with the **Presbyterian Historical Society** (Philadelphia)
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Allegheny County church registers; search the catalog at [familysearch.org/catalog](https://familysearch.org/catalog)

**Research tip:** Identify the family's ethnicity and religion first, then target the specific parish. Searching generically across all Catholic records is far less efficient than going directly to the ethnic parish that served that community.

---

## 5. 🛂 Naturalization & Immigration Records

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)):

- **Naturalization records from the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930)** are held at the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region)
- Before 1906, a person could naturalize in *any* court of record — check federal, state, and local courts
- **Passenger arrival lists** (pre-1891 via customs; 1891+ via Immigration Bureau) are at NARA and indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch; the 1880s–1900s Austro-Hungarian and Italian arrivals at Ellis Island are well indexed
- The 1900 and 1910 censuses record **immigration year** and **years in the US** — use these to focus passenger list searches
- The **Heinz History Center** also holds immigration and ethnic community records

---

## 6. 🗺️ City Directories

Pittsburgh city directories begin in **1813** and provide an annual snapshot of residents with name, occupation, and address. These are invaluable for:
- Tracking a worker's employer from year to year
- Documenting address changes (useful for following mill relocations)
- Filling the gap in the destroyed 1890 census

**Held at:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (complete run from 1813)
**Also accessible:** Ancestry.com (many years digitized); Internet Archive (some free)
Per the FamilySearch Wiki: [Allegheny County Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)

---

## 7. ⚔️ Military Records

Many Pittsburgh steel workers served in the Civil War (if older) or Spanish-American War (1898). Key sources:
- **Civil War service records and pension files** — NARA (indexed on Fold3.com and Ancestry.com)
- **WWI Draft Registration Cards (1917–1918)** — while just outside this window, they record birthplace, employer, and physical description for men born 1872–1900; at NARA and Ancestry.com
- **Pennsylvania adjutant general records** — at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg

---

## 8. 📰 Newspapers

Pittsburgh had a vigorous press during the steel era:
- **Pittsburgh Post-Gazette** (founded 1786) and **Pittsburgh Press** — obituaries, accident reports, labor strikes, and immigration community news
- **Ethnic-language newspapers** (Slovak, Polish, Croatian presses) carried community notices, birth announcements, and death notices inaccessible in English-language papers
- Held at: **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (microfilm); **Newspapers.com** (some years digitized); Pennsylvania State Archives

---

## 9. 🪦 Cemetery Records

Many Pittsburgh mill workers were buried in ethnic Catholic or Protestant cemeteries. Key resources:
- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — crowd-sourced transcriptions and photographs
- **BillionGraves** — indexed cemetery records
- Ethnic parish cemeteries (e.g., Calvary Catholic Cemetery, Allegheny Cemetery) — contact cemetery offices directly for pre-digitization records

---

## 🏛️ Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company records, immigration records, labor history, city directories | In-person and online catalog |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** | Steel industry records, oral histories, industrial photographs | In-person |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1813–), local newspapers, local history books | In-person; some digitized |
| **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Ethnic parish baptism/marriage/burial registers (1840s+) | By appointment |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage licenses (1885+), deeds, probate | In-person |
| **National Archives — Philadelphia (NARA)** | Naturalization records (Court of Common Pleas, 1798–1930), passenger lists | In-person and Ancestry.com |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | State factory inspector reports, state-level vital records post-1906, military records | In-person and online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Census, marriage collections, probate, microfilmed church records | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | City directories, census, passenger lists, death certificates | Subscription |

---

## ⚠️ Key Researcher Quirks

1. **The 1890 census is destroyed.** The only federal snapshot of the height of the steel boom is missing. City directories (1889, 1890, 1891 runs at Carnegie Library) are your best substitute for those years.
2. **Pennsylvania statewide death/birth registration began in 1906**, not before. For deaths and births 1870–1905, look to Allegheny County's own registers (Health Department) and church records — not the state.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court.** Don't limit your search to federal courts — check Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records at NARA Philadelphia.
4. **Company employment records are fragmentary.** Most steel mill HR records did not survive. Contact Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel directly before assuming a collection exists.
5. **Identify ethnicity first, then target the ethnic parish.** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian immigrant families left their best early records in ethnic Catholic parishes, not civil registers. The Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives is the starting point.
6. **The 1880 and 1900 censuses are the strongest federal tools.** The 1880 records parents' birthplaces; the 1900 records immigration year — both are critical for immigrant steel-worker families.
7. **Workers often moved between mill towns.** Families may have lived in Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, or Duquesne (all in Allegheny or neighboring counties) rather than Pittsburgh proper — extend your directory and church searches to adjacent mill towns.

---

*Sources: FamilySearch Wiki — [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy); Wikipedia — Pittsburgh; FamilySearch collections_search (Pennsylvania, scope); external_links_search (Allegheny County, 1860–1910).*

# Locality Research Guide
## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic
**Research period:** August–November 1793 (epidemic window); broader context 1785–1810

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**Philadelphia County** was established in 1682 and has existed continuously since. In 1793 the City of Philadelphia was a distinct municipality *within* Philadelphia County — a smaller, densely settled area bounded roughly by the Delaware River waterfront. **The 1854 Act of Consolidation merged the city and county into a single jurisdiction**, so pre-1854 records may be held under either "Philadelphia City" or "Philadelphia County" headings depending on the repository.

In 1793, **Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration**; that did not begin until 1906. For any death, birth, or marriage in 1793, **church registers are the only systematic vital records**. This is the single most important quirk of this jurisdiction for your research period.

The epidemic ran **August through November 1793**, killing approximately 5,000 of the city's roughly 50,000 residents — about one-tenth of the population. Thousands more fled to surrounding counties and across the Delaware into New Jersey. Sources for those evacuees may therefore lie in **Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, and Bucks Counties (PA)** or **Gloucester and Burlington Counties (NJ)**.

---

## Record Types, Availability & Access

### 🔴 TIER 1 — Epidemic-Specific Sources (highest priority)

#### 1. Published List of the Dead — Mathew Carey
Physician and publisher Mathew Carey compiled a list of persons who died in the epidemic, published in his pamphlet *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia* (multiple editions, 1793–1794). This is a **named-person list** and one of the most direct genealogical sources for epidemic deaths. It is widely available:
- **Library Company of Philadelphia** (physical + digitized)
- **Internet Archive / HathiTrust** (freely searchable online)
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**

#### 2. Committee of the Citizens — Minutes and Reports
The "Committee Appointed by the Citizens of Philadelphia to Attend to and Alleviate the Sufferings of the Afflicted with the Malignant Fever" documented relief efforts, aid recipients, and the dead. Manuscript minutes are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and **HSP**. These name both victims and survivors who received assistance — useful even for families that survived.

#### 3. Bush Hill Hospital Records
The city converted Bush Hill estate into a fever hospital. Records of admissions and deaths there, if they survive, are at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and **HSP**. Coverage is uneven; not all patients were documented.

---

### 🟠 TIER 2 — Church Burial Registers (primary vital source for 1793)

Church registers are **the only systematic record of deaths for this period** in Philadelphia. The epidemic's peak August–November 1793 should be visible as a sharp spike in burial entries. Key congregations whose records survive:

| Congregation | Denomination | Record Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church** | Anglican/Episcopal | HSP; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **St. Peter's Church** | Anglican/Episcopal | HSP; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes')** | Swedish Lutheran | Gloria Dei Church; HSP; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **St. Mary's Church** | Roman Catholic | Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives |
| **Mikveh Israel** | Jewish | Congregation Mikveh Israel; HSP |
| **Philadelphia Monthly Meeting** | Quaker (Friends) | Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College; HSP |
| **First Presbyterian** | Presbyterian | Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia |
| **German Reformed / Lutheran** | German Protestant | HSP; FamilySearch microfilm |
| **African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas** | Episcopalian (Black congregation) | HSP |
| **Mother Bethel AME** | AME (founded 1793) | Mother Bethel; HSP |

**Access level:** Many Philadelphia church registers are available as **browse-only microfilm** on FamilySearch (not name-indexed for this early period). Published transcriptions exist for several congregations via the **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (*Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine*) — check HSP's library for those indexes.

The FamilySearch Wiki confirms: *"Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records."* ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))

**Quirk — African American families:** Richard Allen and Absalom Jones organized the Free African Society to nurse epidemic victims. Records of their community — including the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas and Mother Bethel — are at HSP and within denominational archives; they document Black Philadelphians both as caregivers and victims.

---

### 🟡 TIER 3 — Probate Records (strong secondary source)

Epidemic deaths triggered rapid probate filings. Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, and guardianship petitions for children orphaned by the epidemic are a rich source.

**FamilySearch collection: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (Collection ID 1999196)
- 893,214 indexed records with images
- Date range covers 1793 ✓
- Access: **Indexed + images** — searchable by name on FamilySearch
- URL: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196

**Philadelphia County Orphans' Court** specifically handled guardianship for children whose parents died. These records are at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and some are on FamilySearch microfilm.

---

### 🟡 TIER 4 — Census Records (for context before and after)

| Census | Year | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1790 Federal Census** | 1790 | 3 years before epidemic; establishes household composition going in |
| **1800 Federal Census** | 1800 | 7 years after; identifies survivors, new households, widows/remarriages |
| **Pennsylvania Tax Lists 1782–1793** | 1782–1793 | Annual assessments; can track presence/absence across epidemic years |

The 1790 and 1800 censuses are indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Pennsylvania tax lists for 1793 are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) and on FamilySearch microfilm (browse-only for many counties).

---

### 🟡 TIER 5 — Marriage Records (for surrounding family reconstruction)

**FamilySearch collection: Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (Collection ID 1502909)
- 198,765 indexed records; **no images** (index only)
- Covers 1793 ✓
- Access: **Index only — no images available**
- URL: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909

**FamilySearch collection: Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (Collection ID 1571957)
- 312,045 indexed records with images
- Covers 1793 ✓
- Access: **Indexed + images**
- URL: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957

Marriages in the 1780s–1810s help reconstruct family units — who married before the epidemic, who remarried after.

---

### 🟡 TIER 6 — Newspapers

Philadelphia's newspapers published **lists of epidemic dead**, flight notices, and relief announcements. These are a critical substitute source. Key titles:

- *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*
- *General Advertiser* (Philadelphia)
- *Federal Gazette*
- *Philadelphia Gazette*

**Access:** HSP holds the most complete run of 18th-century Philadelphia newspapers. Some are digitized on **Newspapers.com** (subscription) and **Chronicling America** (free, Library of Congress). Check the **Library Company of Philadelphia** for additional holdings.

---

### 🟢 TIER 7 — Land & Tax Records

Pennsylvania County tax assessments (1782–1806) are a powerful substitute for missing vital records — they track heads of household annually and can show a name disappearing (death, departure) or a widow suddenly assessed in her own name.

- **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg: original tax assessment books
- **HSP**: manuscript duplicates and transcriptions
- **FamilySearch**: some volumes digitized as browse-only microfilm

---

### 🟢 TIER 8 — Court Records / Naturalizations

Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record. Philadelphia's naturalizations are indexed in several published sources:
- **FamilySearch Catalog** for Philadelphia County court records (some microfilmed)
- **Ancestry.com**: Pennsylvania naturalization records
- **Philadelphia City Archives**: Quarter Sessions and Common Pleas Court records

Many post-epidemic guardianship and estate disputes also appear in Quarter Sessions and Common Pleas records.

---

### 🟢 TIER 9 — Military Records

For families with veterans in the epidemic period:
- **Revolutionary War pension files** at NARA (Washington, DC and regional archives) give family composition, ages, and places of residence
- **Fold3.com**: Digitized pension files and service records, searchable by name

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**, Philadelphia | Church records (many originals), Mathew Carey pamphlet, Committee minutes, newspapers, tax records, manuscript collections | On-site; some digitized via HSP Digital Library |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City administrative records, Committee records, Bush Hill records, later vital records | On-site; some records indexed online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Probate (indexed + images), compiled marriages, civil marriages, census records, church microfilm (many browse-only) | Free online |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society**, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church records for Philadelphia | On-site; some microfilmed |
| **Friends Historical Library**, Swarthmore College | Quaker Meeting records (births, marriages, deaths) | On-site; some on FamilySearch |
| **Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives** | Catholic parish registers | On-site by appointment |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | State-level records, tax assessments, military | On-site; some digitized |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | 18th-century printed sources, broadsides, newspapers | On-site |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census records, some Philadelphia church/court records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com / Chronicling America** | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription / Free |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records, some transcribed burial registers | Free online |

---

## Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No civil death registration in 1793.** Pennsylvania statewide registration did not begin until 1906. Church burial registers are the *only* systematic death records for this period — there is no death certificate to find.

2. **City vs. County distinction.** In 1793, "Philadelphia" as a city was a smaller area inside Philadelphia County. Before searching, clarify whether a repository's holdings cover the city proper, the broader county, or both. The 1854 consolidation merged them, so post-1854 finding aids often collapse the distinction.

3. **Epidemic evacuees — search surrounding jurisdictions.** Thousands fled the city August–November 1793. Records of deaths or events during flight may appear in **Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, or Bucks County (PA)** records, or across the Delaware River in **Gloucester or Burlington County (NJ)**.

4. **Mathew Carey's list is a starting point, not a complete registry.** It covers recognized victims but is not exhaustive — especially for the poor, Black residents, and those in peripheral neighborhoods.

5. **The African American community was disproportionately involved.** Richard Allen and Absalom Jones's *Narrative* (1794) is a primary source for the Black experience of the epidemic and names many individuals. HSP holds this and related manuscript material.

6. **Philadelphia church records vary widely in completeness.** Some congregations kept meticulous registers; others left gaps. Always check multiple congregations — many families attended more than one, or were recorded where burial actually took place regardless of membership.

7. **FamilySearch Wiki source.** The FamilySearch Wiki's [Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) page confirms the Carey list, Committee minutes, church burial registers, HSP, and Philadelphia City Archives as the core primary sources for this event.

---

## Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's published list** — freely available on Internet Archive — to confirm whether your ancestor appears among the named dead.
2. **Search the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses** on FamilySearch to bracket the epidemic: who was in the household before, who survived after.
3. **Search the Philadelphia County Probate Records** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) for wills or estate inventories filed 1793–1796 — epidemic deaths generated rapid probate.
4. **Identify the family's congregation** and locate that church's burial register at HSP, a denominational archive, or on FamilySearch microfilm; browse the August–November 1793 entries.
5. **Check Philadelphia newspapers** (HSP, Newspapers.com) for death notices and lists published during the epidemic months.
6. **Search Pennsylvania tax lists 1792–1795** at the Pennsylvania State Archives to track household presence before and absence after.
7. **If the family fled:** check the surrounding county records and NJ records for the same window.

# 🔥 Locality Research Guide — Chicago, Cook County, Illinois
## Tracing Families Affected by the Great Chicago Fire of 1871
**Jurisdiction:** Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States
**Target Period:** ~1840–1900 (fire: October 8–10, 1871)

---

## ⚠️ The Critical Fact: A Hard Record Break at October 1871

The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, wiping out the bulk of the city's accumulated official documentation: deeds, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers. This creates a hard documentary break. Research before the fire and after it require almost entirely different source strategies.

> Source: Wikipedia, *Great Chicago Fire* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire
> FamilySearch Wiki, *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire* — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire

---

## Jurisdictional Context

| Detail | Information |
|---|---|
| **County** | Cook County (formed 1831) |
| **State** | Illinois (admitted 1818) |
| **Vital registration — statewide** | Did NOT begin until **1916** (compliance improved through the 1920s) |
| **Vital registration — Cook County local** | Birth and death records from **1871** (Cook County Clerk's Office); most pre-1871 records destroyed in the fire |
| **Record catastrophe** | October 8–10, 1871: Cook County Courthouse destroyed |
| **Legislative response** | **Burnt Record Act (1872)**: property owners required to re-register deeds; creates a major substitute source |

> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration* — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration

Illinois statewide vital registration did not exist in 1871; Cook County's locally kept birth and death records begin at the fire itself, so **there are effectively no official vital records for Chicago before October 1871.**

---

## Part 1 — Pre-Fire Records (before October 1871)

Most official county records are gone. The following are the surviving and substitute sources for this period.

### 📋 Federal Census Schedules
| Census Year | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1840, 1850, 1860 | ✅ Survived | Held by NARA; indexed and available on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **1870** | ✅ **Survived (key source)** | Taken June 1870 — months before the fire; originals were in Washington, D.C. and were not destroyed. This is your closest pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families. |
| 1880 | ✅ Available post-fire | Full population schedule; Soundex index survives |
| 1890 | ❌ Largely destroyed | Nationwide fire at NARA, 1921; Chicago schedules lost |

> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records* — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records

**Access:** Ancestry.com (subscription) — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | FamilySearch (free)

---

### 🏛️ Naturalization Records (Cook County Courts)
Cook County Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records **survived the fire from the 1840s onward** and are among the most valuable pre-fire sources for immigrant families. They often name the country or town of origin, witnesses, and family members.

- **Held at:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University
- **FamilySearch:** Has microfilmed many of these records
- **Access level:** Partial — check IRAD and FamilySearch

> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records* — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records

---

### 📖 City Directories (1839–)
Chicago city directories were published from **1839** onward and survived the fire because copies were held by publishers and in other locations. They list heads of household, occupations, and addresses — useful for placing a family in a neighborhood and tracking them year to year.

- **Held at:** **Newberry Library** (major collection) | Chicago History Museum | available digitally via Ancestry, Internet Archive
- **Access level:** Physical and digital

> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire* — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire

---

### ✝️ Church Records (pre-1871 survivors)
Some church registers survived because they were held at parish houses rather than the courthouse. Re-established parishes sometimes reconstructed earlier entries from memory, baptismal certificates in family hands, or diocesan copies. **These are the primary pre-fire vital substitute.**

**FamilySearch Collection (indexed + images):**
> **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925**
> Collection ID: 1803978 | ~285,000 records | Dates: 1833–1925
> Covers baptisms, marriages, and burials across multiple denominations for the full period before and after the fire.

- **Catholic parish registers:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds registers for parishes that survived or were reconstituted. The diocesan office often kept copies independent of the parish.
- **Other denominations:** Lutheran, Episcopal, Methodist, and other records vary; check the Newberry Library's denominational collections.

**Access level:** FamilySearch — **indexed + images** (collection 1803978)
Repository: Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic); Newberry Library (general Protestant)

---

### ⚖️ Pre-Fire Reconstructed Court Records (browse-only)
FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of **reconstructed copies of pre-fire county court records**:

> **Image Group 009982110** | 38 images | Coverage: Chicago, Cook County, 1865–1871
> Record type: Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)
> **recordSearchablePercent: 0% | fulltextSearchable: false**
> ⚠️ Browse-only — must be viewed image by image; no name index and no full-text search.

---

### 🗺️ Land / Property Records (pre-fire)
Most pre-fire deeds were destroyed. Substitutes:
- **Bureau of Land Management — General Land Office** (federal land patents): https://glorecords.blm.gov — original federal land grants are held here and were **not** destroyed
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company records** (insurance records documenting property ownership): held at the **Chicago History Museum** — a major substitute source for reconstructing who owned what before the fire

> Source: Wikipedia, *Great Chicago Fire* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire

---

## Part 2 — Post-Fire Records (from October 1871 onward)

Chicago rebuilt rapidly after the fire, and a new documentary record was created almost immediately.

### 📜 Vital Records (post-1871 Cook County)
Cook County began systematic local registration of births and deaths from 1871 onward:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Record Count | Date Range | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cook County Birth Certificates** | 2024189 | ~1,450,000 | 1871–1940 | Indexed + images |
| **Cook County Death Records** | 1913456 | ~980,000 | 1871–1947 | Indexed + images |
| **Cook County Marriage Records** | 1756321 | ~620,000 | 1871–1920 | Indexed + images |

- **Also held at:** Cook County Clerk's Office (originals and certified copies)
- **Note:** For births/deaths before 1916, Cook County's local registration is more complete than any state-level series, since statewide registration didn't begin until 1916.

---

### 🏠 Property Re-recordings (Burnt Record Act, 1872)
Under the Burnt Record Act of 1872, property owners had to re-register their deeds. This creates a substitute for destroyed pre-fire deeds and also documents exactly who was in Chicago at the time of the fire.

> **Image Group 009982111** | 112 images | Coverage: Chicago, Cook County, 1871–1880
> Record type: Post-fire Property Re-recordings
> **recordSearchablePercent: 41% | fulltextSearchable: false**
> ⚠️ Partially indexed — 41% of images are name-searchable; the rest must be browsed image by image.

This volume and the pre-fire reconstructed court record volume (009982110) together form a continuous record trail bridging the pre- and post-fire property landscape — work both together.

---

### 🪖 Military Records
Illinois soldiers in the Civil War (1861–65) are well documented. Service records, pension files, and regimental histories are relevant context for men who were in Chicago in 1871.

- **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/): service records and pension files
- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/): digitized military records
- **Illinois State Archives (Springfield):** adjutant general records and state military rosters

---

### ⚖️ Probate and Court Records (post-1871)
New probate files, guardianships, and court records began accumulating after the fire.

- **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University:** Cook County records post-1871
- **FamilySearch:** Microfilmed many post-fire Cook County records

---

### 📰 Newspapers
Chicago newspapers covered the fire extensively and published long lists of victims, survivors, missing persons, and relief recipients — an irreplaceable direct source for identifying affected families.

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/): historical Chicago Tribune and other papers
- **Chicago History Museum:** clipping files and special fire coverage collections
- **Newberry Library:** extensive newspaper holdings

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Post-fire vital records (collections 2024189, 1913456, 1756321); Church Records 1833–1925 (1803978); microfilmed naturalization and court records; 2 digitized volumes (image groups 009982110–11) | Free online |
| **Newberry Library** (newberry.org) | City directories (1839+), maps, manuscripts, denominational records, newspapers | In-person + partial digital |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, fire photographs, personal papers, newspaper clippings | In-person; some online |
| **IRAD — Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County records post-1871, naturalization records | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | By request |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward (certified copies) | By request / online portal |
| **Illinois State Archives, Springfield** | Military, state census fragments, land patents | In-person + partial digital |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal census, passenger lists, military service and pension files | In-person + Ancestry/FoldJ3 |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents (not destroyed by fire) | Free online |

> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories* — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories

---

## Quirks and Research Gotchas

1. **The 1870 federal census is your most important pre-fire document.** It was enumerated in June 1870 — 15 months before the fire — and the originals were in Washington, D.C. This is the closest official snapshot of Chicago families before the disaster.

2. **Illinois had NO statewide vital registration until 1916.** Cook County's local registration starts at 1871 (the fire). For any birth, marriage, or death before October 1871, you must use church records, census, city directories, or newspaper notices — no civil vital record will exist.

3. **The Burnt Record Act (1872) is not a mere formality.** It required all property owners to re-register their deeds from memory or secondary evidence. The resulting volume (image group 009982111, 41% indexed) documents Chicago property holders immediately after the fire and is a key post-fire starting point.

4. **Pre-fire court record volume (009982110) is browse-only.** The 38 images of reconstructed pre-fire court records have 0% name indexing and are not full-text searchable — plan to browse image by image.

5. **Church records bridge the fire gap.** Collection 1803978 (285,000 records, 1833–1925) is your best continuous source spanning the fire. Catholic parishes submitted copies to the Archdiocese, so diocesan holdings may survive even when the parish register itself burned.

6. **Naturalization records from Cook County courts survived from the 1840s** — one of the most valuable immigrant research sources for the pre-fire period. The IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University and FamilySearch microfilm are the access points.

7. **Newspaper lists of fire victims, missing persons, and relief recipients are primary genealogical sources** — the Chicago Tribune and other papers published extensive lists in October–November 1871. Newspapers.com and the Chicago History Museum are the best access points.

8. **The 1890 census is gone nationwide** (destroyed in a 1921 NARA fire, unrelated to the Chicago fire) — there is no federal census for Chicago between 1880 and 1900.

9. **Federal (not state/county) land patents survived intact** at the BLM General Land Office — original land grants predating the fire are fully accessible online.

10. **Insurance company records at the Chicago History Museum** (especially the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection) document pre-fire property ownership and are a major substitute for destroyed deeds.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence for Fire-Affected Families

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — your baseline pre-fire household snapshot
2. **Search post-fire vital records** (FamilySearch collections 2024189, 1913456, 1756321) to anchor the family in the post-fire period
3. **Search Chicago church records** (collection 1803978, 1833–1925) for births, marriages, and burials spanning the fire
4. **Check city directories** at the Newberry Library for pre-fire presence and post-fire continuity
5. **Search Cook County naturalization records** (IRAD / FamilySearch microfilm) for immigrant ancestors
6. **Browse the post-fire property re-recordings** (image group 009982111, 41% indexed) under the Burnt Record Act
7. **Browse the pre-fire reconstructed court records** (image group 009982110, browse-only) as a supplemental check
8. **Search October–November 1871 Chicago newspapers** for victim, survivor, or relief lists
9. **Contact the Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives** for Catholic parish registers not yet digitized
10. **Check the Chicago History Museum** for insurance records and fire-era personal papers

## 📜 Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s): Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Overview

The 1700s in Louisiana span **two successive colonial regimes**, which directly affects what records exist and where they are held:

| Period | Regime | Governing Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1699–1762 | **French colonial** | Conseil Supérieur (Superior Council) in New Orleans |
| 1762–1800 | **Spanish colonial** | Cabildo (Spanish municipal council); Spanish governors |
| 1800–1803 | French (briefly) | Retrocession; Louisiana Purchase 1803 |

France founded the colony c. 1699, established New Orleans in 1718, and governed under the **Code Noir**, which required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons and made the Catholic Church the only legally recognized church. In 1762 France ceded the territory to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau), shifting the administrative language from French to Spanish while Catholic parish infrastructure continued unbroken.

**Critical quirk for researchers:** Any family whose events straddle 1762 will appear in records held under two colonial regimes, in two languages (French pre-1762, Spanish post-1762). You must search both — they are not redundant but complementary.

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

#### 1. 🏛️ Catholic Parish Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
> *Primary vital record source — no civil registration existed in the 1700s*

- The Catholic Church was the **sole legally recognized church** during the French period; the Code Noir mandated baptism of enslaved persons, so enslaved ancestors often appear in registers under the enslaver's household.
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** holds registers beginning **1720** — the earliest surviving institutional records for the colony.
- **FamilySearch** has digitized these as **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** ([collection 1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)): ~987,654 records with ~493,827 images. This collection begins 1718 and covers the full French (and subsequent Spanish) colonial century. Records are in **French before 1762** and **Spanish after 1762** — the researcher must be able to read the original language or engage a translator.
- Records for parishes outside New Orleans (e.g., Natchitoches Post, Pointe Coupée, Mobile district) survive in varying states; some are held at local diocesan archives rather than FamilySearch.
- **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy: French Colonial Records (1699–1762)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)

---

#### 2. ⚖️ Superior Council Records (Conseil Supérieur)
> *French colonial court and administrative records — unique to the 1699–1762 period*

- The Superior Council was French Louisiana's governing body, producing **land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories** — a rich substitute for the formal probate and deed infrastructure that didn't yet exist.
- These records are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center**, located in the Old U.S. Mint building in New Orleans, and have been **partially digitized**. Contact the Louisiana Historical Center directly for access arrangements.
- For the Spanish colonial period (1762–1800), equivalent administrative records are held by the **Cabildo** (Spanish colonial council), also at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy: French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)

---

#### 3. 📋 Probate Records
> *Estate inventories, wills, guardianship — partially available on FamilySearch*

- **FamilySearch** collection **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** ([collection 2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)): ~456,789 records with ~228,394 images. The 1756 start date falls within the **French colonial period** (14 years before the Spanish takeover), making this a genuine colonial-era resource.
- Probate proceedings in colonial Louisiana were handled through the Superior Council (French period) and its Spanish successor. The FamilySearch collection bridges both regimes.
- Records are in French (pre-1762) and Spanish (post-1762).

---

#### 4. 📜 New Orleans Notarial Archives
> *Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions — from 1730s onward*

- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives** is the **oldest continuous notarial office in North America**, holding instruments from the **1730s** onward: property contracts, marriage settlements, wills, manumission documents, and commercial agreements.
- In French and Spanish law (which governed Louisiana), the notary was central to family property transactions in a way that has no direct English common-law equivalent — these records often contain detailed family relationships.
- Access: **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (physical repository; some records available on microfilm through FamilySearch).
- **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property: Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)

---

#### 5. 🌾 Land Records (Concessions & Grants)
> *French and Spanish colonial land grants follow civil-law traditions*

- French **concessions** and Spanish **land grants** followed civil law (not English common law). They are documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and in records at the **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge).
- The American State Papers are available online via the Library of Congress and Ancestry.com.
- French concession records also appear within Superior Council documents (see above).
- **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property: Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)

---

#### 6. 🇫🇷 Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), France
> *French administrative records — the metropolitan archive for the colony*

- The **ANOM** in Aix-en-Provence, France holds French colonial administrative correspondence, **census rolls (dénombrements)** for the colony, and military/militia records relating to Louisiana from the French period.
- Colonial censuses taken during French rule (several survive from the 1720s–1750s) enumerated free households and sometimes enslaved persons.
- The ANOM has an online portal ([anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)) where some finding aids and digitized documents are accessible. Physical or correspondence research may still be required for original documents.
- All records are in **French**; some require paleographic skill (17th–18th-century French script).
- **Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy: French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)

---

#### 7. 🪖 Military Records
> *Colonial militia and garrison records*

- French colonial militia and garrison records are held principally at the **ANOM** and at the **Archives nationales de France** (Paris, Série Colonies).
- Spanish colonial militia records (post-1762) may be held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain), which is the premier repository for Spanish colonial American records, with some finding aids available online.

---

#### 8. 👨‍👩‍👧 Colonial Census Rolls (Dénombrements)
> *Household enumerations — substitute for census records*

- Several colonial household censuses survive from the French period, taken in the 1720s–1750s. These named heads of household, free family members, enslaved persons, and sometimes livestock.
- Held at the **ANOM** (France). Some have been transcribed and published by Louisiana genealogical societies (e.g., Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society).

---

#### 9. ⛪ Acadian (Cajun) Records — If Applicable
> *Relevant for families arriving 1755–1785*

- If your ancestor was an Acadian refugee expelled from Nova Scotia (Grand Dérangement, 1755), their pre-Louisiana records are in **Nova Scotia/Canada** and **France** (port records at Saint-Malo, Rochefort, and Nantes).
- Acadian arrivals in Louisiana are documented in both French and Spanish colonial records and in published compilations such as **Bona Arsenault's *History and Genealogy of the Acadians***.

---

### FamilySearch Collections Overlapping the 1700s

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Louisiana, Church Records | [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) | 1718–1925 | ~987,654 | ~493,827 | Records + images on FamilySearch |
| Louisiana, Probate Records | [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) | 1756–1984 | ~456,789 | ~228,394 | Records + images on FamilySearch |

> Two other Louisiana collections on FamilySearch (Parish Marriages 1837–1957; Statewide Death Index 1819–1964) are **post-colonial** and do not apply to the 1700s.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Location | Primary Holdings for 1700s |
|---|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** | Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records, Spanish Cabildo records |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | New Orleans | Notarial acts from 1730s — contracts, wills, marriage settlements |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Baton Rouge | Colonial land concessions and grants |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** | Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls, military records |
| **Archivo General de Indias** | Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial (post-1762) administrative and military records |
| **FamilySearch** | Online | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984 |

---

### ⚠️ Key Quirks for Colonial Louisiana Research

1. **Two languages, two regimes.** French before 1762, Spanish 1762–1800. Search both eras' records — they are not redundant.
2. **No civil registration.** Catholic parish registers are the only official vital records. The Church was the sole recognized institution for births, marriages, and deaths.
3. **Code Noir baptism requirement.** Enslaved ancestors may appear in Catholic registers — often identified by first name only, with the enslaver's surname noted. This is frequently the only documentary trace.
4. **Civil-law property tradition.** Louisiana followed French/Spanish civil law, not English common law. Notarial records are far richer and more central to family research than in other US states.
5. **Records in foreign archives.** Major administrative records are in France (ANOM) and Spain (Archivo General de Indias) — essential for the colonial period and unavailable through most US-based databases.
6. **"Parishes" not counties.** Louisiana's colonial and ecclesiastical units were **posts** and **parishes**, not counties. This affects how records are filed and indexed.
7. **FamilySearch coverage gap.** FamilySearch has only 4 collections for Louisiana total; the 1700s are thinly indexed online. Expect significant physical or correspondence-based archival research for deep colonial work.

---

*Sources: [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy: French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records); [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Land and Property: Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants); [Wikipedia — French Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana); FamilySearch collections_search (scope: Louisiana).*

---

**Where to start:** Open FamilySearch's [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) and search by surname. Then contact the **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) about Superior Council records for any legal, property, or court event in your ancestor's life. For anyone whose story begins before 1762, the **ANOM** in France is the next essential stop.
