---

## 🏭 Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide
**Period: c. 1870–1900**

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania's **anthracite coal region** spans **Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties** in northeastern Pennsylvania. The **bituminous region** covers western Pennsylvania, principally Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, and Indiana counties.

**Critical boundary change:** Lackawanna County was carved out of Luzerne County in **1878**. If your ancestor lived in Scranton or surrounding towns before 1878, records will be filed under **Luzerne County**, not Lackawanna. Search both county series as one continuous trail.

Immigration drove explosive population growth: the region drew waves of **Irish, Welsh, and German** miners from the 1820s–1860s, followed by **Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian** immigrants from the 1880s–1900s. That ethnic sequence shapes which church and language records apply to your family.

---

### 1. 🪨 Mining-Specific Records *(unique to coal towns)*

These are the record classes you won't find elsewhere — start here if you know your ancestor was a miner.

| Record | What It Contains | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **State Mine Inspector Reports** (from 1870) | Fatal accident lists: name, age, nationality, cause of death, colliery | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Physical; published annual reports may be browsable in some libraries |
| **Mine Worker Employment Cards** (Schuylkill Co.) | Employee data 1870–1900; 410 images on FamilySearch, image group 002240015 | FamilySearch | **Indexed (95%) + full-text searchable** — searchable by name |
| **Mine Accident Reports** (Luzerne Co.) | Accident records 1870–1895; 287 images on FamilySearch, image group 002240016 | FamilySearch | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text; must be browsed image by image |
| **Colliery Payroll Ledgers** (Lackawanna Co.) | Pay records 1878–1900; 199 images on FamilySearch, image group 002240017 | FamilySearch | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text |
| **Company employment records** (payrolls, accident reports) | Survive fragmentarily for multiple collieries | Pennsylvania State Archives; Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Physical access; not digitized |
| **UMWA union records** (from 1890) | Membership rolls, grievance files of United Mine Workers of America | UMWA Archives; Pennsylvania State Archives | Physical; limited digitization |

> **FamilySearch note:** The statewide volume search returned 23 total digitized volumes for Pennsylvania 1870–1900; only the first page (3 volumes) was returned. There are likely additional volumes not shown here — browse FamilySearch's catalog under Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties directly to find them all.

---

### 2. ✝️ Church Records *(the primary vital record for 1870–1906)*

**Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906** ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)). For the entire 1870–1900 window, **church registers are your main source** for births, baptisms, marriages, and burials.

Ethnic parishes served specific mining communities — match the national origin of the family to the parish type:

| Ancestry | Denomination | Records Language |
|---|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic | Latin/English |
| Welsh | Congregational, Presbyterian, Methodist | English |
| German | Lutheran, German Reformed | German |
| Polish | Roman Catholic (Polish national parishes) | Polish/Latin |
| Lithuanian | Roman Catholic | Lithuanian/Latin |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic | Slovak/Latin |
| Italian | Roman Catholic | Italian/Latin |
| Ukrainian | Greek Catholic, Ukrainian Orthodox | Ukrainian/Church Slavonic |

> ⚠️ **Language warning:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian Catholic registers are in non-English. You will need to read or translate the original language to use these records.

**Where to find church records:**
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania Catholic and Protestant parish registers — search the FamilySearch catalog by county and town
- Diocesan archives (Diocese of Scranton, Diocese of Allentown, Diocese of Harrisburg) hold registers not microfilmed
- Local parishes may retain original registers

**FamilySearch collection:** [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — 524,189 records, 312,045 images. Overlaps the later part of the period.

---

### 3. 📋 Civil Vital Records

| Record | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Birth & death registration** | **None statewide before 1906** | Philadelphia registered from 1860; Allegheny County from 1870. For the coal counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland), no civil birth/death records exist before 1906 — use church records |
| **Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968** | Starts after the target period | [FamilySearch collection 2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) — 4.2 million records. Useful for miners who died in the early 1900s, often listing birthplace, parents, and cause of death |
| **Marriage licenses/bonds** | County level from colonial period | Held at county courthouse (Register of Deeds). FamilySearch collections cover parts of the period |
| [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 312,045 records | Overlaps the target period |
| [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 198,765 records — **no images** | Index only; compiled abstracts |

---

### 4. 🗺️ Federal Census Records

Federal census schedules (1870, 1880, 1900) are available and **list occupation as "miner"**, making coal families easy to identify. The 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire — it is a nearly complete gap.

| Census | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1870** | Lists all household members, birthplace, occupation |
| **1880** | Adds relationship to head of household; includes birthplace of parents |
| **1890** | Destroyed — essentially no records survive for most families |
| **1900** | Adds month/year of birth, years in the US, naturalization status, and number of children |
| **Mortality Schedules, 1870–1885** | List deaths in the year preceding enumeration — valuable for miners killed in accidents. Available on Ancestry and FamilySearch |

---

### 5. 🚢 Immigration & Naturalization

Immigration records are **essential** for coal mining families — most workers in the 1870–1900 period arrived from abroad.

| Record | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Passenger lists** | Philadelphia and New York were primary ports of entry | NARA; indexed on Ancestry ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) and FamilySearch |
| **Naturalization petitions & declarations of intent** | Pre-1906: filed in any court of record — county courts of common pleas, federal district courts | **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are at the Pennsylvania State Archives ([wiki source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)) |
| **County naturalization records** | Luzerne and Lackawanna counties — at respective county courthouses and Pennsylvania State Archives | Physical; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |

> ⚠️ **Pre-1906 naturalization quirk:** Before the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization was established in 1906, a miner could naturalize in *any* court of record — local, state, or federal. Check the county court of common pleas for the county where the miner lived, not just federal courts.

---

### 6. ⚖️ Probate, Court & Land Records

Held at the **county Register of Wills** (probate) and **county courthouse** (deeds, court records) from each county's date of formation.

| Record | FamilySearch Collection | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Probate records** | [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records | Wills, inventories, administrations, guardianships — valuable for tracing heirs and assets |
| **Deed / land records** | County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives Land Office holds original warrants/patents | Miners often rented company housing, but some purchased land |
| **Tax records** | County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives | Assessment lists serve as census substitutes and can place a family in a specific township |
| **Court records** | County courthouse | Naturalization petitions (pre-1906), guardianship, name changes |

---

### 7. 🎖️ Military Records

Many coal miners were veterans of the Civil War (1861–1865) or had sons who served in the Spanish-American War (1898).

- **Civil War service & pension records**: NARA ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/), [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) — pension files contain detailed family information including wife's maiden name, children, and physical description
- **Pennsylvania Civil War muster rolls**: Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Spanish-American War draft and muster**: NARA

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers & Cemetery Records

| Source | Notes |
|---|---|

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts — Early Colonial Period (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628. The two colonies merged in 1691 to form the **Province of Massachusetts Bay** under a new royal charter.
- **Administrative centers:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of England / Crown (post-1691: Province under English Crown)
- **Population during period:** No census data available for this period; the Great Migration of 1630–1640 brought approximately 20,000 settlers. Population grew steadily through the century.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, fur trade, timber, and early mercantile trade
- **Ethnic/national composition:** Overwhelmingly English; very small numbers of other Europeans and enslaved Africans by late 1600s
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) — the established church of both colonies; small numbers of Anglicans, Quakers (largely persecuted), Baptists
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630–1643); Pequot War (1637); King Philip's War (1675–1676); King William's War (1689–1697); merger of colonies (1691)

---

## Boundary changes

- **1620:** Plymouth Colony established — covers southeastern Massachusetts and Cape Cod. Its records are a **separate jurisdiction** from Massachusetts Bay, published independently, and must be searched separately.
- **1628/1630:** Massachusetts Bay Colony established — covers Boston and surrounding settlements.
- **1643:** Four original counties created within Massachusetts Bay: **Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Norfolk**. Probate, land, and court records are organized at the county level from this point.
- **1685:** Three new counties carved out: **Plymouth, Bristol, and Barnstable** — covering territory that had been Plymouth Colony.
- **1691:** Plymouth Colony absorbed into Massachusetts Bay under the new Province of Massachusetts Bay charter. After 1691, all records are unified under one provincial jurisdiction, though county-level organization continues.

> **Critical quirk:** If you do not know whether your ancestor lived in Plymouth Colony or Massachusetts Bay Colony territory, you must search **both** record sets for the pre-1691 period. Records from each colony are held and published separately.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (town-level registration)

- **Start date — town level:** The General Court of Massachusetts Bay mandated that town clerks record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)). This is **town-level** registration, not statewide. Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1841.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by individual town clerks; quality and completeness vary by town and decade. Earlier records (1620s–1630s) are sparser; coverage improves through the mid-1600s.
- **Published compilations:** The multi-volume **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series (Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is the standard starting point. Available at NEHGS, many research libraries, and partially on FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — **3,456,789 records / 1,728,394 images** — **Indexed + images**
- **Plymouth Colony vitals:** Recorded separately; published in the *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (12-volume series). Search these independently for pre-1691 Plymouth territory.
- **Gaps:** Some towns have no surviving records for the earliest decades; fire and loss account for occasional gaps.

### Church records

- **Denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) meetings were the dominant and established church. As the only legally recognized church through most of the 1600s, church membership and vital events were recorded in Congregational registers. Quakers kept their own meeting records (though suppressed early on); small Baptist congregations formed by the 1660s–1670s.
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments) — all genealogically valuable.
- **Published records:** Many early Congregational church records have been published in the *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* series and in local historical society publications.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — **987,654 records / 493,827 images** — **Indexed + images**
- **Where held:** Original registers at individual churches; microfilm and digitized copies at NEHGS and FamilySearch. Denominational archives at various repositories.
- **Language:** English

> **Tip:** For early Puritan families, Congregational church records are often the richest source for family relationships, dates, and community context — especially when town clerk records are missing.

### Census records

- **No census records exist for this period.** The first federal census was 1790; Massachusetts state censuses began later.
- **Substitutes:** Tax lists, militia muster rolls, church membership lists, and town meeting records serve as population surrogates. Plymouth Colony conducted occasional enumerations of men able to bear arms.

### Probate and court records

- **Probate records begin in the 1630s** at county probate courts — among the earliest surviving probate records in North America ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)).
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate), inventories of personal property, guardianships, estate accounts.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — **567,890 records / 283,945 images** — available on FamilySearch; check individual volumes for name-indexing vs. browse-only status.
- **County organization:** Filed at the county level — Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk (from 1643); Plymouth, Bristol, Barnstable (from 1685). Search the county where your ancestor lived.
- **Colonial court records:** The General Court (legislature/high court), county courts, and Courts of General Sessions generated civil and criminal records documenting disputes, land disputes, and administrative actions. These are at the **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) and have been partially published and microfilmed ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Military and Court Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)).
- **Plymouth Colony probate:** Held separately; published in *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth*.

### Land records

- **System:** Metes and bounds (not rectangular survey — Massachusetts is an original colony)
- **Start date:** County registries of deeds hold records from the **1630s** onward in remarkably complete runs ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages. Town proprietors' records document the original laying out of lots to founding settlers — an important source for the earliest residents.
- **Where held:** **County registries of deeds** (one per county, at county seat). Many early deed books have been microfilmed by FamilySearch; some are digitized online. Original volumes remain at county registries.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Document land divisions to original settlers; held in town archives or published in local histories — a critical source for the 1620s–1640s settlers.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts in this period:**
  - **King Philip's War (1675–1676):** The most destructive war in colonial New England. Militia muster rolls and lists of men killed or captured survive.
  - **King William's War (1689–1697):** Colonial forces mobilized against French Canada.
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, pay vouchers, lists of participants — partially published and available at the **Massachusetts Archives**.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); partially published by the Massachusetts Historical Society and other scholarly series.
- **Note:** There were no formal pension or bounty land systems in the colonial period. Service is documented mainly through colonial legislative and administrative records.

### Cemetery records

- **Church burial grounds** were the primary burial sites; Congregational meetinghouses typically had adjacent graveyards.
- **Online coverage:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many historic New England cemeteries, including gravestone transcriptions and photographs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records (where they survive) are held by individual town or church archives. Many early gravestone inscriptions have been transcribed and published in local histories and cemetery surveys.
- **Colonial gravestone surveys:** The Association for Gravestone Studies has documented many early New England stones.

### Passenger and immigration records

- **FamilySearch passenger list collection** ([Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312)) covers **1820–1891 only** — it does **not** cover the 1620–1700 period.
- **For colonial-era arrivals:** Published ship passenger lists are the primary resource:
  - *The Great Migration: Immigrants to New England, 1620–1643* — NEHGS multi-volume scholarly study documenting every known settler; available at NEHGS and research libraries.
  - Published colonial-era passenger lists in the NEHGS *Register* and in Coldham's *Complete Book of Emigrants*.
  - Winthrop's fleet (1630) and other voyages are documented in published histories and NEHGS finding aids.
- **Where held:** NEHGS (Boston); published volumes in research libraries; partial digitization online.

### Tax records

- **Colonial tax records** include both poll taxes and property valuations.
- **Town and colony level** — assessment lists and rate books survive for many towns from the mid-1600s onward.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); town archives; partially published in local histories.
- **Substitute value:** Tax and rate lists can substitute for the missing census, establishing residence and relative wealth.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Every Massachusetts town maintained meeting records documenting admissions of inhabitants, land grants, appointments, and local governance from the founding of each town. These name every participating adult male resident. Held at **town archives** (town clerk's office); some published.
- **Great Migration Study Series (NEHGS):** A definitive scholarly reconstruction of every known immigrant to New England 1620–1643, with full source citations, family reconstruction, and English origins when known. **Essential first stop** for any family arriving in this period.
- **Colonial Society of Massachusetts / Massachusetts Historical Society publications:** Hundreds of volumes of published transcripts of court records, church records, correspondence, and legislative proceedings.
- **Deposition records:** Court depositions (especially in land disputes and defamation cases) frequently record ages, family relationships, and community knowledge. Found in colonial court records at Massachusetts Archives.

---

---

## Records NOT online (or not fully online)

- **Town meeting records and town proprietors' records** — most remain in individual town archives; some published, many not digitized.
- **County deed books (pre-1700)** — microfilmed by FamilySearch but many early volumes are browse-only, not name-indexed.
- **Colonial court records** (General Court, county courts) — largely in the Massachusetts Archives; partially published, partially on FamilySearch microfilm, but not comprehensively indexed online.
- **Congregational church records** — many individual church registers have not been digitized; published volumes in libraries.
- **Colonial-era passenger lists** — the FamilySearch passenger list collection starts 1820; pre-1700 arrivals must be traced through published scholarly compilations (NEHGS Great Migration study, Coldham's emigrants volumes).

---

## Known record losses

- Some town records were lost or damaged during King Philip's War (1675–1676), when numerous towns were burned or attacked.
- Early records for some towns with short-lived settlements simply were never created or did not survive.
- Plymouth Colony records for the very earliest years (1620–1627) are sparse; the most complete run begins with the formal establishment of colonial governance.
- No courthouse fires of the magnitude seen in southern states affected colonial Massachusetts records, making this **one of the most intact early record jurisdictions in America**.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the Great Migration study.** If your ancestor arrived before 1643, the NEHGS *Great Migration* series ([AmericanAncestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org)) gives a fully sourced family reconstruction and, often, the English place of origin.

2. **Plymouth Colony is a separate jurisdiction.** Pre-1691 Plymouth Colony records (southeastern MA, Cape Cod) are published in *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Always determine which colony your ancestor resided in before 1691. ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial))

3. **Town vital records were mandated at the town level from 1639** — not at the state level. Statewide registration began in 1841. For your target period, search the individual town's records. Published Vital Records to 1850 volumes exist for over 200 towns. ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

4. **Congregational church records parallel — and sometimes predate — town vital records.** A Puritan family that appears incomplete in town records should be cross-checked against the Congregational meeting records, which often supply baptism dates, membership lists, and family relationships. ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))

5. **Search probate and land records together.** Colonial wills and estate inventories name heirs, relationships, and neighbors. Land deeds frequently name family members in grantee relationships. Both series run from the 1630s and are remarkably well-preserved. ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial))

6. **County organization is the key to routing searches.** Probate, land, and court records are organized at the county level. Know which county your ancestor's town fell under — and note that county boundaries shifted in 1685 when Plymouth, Bristol, and Barnstable Counties were established.

7. **King Philip's War records (1675–1676)** — militia rolls and casualty lists are at the Massachusetts Archives and partially published. If your ancestor was an adult male in the 1670s, there is a high probability of a militia record. ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Military and Court Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military))

8. **Court depositions are an underused source.** Colonial court proceedings frequently record ages, family relationships, residency history, and community testimony — use them to reconstruct life events not captured in vital or church records.

9. **Efficient research sequence for this period:** Great Migration study → Vital Records to 1850 series → Congregational church records → Probate records (county) → Land deeds (county) → Town meeting / proprietors' records → Colonial court records (Massachusetts Archives) → Military records if 1675–1700.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts — Early Colonial Period (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628. Merged in 1691 to form Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **Administrative centers:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Population:** Great Migration 1630–1640 brought ~20,000 settlers; no census data for this period
- **Religion:** Congregational (Puritan) — established church; small numbers of Quakers, Baptists by late 1600s
- **Key events:** Great Migration (1630–1643); Pequot War (1637); King Philip's War (1675–1676); King William's War (1689–1697); merger of colonies (1691)

## Boundary changes
- 1620: Plymouth Colony — southeastern MA, Cape Cod. Separate jurisdiction; records published independently.
- 1628/1630: Massachusetts Bay Colony — Boston and surrounding settlements.
- 1643: Four original counties created: Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk. Probate, land, court records organized at county level from this point.
- 1685: Plymouth, Bristol, Barnstable counties carved out of Plymouth Colony territory.
- 1691: Plymouth Colony absorbed into Province of Massachusetts Bay. All records unified after this date.

**Critical:** For pre-1691 research, determine which colony your ancestor lived in and search that jurisdiction's separate records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (town-level registration)
- **Start date:** Town level from **1639** (mandated by General Court); **statewide** registration began 1841 only
- **FamilySearch:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — 3,456,789 records / 1,728,394 images — **Indexed + images**
- **Published series:** "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" (Tanner-Corbin) covers 200+ towns
- **Plymouth Colony vitals:** Published separately in *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (12 vols)

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) — the established and dominant church; Quaker meeting records; Baptist from 1660s–70s
- **FamilySearch:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — 987,654 records / 493,827 images — **Indexed + images**
- Many records also published in Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society volumes
- Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)

### Census records
- **No census records for this period.** Federal census begins 1790.
- **Substitutes:** Tax lists, militia muster rolls, church membership lists, town meeting records

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — 567,890 records / 283,945 images
- Filed at county level (search by county of residence)
- Colonial court records (General Court, county courts, Courts of General Sessions): Massachusetts Archives, Boston; partially published
- Plymouth Colony probate: published in *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth*
- Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)

### Land records
- **System:** Metes and bounds
- **Start:** County registries of deeds from **1630s** onward in remarkably complete runs
- Town proprietors' records document original land grants to founding settlers — held in town archives, some published
- Many early deed books microfilmed by FamilySearch; originals at county registries of deeds

### Military records
- King Philip's War (1675–1676): militia muster rolls and casualty lists at Massachusetts Archives; partially published
- King William's War (1689–1697): colonial forces documented in Massachusetts Archives records
- Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Military and Court Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)

### Cemetery records
- Church burial grounds were primary sites adjacent to meetinghouses
- [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) — transcriptions and photographs for many historic New England cemeteries
- Association for Gravestone Studies has documented many early New England stones

### Immigration/passenger records
- **FamilySearch Passenger Lists start 1820 — does not cover colonial period**
- For 1620–1700 arrivals: NEHGS *Great Migration* study (every known settler 1620–1643 with full sources); Coldham's *Complete Book of Emigrants*; published fleet lists (Winthrop's fleet, etc.)
- Available at NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org and research libraries

### Tax records
- Colonial poll and property assessment lists from mid-1600s onward
- Held at Massachusetts Archives and town archives; partially published
- Substitute for missing census; establishes residence and relative wealth

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Name all adult male residents; document land grants and governance from each town's founding. Held at town clerk offices; some published.
- **Great Migration Study (NEHGS):** Definitive scholarly reconstruction of every known immigrant 1620–1643. Essential first stop.
- **Court depositions:** Record ages, family relationships, residence history. Found in colonial court records at Massachusetts Archives.
- **Colonial Society of Massachusetts / Massachusetts Historical Society publications:** Hundreds of volumes of published transcripts.

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620–1890; Church Records 1630–1920; Probate Records 1635–1991 | Free |
| NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org | Great Migration study, Vital Records to 1850, NEHGS Register, manuscripts | Subscription |
| Ancestry.com | MA vital, probate, land record digitizations | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| Fold3 | Colonial-era military records | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony records from 1620s; court records; military rolls; tax lists | In-person; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| NEHGS, Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study; manuscripts | In-person; online via AmericanAncestors.org |
| Massachusetts Historical Society | Colonial correspondence, diaries, published documentary series | In-person; some digitized |
| County registries of deeds | Deed books from 1630s (one per county) | In-person at county seat; some microfilmed |
| County probate courts | Probate files from 1630s | In-person; FamilySearch microfilm/digitization |
| Town clerk offices | Town vital records and town meeting records | In-person; many published or microfilmed |

## Records NOT online
- Town meeting and proprietors' records — mostly in individual town archives
- County deed books pre-1700 — microfilmed but largely browse-only
- Colonial court records — Massachusetts Archives; partially published, not comprehensively indexed
- Most individual Congregational church registers not fully digitized
- Colonial-era passenger lists — must use published scholarly compilations

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675–1676) destroyed records in several burned towns
- Earliest Plymouth Colony records (1620–1627) are sparse
- Massachusetts is overall one of the most intact early record jurisdictions in America

## Research tips
1. Start with the Great Migration study for any ancestor arriving before 1643
2. Plymouth Colony (pre-1691) is a separate jurisdiction — determine colony membership before routing searches
3. Town vital registration began 1639 at town level; statewide registration only from 1841 — always search individual town records
4. Congregational church records parallel town records; cross-check both for Puritan families
5. Search probate and land records together — wills name heirs; deeds name family members
6. Know the county of residence for routing probate, land, and court record searches
7. King Philip's War militia rolls document virtually all adult males in the 1670s
8. Efficient sequence: Great Migration study → Vital Records to 1850 → Church records → Probate → Land deeds → Town meeting records → Colonial court records → Military records

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / State of Oklahoma (1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory organized **May 2, 1890** under the Organic Act of Congress, carved from the former Unassigned Lands of Indian Territory. Oklahoma achieved statehood **November 16, 1907**, combining Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east).
- **Administrative centers:** Guthrie was the territorial capital (1890–1910); Oklahoma City became the state capital in 1910.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before 1890, the Unassigned Lands were administered directly by the U.S. federal government. Indian Territory (eastern half) had no territorial government and was governed through the Five Civilized Tribes' own national governments under federal supervision.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this fixture; however, the Land Run of 1889 alone drew an estimated **50,000 participants** racing to claim roughly **2 million acres** (Wikipedia). By 1900, Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory combined held over 790,000 people (federal census).
- **Economy:** Subsistence homesteading, cattle ranching, and early agriculture (cotton in the south, wheat in the north). The Five Tribes in Indian Territory also had coal mining operations. Oil was discovered at Bartlesville in 1897 and became economically dominant near statehood.
- **Ethnic composition:** The settler population came overwhelmingly from **Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas**. African American "Exodusters" and freedmen from the Five Tribes formed significant communities (several all-Black towns were founded in Indian Territory). The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole — occupied Indian Territory under their own governance.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian missions had operated in Indian Territory decades before the Land Run. After 1889, congregations of these denominations plus Quakers, Catholics, and smaller groups established quickly in the new towns.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889; additional land runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened the Cherokee Outlet and other areas; Dawes Commission enrollment of tribal members (1898–1914); statehood 1907.

---

## Boundary changes

This is a **two-phase jurisdictional split** that directly affects which repository holds a given record:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Authority |
|--------|-------------|-----------|
| Pre-1890 | Unassigned Lands / Indian Territory | U.S. federal government (GLO, Department of the Interior) |
| 1890–1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** (west) + **Indian Territory** (east, still no territorial govt.) | Territorial courts under federal supervision; Five Tribes' national courts in I.T. |
| 1907– | State of Oklahoma | State of Oklahoma; NARA holds earlier territorial records |

> **Critical quirk:** Before 1907, Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were **legally separate jurisdictions** with separate court systems and separate record series. A family in Muskogee (Indian Territory) will appear in entirely different records than a family in Guthrie (Oklahoma Territory). Determine which territory your ancestor was in before routing your search.

---

## Available record types

### 🏆 Federal land / homestead records — *the premier source for Land Run families*

- **System:** Federal rectangular survey (public-land state). The General Land Office administered all claims.
- **What exists:** Homestead applications, proof-of-settlement affidavits (with named witnesses), final patents, and — importantly — **rejected applications**, which also survive and can contain detailed family information. Land offices opened at **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher** in April 1889; additional offices opened as subsequent land runs proceeded.
- **Where held:**
  - **NARA Washington, D.C.** — Record Group 49 (General Land Office case files); the full homestead case file, not just the patent, lives here.
  - **BLM General Land Office Records website** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free, searchable index of patents with images; start here.
  - **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (Collection ID 1541872): **234,567 records / 117,283 images**, indexed + images. ([familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872))
- **Digitization level:** **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch; full patents free on BLM GLO; NARA case files require an in-person visit or paid copy request.
- **Research note:** The FamilySearch wiki confirms homestead files typically include the original application, proof of settlement with witnesses, and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive ([Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)).

---

### Census records

- **1890 federal census:** The national 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921. However, **Oklahoma Territory has a surviving 1890 special census** — one of the rarest 1890 census survivals in the nation. Held by the **Oklahoma Historical Society**; FamilySearch has partial coverage. This is a critical document for Land Run families.
- **1900 federal census:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were enumerated as **separate entities** in 1900 — search both. Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1910 federal census:** Oklahoma is enumerated as a state. Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **County/territorial censuses:** County-level tax rolls and some territorial enumerations from the 1890s survive and help document early settlers in intercensal years. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds many of these ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)).

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Statewide registration:** Oklahoma did **not** have statewide civil registration until **1908** (one year after statehood). Before that, there was no systematic territorial requirement.
- **What exists before 1908:** Marriage records begin at the **county level from 1890** when counties were formally organized under the territorial government. Birth and death registration before 1908 is largely absent or fragmentary.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (Collection ID 2134789): **456,789 records / 228,394 images**, indexed + images. ([familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789))
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below), family bibles, and newspaper notices are the main substitutes for births and deaths before 1908.
- **Where held:** County clerks' offices; FamilySearch has the digitized county marriage series.

---

### Church / mission records

- **Context:** Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian missions operated in Indian Territory for decades before the Land Run. After April 1889, new congregations formed rapidly in settler towns — though records begin sporadically ([Oklahoma Territorial Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)).
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (Collection ID 1654321): **123,456 records / 61,728 images**, indexed + images. ([familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321))
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized); individual denominational archives; Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Language:** English.

---

### Indian censuses, tribal rolls, and Dawes Roll

- **Context:** Any family with Native American ancestry — or any settler family living within Indian Territory — needs these records.
- **Dawes Roll (1898–1914):** The definitive enrollment of members of the Five Civilized Tribes, required for allotment. Includes name, age, sex, and blood degree. Essential for Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole ancestry.
- **Annual Indian censuses:** Federal agents enumerated tribal members annually.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (Collection ID 1987432): **567,890 records / 283,945 images**, indexed + images. ([familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432))
- **Other holdings:** The **Five Civilized Tribes Agency records** are at NARA Fort Worth (Record Group 75).

---

### Territorial and court records

- **Territorial district courts (Oklahoma Territory, 1890–1907):** Handled civil, criminal, probate, and naturalization cases. Records are at **NARA at Fort Worth, Texas** and the **Oklahoma State Archives**.
- **U.S. Court for the Indian Territory (Indian Territory, 1890–1907):** Headquartered in Muskogee; separate from the Oklahoma Territory court system. Records also at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Naturalization:** Before September 27, 1906, any court of record could naturalize — meaning declarations of intention and petitions may be filed in territorial district courts. Check NARA Fort Worth for these.
- **Probate:** Filed at the district court level in the territorial period; transferred to county district courts after 1907.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical only** or **microfilm** at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives; limited online availability ([Oklahoma Territorial Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)).

---

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War veterans were heavily represented among 1889 settlers (many were Union veterans using land-run rights). Spanish-American War (1898) drew Oklahoma Territory volunteers. WWI draft (1917–1918) covers sons of Land Run settlers.
- **Where held:**
  - NARA Washington, D.C.: Civil War service records and pension files (free on Fold3 for some series; Ancestry).
  - **Fold3** (subscription): Digitized pension files, service records, draft registrations — [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)
  - **Oklahoma State Archives:** State adjutant general records for Oklahoma National Guard.

---

### Cemetery records

- **Online:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com) has broad Oklahoma coverage, including many early homestead-era burials. Many early cemeteries were established on or near homestead claims.
- **Physical:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held by local governments or historical societies.
- **Note:** Early graves on homestead land may be unlisted in any database — land records (survey plats) sometimes note the location of family burial plots.

---

### Newspaper records

- **Context:** Towns established in the 1889 Land Run (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Norman, Oklahoma City, Stillwater) founded newspapers almost immediately. These carry land-claim notices, probate legal notices, marriage announcements, and obituaries.
- **Where held:**
  - [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) (subscription): Historical Oklahoma newspapers.
  - **Oklahoma Department of Libraries — Oklahoma Digital Prairie**: Free digitized Oklahoma newspapers.
  - **Oklahoma Historical Society**: Large newspaper microfilm collection.

---

### Tax records

- **What exists:** County-level property tax rolls from the 1890s onward document settlers in the territorial period. These substitute for census gaps and confirm residence.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; county clerks' offices; Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical or microfilm only**.

---

### Immigration and naturalization

- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any territorial or federal court of record — check NARA Fort Worth's territorial court records. Post-1906, naturalization was centralized through the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization (NARA).
- **Origins research:** The wiki confirms that many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states — tracing them requires searching **departure-state records** before turning to Oklahoma sources ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)).

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Early Land Records 1834–1907 (234K records); Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959 (568K records); County Marriages 1890–1995 (457K records); Mission & Church Records 1820–1965 (123K records) | Free |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Oklahoma land patents — indexed + images | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1900, 1910); various Oklahoma collections | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records, pensions, WWI draft | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Some digitized federal records; online ordering portal | Free / fee for copies |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** | RG 49 — GLO homestead case files (the full file, not just the patent) | In-person or paid copy request |
| **NARA at Fort Worth, TX** | Oklahoma & Indian Territory court records (1890–1907); Five Civilized Tribes Agency records (RG 75) | In-person or written request |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City** | 1890 territorial census; county tax rolls; newspapers; early state records | In-person; some digitized |
| **Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City** | Territorial and state government records; court records | In-person / online request |
| **County courthouses** | Marriage licenses (from 1890), deed books, probate files | In-person / mail |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Full homestead case files** (NARA RG 49): Only the patent is free online via BLM GLO. The underlying application and proof-of-settlement file — often containing the most genealogical detail — must be ordered from NARA Washington.
- **Territorial court records** (NARA Fort Worth): Civil, criminal, probate, and pre-1906 naturalization records from Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory district courts are largely microfilm or physical only.
- **County tax rolls (1890s):** Largely held physically at the Oklahoma Historical Society and county repositories.
- **Most early church registers:** Individual congregation records from 1889–1900 are not broadly digitized; contact the Oklahoma Historical Society or relevant denominational archives.

---

## Known record losses and gaps

- **1890 federal census:** The national enumeration was largely destroyed by fire in 1921. The **Oklahoma Territory 1890 special census is a rare exception** and survives — use it. Indian Territory was not covered by a similar survivor.
- **Vital records before 1908:** No statewide birth or death registration existed in the territorial period; county-level recording was inconsistent before statehood. Church and newspaper records are the primary substitutes.
- **Early county records:** Some territorial-era county records were poorly preserved when counties reorganized at statehood.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start at BLM GLO** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) for any Land Run ancestor — the patent is free and names the patentee, legal description, and date. Then order the full homestead case file from NARA for the settlement proof with witnesses.

2. **Know your territory.** Oklahoma Territory (west, organized 1890) and Indian Territory (east, governed by Five Tribes) were separate jurisdictions with separate records until 1907. The 1900 federal census enumerates them separately — search both.

3. **Trace the origin state first.** The wiki confirms most settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)). Identifying where the family lived before 1889 often unlocks birth, marriage, and earlier census records that Oklahoma itself cannot provide.

4. **The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is irreplaceable.** It is one of very few surviving 1890 census-era records in the entire country and specifically documents the first wave of Land Run settlers. Check the Oklahoma Historical Society and FamilySearch for coverage.

5. **Contested "Sooner" claims and rejected homestead applications** survive in the NARA GLO case files and may also appear in territorial district court litigation — both can contain richer family detail than a straight patent record.

6. **For any family with Native American ancestry or who lived in Indian Territory**, the Dawes Roll (FamilySearch collection 1987432) and NARA Fort Worth's Five Civilized Tribes Agency records (RG 75) are mandatory stops, not optional ones.

7. **Pre-1906 naturalizations** can appear in any territorial district court — check NARA Fort Worth before assuming the record is in a federal naturalization series.

8. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Oklahoma** returned only generic content in this survey — consult the [Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records) and [Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records) pages directly for the most current guidance on holdings and digitization status.

---

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1780–1819 (Pre-Statehood / Mississippi Territory Era)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Around 1800, present-day Alabama was not yet a separate political entity. The full succession that produced its records is:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French Louisiana / Mobile District | Mobile founded 1702 |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | Mobile area only |
| 1780–1798 | Spanish Mobile District | Upper areas still contested |
| **1798–1817** | **Mississippi Territory** | All of present-day AL + MS combined |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Separated from Mississippi |
| Dec. 1819+ | State of Alabama | Statehood |

*(Sources: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama; FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*

**Key county formations within present-day Alabama during the target period:**
- **Washington County** (est. 1800) — the first Alabama county; covers the Mobile / southwest Alabama area; the only Alabama county with records before 1808
- **Madison County** (est. 1808) — north Alabama, Tennessee Valley
- **Baldwin County** (est. 1809) — southwest Alabama, east of Mobile Bay
- **Clarke County** (est. 1812) — central southwest Alabama

**Critical regional split:** Mobile area (southwest) and north Alabama are essentially *two different research problems*. Mobile has Catholic colonial registers back to 1702. North Alabama was largely Creek and Cherokee territory in 1800 — virtually no European/American records exist there before 1808, and settlement only boomed after the Creek War of 1813–1814.

**Spanish Mobile:** Mobile remained under Spanish control until **1813**, even though the rest of the Mississippi Territory became American in 1798. Mobile-area records from 1780–1813 are Spanish colonial records, not U.S. territorial records.

---

## Record Types, Availability, and Access

### 1. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**No statewide civil registration existed.** Alabama did not require statewide vital registration until 1908. For 1800, births, marriages, and deaths are documented *only* in church registers and county marriage books (from county organization onward), or inferred from land, probate, and census records.

**County marriage registers** begin when each county was organized:
> **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* — Collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) — 612,345 records / 306,172 images — **Digitization level: Indexed + images.** The earliest marriages in this collection date to 1809, coinciding with the first county organization in north and south Alabama.

For vital events before 1809, or in any area without a county court, church records are the only surviving source (see §4 below).

---

### 2. Census and Population Records

**Federal census:** The 1810 federal census (Mississippi Territory) and 1820 census (Alabama, first year of statehood) are the earliest federal enumerations covering present-day Alabama. The 1810 census covers Washington County and the newly organized territories; most of north Alabama was not yet enumerated as settled territory.

**Territorial censuses (critical for c. 1800):** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that Mississippi Territory censuses for **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*

> **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* — Collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) — 287,634 records — **Digitization level: Name-indexed; no images attached.**

> **FamilySearch collection (Mississippi-side):** *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* — Collection [1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) — 198,340 records — **Digitization level: Name-indexed; no images.** Because Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory through 1817, pre-1817 records may appear here.

**Tax lists as census substitutes:** Territorial-period tax lists (especially Washington County from c. 1800, Madison County from c. 1808) survive at ADAH and function as the best census substitute when no federal enumeration exists for an area. These are largely physical/microfilm at ADAH; check their online catalog at https://www.alabamaarchives.gov.

---

### 3. Land Records — The Richest Pre-Statehood Source

For families who owned or claimed land, land records predate nearly every other American-era record type. Multiple systems operated simultaneously:

**a) Federal land patents (BLM GLO):** After the U.S. acquired the territory, federal patents were issued through land offices at St. Stephens (southwest Alabama, from c. 1800s) and Huntsville (north Alabama, from 1811). These are the first surviving U.S.-government record for many families.
> **Access:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office Records — https://glorecords.blm.gov — fully digitized, free, name-searchable. **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**

**b) Spanish and British colonial grants (Mobile area):** The FamilySearch Wiki identifies colonial-era land grants as the earliest land records for present-day Alabama. Spanish records of the Mobile District (including land grants) are held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

**c) Mississippi Territory-era land records:**
> **FamilySearch collection:** *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* — Collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) — 312,450 records / 156,225 images — **Digitization level: Indexed + images.** This collection covers the Mississippi Territory period and will include pre-1817 Alabama land records under the territorial name.

---

### 4. Church Records

**Catholic (Mobile area):** The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, Mobile, holds sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) reaching back into the Spanish and French colonial periods — the oldest continuous church registers in present-day Alabama. Pre-1763 registers are in French; 1780–1813 registers are largely in Spanish and Latin.

**Baptist and Methodist (American settlements):** Protestant settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after c. 1800 brought frontier churches with them. Individual congregation records from the territorial period are scattered among state and denominational archives, often surviving only in physical or microfilm form.

> **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* — Collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) — 156,789 records / 78,394 images — **Digitization level: Indexed + images.** Earliest entries begin at 1803. This is the primary FamilySearch source for early Protestant church registers in Alabama.

⚠️ **Language note:** Mobile-area Catholic registers in French (pre-1763) and Spanish (1780–1813) require reading in those original languages.

---

### 5. Probate Records

> **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* — Collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) — 438,210 records / 219,105 images — **Digitization level: Indexed + images.** Earliest entries date to 1809, matching the earliest functioning county probate courts.

For pre-1809 probate matters (Washington County, est. 1800), records would have been handled by the territorial court. Physical records at ADAH or Washington County Courthouse.

---

### 6. Court Records

Territorial courts handled civil/criminal matters, naturalizations, and guardianship. Washington County's court records from 1800 are the earliest; Madison County's from 1808.

> **FamilySearch collection:** *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* — Collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) — 245,670 records / 122,835 images — **Digitization level: Indexed + images.** Because Alabama was Mississippi Territory through 1817, early Alabama court proceedings may appear here alongside Mississippi records.

ADAH holds original territorial court records for Washington and Madison counties.

---

### 7. Colonial Records (Mobile District, Pre-1798)

This is a specialized but important track for Mobile-area families:

| Colonial Power | Record Types | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| French (1702–1763) | Church registers, census, land concessions | Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at **Mobile Municipal Archives** |
| British (1763–1780) | Colonial office files, land grants | National Archives (Kew, UK); Colonial Office series |
| Spanish (1780–1813) | Census *padrones*, church registers, land grants | **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville; copies at **Library of Congress** |

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

**Digitization level:** Largely physical or microfilm at the originating archives. Some finding aids are online. No digitized browse-only volumes for these records appeared in FamilySearch's systems.

---

### 8. Military Records

- **Creek War (1813–1814):** Service records and pension files at NARA — available on Fold3.com (subscription) and Ancestry. This war drove the mass post-1814 settlement of Alabama; pension files and bounty land warrants often reveal family data for families who arrived in Alabama in the years just after your target period.
- **Territorial militia rolls:** The FamilySearch Wiki lists militia rolls among surviving Mississippi Territory records held at ADAH. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*
- **Revolutionary War pensions:** Settlers arriving from the Carolinas/Georgia may have pension files at NARA (Fold3, Ancestry).

---

### 9. Newspapers

Alabama's earliest newspapers date to c. 1811–1812. The **Chronicling America** project (Library of Congress, https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) holds early Alabama newspaper runs and is free and full-text searchable online. Legal notices, land sales, and estate notices in these papers are a useful supplement when other records are absent.

---

## Digitized Browse-Only Volumes — Honest Gap Report

**FamilySearch's Records Management System (RMS) returned zero digitized volumes under "Alabama, United States" for the pre-statehood period**, both with and without the 1780–1820 date filter. This means there are no browse-only image volumes cataloged under that standardPlace for this era in FamilySearch's system — a genuine digitization gap.

This does not mean records don't exist — it means they aren't currently cataloged as digitized volumes under that place name in FamilySearch. Pre-statehood Alabama records at ADAH and county courthouses may be on microfilm, available through the FamilySearch microfilm catalog (catalog.familysearch.org — search by county name) or on-site at ADAH.

**Where to look for browse-only volumes outside FamilySearch:**
- **Alabama Department of Archives and History** — https://www.alabamaarchives.gov — primary repository for territorial-era physical and microfilm holdings
- **BLM General Land Office** — https://glorecords.blm.gov — digitized and browsable by land office and survey
- **FamilySearch Catalog** — https://www.familysearch.org/catalog — search "Washington County, Alabama" or "Madison County, Alabama" for microfilmed county records not yet in the RMS

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What's Held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)** | Territorial censuses (1801–1810), tax lists, militia rolls, early court records | On-site; catalog at alabamaarchives.gov |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents from Alabama land offices | Free: glorecords.blm.gov |
| **NARA** | Federal census (1810, 1820), military / pension records | In-person; digitized on Ancestry & Fold3 |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** | Spanish colonial records (land grants, census, church) | Physical; copies at Library of Congress |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence** | French colonial records (1702–1763) | Physical; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | French colonial microfilm; local Mobile records | On-site |
| **FamilySearch.org** | County marriages (1809+), church records (1803+), probate (1809+), census substitutes | Free online |
| **Fold3 / Ancestry** | Military records, federal census, some territorial records | Subscription |

---

## Key Quirks and Gotchas

1. **Pre-1817 Alabama = Mississippi Territory.** All records generated before 1817 carry a Mississippi Territory (not Alabama) jurisdiction. Search Mississippi Territory/state FamilySearch collections in parallel with Alabama collections — the jurisdictional dividing line is 1817, not 1800.
2. **No statewide civil vital registration until 1908.** Births, marriages, and deaths in 1800 appear only in church registers, county marriage books (from county organization), or inferred from other records.
3. **Mobile and north Alabama are completely different research tracks.** Mobile has Catholic colonial registers from 1702 and continuous European-era records. North Alabama (Madison County and beyond) has essentially no records before 1808, and American settlement was sparse until after the Creek War of 1813–1814.
4. **Washington County (est. 1800) is the only Alabama county with records before 1808.** If your family was in Alabama before 1808, they were almost certainly in the Mobile / Washington County area — search there first.
5. **Mobile was Spanish until 1813.** Mobile-area families in 1800 generated Spanish colonial records (padrones, church registers, land grants), not U.S. territorial records.
6. **Land records are the richest American-era source for this period.** BLM GLO patents are digitized, free, and name-searchable — often the first surviving U.S. record for a family.
7. **FamilySearch volume search gap.** No digitized browse-only volumes for pre-1819 Alabama appear in FamilySearch's RMS. Go directly to ADAH and the FamilySearch microfilm catalog for un-digitized territorial holdings.
8. **Colonial records require non-English language skills.** French (pre-1763 Mobile), Spanish (1780–1813 Mobile), and Latin (church registers) appear throughout Mobile-area pre-statehood records.

# Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide
**Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Lackawanna · Northumberland Counties, 1860–1900**
*Focus: Irish Immigrant Coal Miners*

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The five anthracite counties span northeastern and east-central Pennsylvania:

| County | Formed | Parent(s) | County Seat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Northumberland | 1772 | Lancaster, Berks, Cumberland, Bedford, Northampton | Sunbury |
| Luzerne | 1786 | Northumberland | Wilkes-Barre |
| Schuylkill | 1811 | Berks & Northampton | Pottsville |
| Carbon | 1843 | Monroe & Northampton | Mauch Chunk (now Jim Thorpe) |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | **Luzerne** | **Scranton** |

**🔑 Critical temporal split — Lackawanna/Luzerne:** Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878. Every record for Scranton and surrounding communities before that date — naturalizations, deeds, probate, court filings — is filed under **Luzerne County**. Switch to Lackawanna only from 1878 forward. This is not a statewide rule: it applies only to the specific territory that became Lackawanna.

**Population scale (Schuylkill County, confirmed by tool):** 89,510 in 1860 → 116,428 in 1870 → 129,974 in 1880 → 172,927 in 1900. Growth driven by anthracite coal mining; large immigrant population (Irish, Welsh, German, later Eastern European) from the 1840s onward.

---

## ⚠️ Critical Warning: Civil Registration Gap, 1860–1906

Pennsylvania **did not require statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during most of the 1860–1890 target window. The statewide death certificate series begins in 1906 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4.2 million records, fully indexed — but **this starts after your research period**). For Irish miners dying in the 1870s and 1880s, **no Pennsylvania death certificate exists**. Church records and mine accident reports fill this void.

---

## Record Types and Availability

### 1. Federal Census Records ✅ Indexed + Images — *Start Here*

Pennsylvania is covered in every decennial federal census 1790–1940. Key censuses for this research:

- **1860 & 1870:** Name, age, birthplace, occupation. Irish-born miners appear as "Ireland" under birthplace; occupation reads "miner" or "laborer."
- **1880:** First census to record the relationship of each household member to the head — the most valuable for proving family structure in this period. ([Pennsylvania,\_United\_States\_Genealogy#Census\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records))
- **1890:** Population schedules almost entirely destroyed. Use 1880 and 1900 to bracket this decade.
- **1900:** Records birth month/year, years in the US, and parents' birthplaces — critical for the immigrant generation.

**Mortality Schedules (1850–1885):** List individuals who died in the year preceding each census; mine accident deaths appear here.

**Access:** Fully name-indexed and free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry.

---

### 2. Naturalization Records ⚠️ Browse-Only / Partially Indexed — *Most Valuable Irish-Specific Source*

Naturalization documents name the country of origin and often the county of birth in Ireland — frequently the only record that does so.

**Pre-1906 (your entire target window):** Naturalizations were scattered across county courts — Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts all had jurisdiction. A Declaration of Intent ("first papers") and Petition for Naturalization ("second papers") were filed separately, sometimes years apart and in different counties as miners moved between coalfields. ([Pennsylvania\_Naturalization\_Records#County\_Court\_Naturalizations](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records))

**FamilySearch digitized volumes for Schuylkill County** (from `volume_search`):
- Naturalization Records, 1849–1915: **298 images · 0% name-indexed · not full-text searchable · browse-only** — must be examined image by image

**Pennsylvania state-level naturalization volume** (from `volume_search`):
- Naturalization Records, 1790–1915: **351 images · 15% name-indexed** — partially searchable by name; the remaining 85% must be browsed

**Post-September 1906:** Centralized under NARA Philadelphia (Record Group 85) for eastern Pennsylvania federal courts.

**Strategy:** Check all three court types for every county where the ancestor lived. A miner who moved between Schuylkill and Luzerne may have filed papers in either or both.

---

### 3. Church Records ⚠️ Browse-Only Images / Physical Archives — *Primary Vital Source, 1860–1890*

Because civil vital registration did not cover this period, Catholic and Protestant parish registers are the only consistent source of baptisms, marriages, and burials for Irish mining families.

Irish miners were overwhelmingly **Roman Catholic**:
- **Diocese of Scranton** (established 1868): Covers Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon, and adjoining counties. Diocesan Archives in Scranton holds or has inventory of surviving parish registers. Contact: [Diocese of Scranton Archives](https://dioceseofscranton.org)
- **Diocese of Allentown / Archdiocese of Philadelphia** (earlier period): Covers Schuylkill and Northumberland counties.

**FamilySearch digitized volumes for Schuylkill County** (from `volume_search`):
- Church Records, 1842–1895: **187 images · 0% name-indexed · not full-text · browse-only** · languages: English and German — some entries are in German (Protestant records); must be browsed page by page

**Strategy:** Identify the colliery or "patch town" where the ancestor worked. Company-built patch towns each had a serving parish — knowing the colliery name gets you to the right church. The **FamilySearch Catalog** (catalog.familysearch.org) holds many Pennsylvania Catholic register microfilms; search by county, then by parish name.

---

### 4. Marriage Records ✅ / ⚠️ Mixed — Indexed for Later Years, Gaps Earlier

**State-level indexed collections on FamilySearch** (from `collections_search`):

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | 1921317 | 1885–1950 | 524,189 records · 1,048,378 persons · 312,045 images | ✅ Indexed |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1571957 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 records · 624,090 persons · 156,023 images | ✅ Indexed |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | 1502909 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 records · 397,530 persons · **0 images** | ⚠️ Index only, no images |

**Schuylkill County digitized volume** (from `volume_search`):
- Marriage Records, 1870–1910: **94 images · 0% indexed · browse-only**

**Gap:** County marriage records for 1860–1885 fall largely outside the indexed state collections. Church marriage registers are the primary source for this window.

---

### 5. Probate Records ⚠️ Browse-Only — Lower Priority for Wage Laborers

Most Irish immigrant miners were wage laborers who left little estate. Check probate if the ancestor owned property or operated a business.

**Schuylkill County digitized volumes** (from `volume_search`):
- Probate Records, 1851–1930: **412 images · 0% indexed · browse-only**

**State-level collection** (from `collections_search`):
- *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection 1999196): 2,304,118 images — **0 persons indexed · browse-only**

**Physical repository:** County Orphans' Court / Register of Wills at each county courthouse.

---

### 6. Deed and Land Records ⚠️ Partially Indexed

Company-owned housing ("company houses") was the norm in patch towns, so many miners never purchased land. But some did buy property over time, and deed grantee indexes confirm presence in a locality.

**Schuylkill County digitized volumes** (from `volume_search`):
- Deed Records, 1815–1900: **543 images · 22% name-indexed** — partially searchable; the remaining 78% must be browsed

**Physical repository:** County Recorder of Deeds at each county courthouse.

---

### 7. ⛏️ Coal Mining Company Records — *Specialized to This Region* ★★★

This record class is unique to the anthracite coal region and is the most direct source for identifying individual Irish miners in their work context.

**What survives:** Major operators — Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, Lehigh Coal and Navigation Company, Delaware and Hudson Coal Company, and others — kept payroll ledgers naming workers by colliery, listing wages, and sometimes noting nationality or prior residence.

From the FamilySearch Wiki, *Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Coal Mining Records*:
> *"Mining company employment records, where they survive, list worker names, nationalities, and sometimes prior residence. The Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds payroll ledgers for several collieries."*
> — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill\_County,\_Pennsylvania\_Genealogy#Coal\_Mining\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records)

**Mine inspection / accident reports:** The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines (established 1870) published annual reports listing mine fatalities and sometimes the names of the deceased. Available at the Pennsylvania State Archives and in historical society collections.

**Key repositories:**
- **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) — colliery payroll ledgers
- **Lackawanna County Historical Society** (Scranton) — Delaware & Hudson records
- **Luzerne County Historical Society** (Wilkes-Barre) — Wyoming Valley operators
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) — Bureau of Mines annual reports
- **Hagley Museum and Library** (Wilmington, DE) — corporate archives of major anthracite companies (finding aids at hagley.org)

---

### 8. ⚖️ Molly Maguires Court Records — *Specialized Coal-Region Index* ★★★

From the FamilySearch Wiki, *Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Molly Maguires*:
> *"The Molly Maguires, a secret society active among Irish miners in Schuylkill County during the 1860s–1870s, generated extensive court records and newspaper coverage. Trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports **name hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families**, providing a rich (if adversarial) genealogical source for this community."*
> — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill\_County,\_Pennsylvania\_Genealogy#Molly\_Maguires](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)

The trials (1876–1877) were held in Pottsville (Schuylkill County) and Mauch Chunk (Carbon County). Trial transcripts and Pinkerton detective agency reports are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**. Even if your ancestor was not accused, witnesses, neighbors, and bystanders are named extensively throughout. This is a de facto index into the Irish mining community of Schuylkill and Carbon counties in the 1860s–1870s.

---

### 9. Military Records ✅ Indexed (Federal) — *Very High Yield for Irish Miners*

Many Irish coal-region miners served in the Civil War (1861–1865).

- **Civil War pension files** (NARA): Among the richest genealogical sources available. Widow's pension applications routinely document marriage date/place, children's births, the soldier's Irish birthplace, and naturalization status — often the only record linking an Irish immigrant to his home county.
- **Civil War draft registrations, 1863–1865** (NARA Series M1872/M1880): Name, age, occupation, birthplace — covers all men in the coal counties.
- **Compiled Service Records**: Indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- **Pennsylvania GAR records** (Grand Army of the Republic): Post records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### 10. Newspapers ⚠️ Partially Digitized — *Deaths, Accidents, Molly Maguires Coverage*

Local papers published births, marriages, deaths, mine accident notices, and extensive trial coverage.

**Key papers:**
- ***Miners' Journal*** (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) — continuous from 1825; partially digitized and full-text searchable at **Chronicling America** (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov, free); complete run at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County
- *Scranton Republican* and *Scranton Times* — Lackawanna County from 1860s
- *Wilkes-Barre Record* and *Luzerne Union* — Luzerne County

Search Chronicling America by county and surname — free and often overlooked.

---

### 11. Passenger Lists and Immigration Records ✅ Indexed — *Establishes Irish Origin*

Irish immigrants to the coal region typically arrived through **Philadelphia** or **New York** (Castle Garden 1855–1891; Ellis Island from 1892). The Famine-generation arrivals (1845–1855) predate the target research window but establish the critical connection to Ireland.

- **Philadelphia passenger lists** (NARA M425, M360): Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **New York passenger lists** (NARA M237): Indexed and searchable.
- Liverpool was the common transit port: look for "Liverpool" as departure port, "Philadelphia" or "New York" as destination.
- The 1900 census column "years in the US" lets you calculate an approximate arrival year, narrowing the passenger list search.

---
